When the human lifespan was one hundred years, there was the ṛṣi Pāṇini, who was born with great wisdom and broad learning. Pitying the decadence of the age, he wished to prune away the superficial and false, and to edit and refine the cumbersome and redundant. He traveled to various regions to inquire after the Way, and upon meeting Maheśvara (自在天), he expressed his intention to compose a work. Maheśvara said, "Excellent! I shall assist you." Having received these instructions, the ṛṣi withdrew and applied his mind to deep reflection, collecting a vast array of words to compose a lexicon consisting of one thousand stanzas, each containing thirty-two syllables. It exhausted the depths of both the present and the past, and summarized the entirety of literary language. He sealed it and presented it to the king, who found it most extraordinary and issued a decree throughout the kingdom to make it universally studied, rewarding anyone who could recite it with mastery with one thousand gold coins. This is why the tradition of teacher and student has been passed down and flourished in the present age. Consequently, the Brahmins in this town are men of great learning and high talent, possessing broad knowledge and excellent memories. In the town of Śalātura (婆羅覩邏邑) there is a stūpa, which is the place where an Arhat converted the later followers of the sage Pāṇini. Five hundred years after the Tathāgata had passed away, a great Arhat traveling from the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國) arrived here and saw a Brahmin beating and scolding a young boy. The Arhat asked the Brahmin, "Why are you tormenting this child?" The Brahmin replied, "I am making him study the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra* (聲明論), but his progress is not timely." The Arhat smiled gently. The old Brahmin said, "The nature of a Śramaṇa is compassion and pity for all living beings. I wish to hear the reason for your laughter." The Arhat said, "It is not easy to speak of this, for I fear it will cause deep doubt. Have you ever heard that the sage Pāṇini composed the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra* and left it as a teaching for the world?" The Brahmin replied, "The children of this town, as later followers, look up to his virtue, and his image is still here." The Arhat said, "This child of yours is that very sage. Because he possessed a powerful memory, he indulged in the study of worldly texts, discussing only heterodox doctrines without investigating the true principles. His spiritual wisdom was wasted in vain, and his transmigration has not yet ceased; it is only by riding on the merit of his remaining good deeds that he has become your beloved son. However, the literary expressions of worldly texts merely exhaust one's efforts; how can they compare to the holy teachings of the Tathāgata, which nourish merit and wisdom in the dark? Formerly, on the shore of the Southern Sea, there was a withered tree where five hundred bats lived in holes." Some merchants stopped under this tree. At that time, it was windy and cold, and everyone was hungry and freezing. They gathered firewood and brush, and kindled a fire beneath it. The smoke and flames gradually intensified, and the withered tree caught fire. Among the merchants, there was one trader who, after the middle of the night, was reciting the Abhidharma-piṭaka (阿毘達磨藏). Although those bats were distressed by the fire, they loved the sound of the Dharma and endured it without leaving, and thus they met their end there. Following their karma, they were reborn, all obtaining human bodies. They left their homes to study and practice, and by virtue of having heard the sound of the Dharma, they were intelligent and wise, all attaining the holy fruit and becoming fields of merit for the world. Recently, King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王) and the Venerable Pārśva (脇尊者) summoned five hundred sages in the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國) to compose the Vibhāṣā-śāstra (毘婆沙論); these are the very same five hundred bats from the withered tree. Although I am unworthy, I am one of that number. This shows that the superior and the inferior are truly different, and the flying and the crawling are vastly distinct. You should now allow your beloved son to leave home; the merit of leaving home is beyond description."  When the Arhat had spoken these words, he displayed his supernatural powers and suddenly vanished. The brahmin was deeply filled with reverence and wonder, and after praising the goodness of this for a long time, he told his neighbors everything. He then allowed his son to leave home to study and practice, and consequently turned to the faith, honoring the Triple Gem. The villagers followed his transformation, and their devotion remains intense to this day.  Traveling north from the city of Udakahāṇḍa (烏鐸迦漢荼城), crossing mountains and wading through rivers for more than six hundred li, one arrives at the country of Uḍḍiyāna (烏仗那國) (Original note: In the language of the Tang, this means "garden," as it was formerly the pleasure garden of a Cakravartin king). It was formerly called Wuchang (烏場) or sometimes Wucha (烏茶), but both are incorrect. It is within the territory of North India.

Four or five li to the east of the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城) there is a stūpa that displays many miraculous signs. It is the place where the Buddha, in a former life as the Rishi of Patience (忍辱仙人), had his limbs severed by King Kali (羯利王; in the Tang language this means "Strife" [鬪諍]; the older transcription "Goli" [哥利] is incorrect).

More than four hundred *li* to the south of the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城), one reaches Mount Hiḍḍa (醯羅山). The valley stream branches to the west, but as one ascends eastward against the current, various flowers and strange fruits cover the gullies and line the cliffs. The peaks and crags are perilous, and the streams and valleys wind and meander; sometimes one hears the sound of loud talking, and sometimes one hears the strains of music. Square stones resemble pagodas, appearing as if fashioned by craftsmen, stretching out in succession and spreading through the cliffs and valleys. This is where the Tathāgata in a former life sacrificed his body and life to hear half a stanza (Original note: Formerly it was called *jie* (伽), which is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit. Some call it *jieta* (偈他), which is a corruption of the Sanskrit sound. Following the correct pronunciation now, it should be called *gāthā* (伽他). *Gāthā* means *song* (頌) in the language of Tang, a *song* being thirty-two syllables) of the Dharma.

More than two hundred li south of the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城), by the side of a great mountain (Pravaragiri), one reaches the Mahāvana (唐言大林 - "Great Forest" in the language of Tang) Monastery. This is where the Tathāgata, in a former life when practicing the bodhisattva path as a king named Sarvadatta (唐言一切施 - "All-Bestowing" in the language of Tang), having fled his enemies and abandoned his kingdom, traveled in secret to this place and encountered a poor brahmin who had come to beg for alms. Having already lost his royal position and having nothing to give, he ordered the brahmin to bind him and take him captive to the enemy king, hoping that the reward money could be used as a gift of charity in return.

Thirty or forty li to the northwest of the Mahāvana (Great Forest) Monastery, descending the mountain, one reaches the Mayū (Mayuṇḍa) Monastery. There is a stūpa over one hundred feet high. On a large square stone at its side are the footprints of the Tathāgata, left when the Buddha formerly stepped upon this stone and emitted a koṭi of rays of light to illuminate the Mahāvana Monastery, while preaching Jātaka stories for the sake of all humans and devas. Below the base of this stūpa is a stone, yellowish-white in color, which is always moist and oily. It is here that the Tathāgata, in the past while practicing the bodhisattva path, split his bones to write down the scriptures in order to hear the true Dharma.

Sixty or seventy li to the west of the Mayū Monastery (摩愉伽藍), one reaches a stupa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). This is where the Tathāgata, in a former life while practicing the conduct of a Bodhisattva, was known as King Viśvaka (毘迦王; in the language of Tang, this means "giving"; the older term "King Śibi" [尸毘王] is incorrect). Seeking the fruit of Buddhahood, he here cut his own flesh to ransom a dove from a hawk.

Traveling more than two hundred *li* northwest from the place where the dove was ransomed, one enters the Sanirāja River valley and reaches the Sarpauṣadhi (which means "Snake Medicine" in the language of Tang) Monastery. There is a *stūpa* here, more than eighty feet high. It is said that in the past, when the Tathāgata was Indra, a time of famine and pestilence occurred; medical treatments were ineffective, and deaths followed one after another. Indra, moved by compassion and wishing to provide relief, transformed his body into that of a giant python, lying dead in the valley, and proclaimed it to all from the air. Those who heard were moved and rejoiced, rushing to the site; as they cut pieces from the body, it would immediately regenerate, curing their hunger and their illnesses. Not far to the side is a large *stūpa* of Soma. It is said that in the past, when the Tathāgata was Indra, during a time of pestilence, he took pity on all sentient beings and transformed his body into a Soma snake; all who consumed it were restored to health and comfort. Beside the stone cliff to the north of the Sanirāja River, there is a *stūpa*. Sick people who come here to pray are often cured of their ailments. In the past, when the Tathāgata was a peacock king, he came to this place with his flock; driven by heat and thirst, they sought water but could not find any, so the peacock king pecked the cliff with his beak, causing a spring to gush forth. This has now become a pool, and drinking from or bathing in it cures illnesses. The tracks of the peacock are still visible on the stone.

More than fifty li to the west of the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城), crossing a great river, one arrives at the Rohitaka (盧醯呾迦; in Tang language, "Red") Stupa, which is over fifty feet high and was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, when the Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path, he was a great king named Maitrībala (慈力), who here pierced his body to draw blood to feed five Yakṣas (藥叉; formerly called "Ye-cha" [夜叉], which is incorrect).

More than thirty li to the northeast of the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城), one reaches the Adbhuta (遏部多; in Chinese, "Miraculous") stone stupa, which is over forty feet high. In the past, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here to instruct humans and devas; after the Tathāgata departed, it emerged from the earth. The common people revere it, and offerings of incense and flowers never cease.

Crossing the great river thirty or forty li to the west of the stone stūpa, one arrives at a vihāra (mūla-gandha-kuṭī) containing an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (in Tang language, Guanzizai. When the characters are combined and the sounds are linked, the Sanskrit is as above; when the text is separated and the sounds are analyzed, "Avalokita" is translated as "Guan" [Observing], and "Īśvara" is translated as "Zizai" [Sovereign]. Former translations such as Guangshiyin, or Guanshiyin, or Guanshizizai, are all erroneous). His majestic spiritual influence is secretly bestowed, his miraculous traces are clearly manifest, and both the ordained and the laity flock there, offering worship without interruption.

One hundred and fifty li northwest of the statue of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, one arrives at the mountain of Lamboura (藍勃盧山). On the mountain ridge is a dragon lake, over thirty li in circumference; its green waves are vast and expansive, and its clear waters are as bright as a mirror. In the past, when King Virūḍhaka (毘盧釋迦王) attacked the Śākyas, four men resisted the army; they were expelled by their kinsmen and each fled in a different direction. One of these Śākyas, having left the capital, was exhausted from his travels and stopped midway. At that time, a wild goose flew before him; since it was tame and friendly, he mounted it. The goose flew and landed beside this lake. The Śākya, wandering aimlessly and having traveled far to a foreign land, was lost and did not know the way, so he took a nap in the shade of a tree. The young daughter of the dragon of the lake was wandering along the water's edge when she suddenly saw the Śākya; fearing her appearance was inappropriate, she transformed into human form and approached to stroke him. The Śākya was startled awake and asked, "I am a weary traveler, why do you show me such intimacy?" He then pressed her with great earnestness, forcing himself upon her in the wilderness. The woman said, "I have my parents' instructions, which I respect and do not violate. Although I am honored by your attention, I have not received their command." The Śākya asked, "The mountain valleys are dark and remote; where is your home?" She replied, "I am the dragon daughter of this lake. I respectfully heard that your noble clan was wandering in exile, and as I happened to be out for a stroll, I dared to offer comfort for your fatigue. As for the matter of intimate relations, I have not heard of such an intention. Furthermore, due to accumulated karma, I have received this dragon body; humans and animals follow different paths, and such a thing is unheard of." The Śākya said, "If you grant me this one word, my long-held desire will be fulfilled." The dragon girl said, "I respectfully hear your command; I submit to whatever you decide." The Śākya then made a vow in his heart: "By whatever power of merit I possess, let this dragon girl's entire body be transformed into that of a human." Moved by the power of his merit, the dragon then changed her form; having attained a human body, she was deeply overjoyed. She thanked the Śākya, saying, "Due to my accumulated evil karma, I have been wandering in the lower realms. Fortunately, I have received your kind attention, and through the application of your merit, this wretched body held for vast kalpas has been transformed in an instant. I wish to repay this virtue, but even shattering my body would not be enough. I desire to accompany you, but I am constrained by the opinions of others. I wish to inform my parents, and then prepare the rites."  The dragon girl returned to the pool and told her parents, "Today while out on an excursion, I suddenly met a member of the Śākya clan; moved by the power of his merit, I have been transformed into a human. My heart is set on a happy union, and I venture to state the facts." The Dragon King, pleased with the human realm and holding the holy clan in high regard, acceded to his daughter's request. He then emerged from the pool and thanked the Śākya, saying, "You have not shunned those of a different species, but have lowered your noble status to accommodate the lowly. I wish for you to visit my dwelling, where I dare to offer you my service."  The Śākya accepted the Dragon King's invitation and went to his residence. There, within the dragon palace, they prepared the rites for a personal wedding, and in the joy of their new union, they indulged in the utmost pleasure. However, the Śākya, seeing the dragon's form, felt constant fear and disgust, and wished to take his leave. The Dragon King stopped him, saying, "I hope you will not go far away, but reside in this neighborhood. I shall cause you to occupy territory, bear a great title, command subjects, and enjoy a long-lasting dynasty." The Śākya declined, saying, "This is not what I desire." The Dragon King placed a precious sword into a chest and covered it with a fine white cotton cloth. He said to the Śākya, "I hope you will take this cloth and present it to the king. The king will surely receive this tribute from a man from afar in person, and at that moment, you can slay him. By then seizing his kingdom, would that not be excellent?" The Śākya accepted the dragon’s instructions and went to present it. As the King of Udyāna (烏仗那) personally lifted the cloth, the Śākya seized his sleeve and stabbed him. The attendants and guards were in an uproar on the palace steps, but the Śākya brandished his sword and declared, "The sword I wield was bestowed upon me by the divine dragon to execute those who do not submit and to behead those who are not loyal." All were awed by his divine martial prowess and elevated him to the high throne. Thereupon, he reformed the corrupt administration, honored the virtuous, and relieved the suffering. Having done this, he mobilized a great assembly and prepared a royal procession to go to the dragon palace to report his success and bring the dragon girl back to the capital. Because the dragon girl’s past karma was not yet exhausted and residual retribution remained, whenever they were in private, nine dragon heads would emerge from her head. The Śākya, fearful and disgusted, did not know what plan to devise, but when he caught her sleeping, he cut them off with a sharp blade. The dragon girl, startled from her sleep, said, "This is not to the benefit of our descendants; not only is my life somewhat injured, but your offspring shall suffer from headaches." Therefore, the people of this country often suffer from this affliction; although it is not continuous, it flares up from time to time. After the Śākya passed away, his son succeeded to the throne; this was King Uttarasena (嗢嗾羅犀那; Tang dynasty translation: "Superior Army"). After King Uttarasena (嗢嗾羅犀那) succeeded to the throne, his mother lost her sight. The Tathāgata, having subdued the dragon Apalāla (阿波邏羅), was returning and descended through the air into the palace. King Uttarasena happened to be out hunting, so the Tathāgata briefly explained the essentials of the Dharma to his mother. Having encountered the Holy One and heard the Dharma, she immediately regained her sight. The Tathāgata asked, "Your son is of my clan; where is he now?" The mother replied, "He went out hunting this morning and is now on his way back." The Tathāgata and the great assembly were about to depart. The King’s mother said, "It is only by my good fortune that I gave birth into this holy clan; the Tathāgata has shown great compassion by personally visiting us. My son is just now returning, so I pray you stay and wait a moment." The World-Honored One said, "This man is of my clan. He can be awakened to faith by hearing the teachings; he does not require personal instruction to arouse his resolve. I shall depart. When he returns, tell him: 'The Tathāgata is going from here to the city of Kuśinagara (拘尸城) to enter nirvāṇa among the śāla trees; you should obtain the relics and make offerings to them yourself.'" The Tathāgata and the great assembly then rose into the void and departed. King Uttarasena was out hunting and saw from afar a brilliant light shining in the palace; suspecting a fire, he stopped his hunt and returned. He then saw that his mother had regained her sight, and he asked joyfully, "How long was I gone that such an auspicious response occurred, restoring my mother's vision as it was before?" The mother replied, "After you went out, the Tathāgata arrived here; upon hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, I regained my sight." "The Tathāgata has gone from here to the śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara (拘尸城) to enter nirvana; he summons you to come quickly to receive a portion of his relics." When the king heard this, he wailed with grief and collapsed to the ground. After a long time, he regained his senses and ordered his carriage to hasten to the site. By the time he arrived between the twin trees, the Buddha had already entered nirvana. At that time, the various kings looked down upon his borderland status and, treasuring the relics, did not wish to share them with him. Then, the assembly of devas and humans restated the Buddha’s intention; having heard this, the kings finally granted him an equal share.

Going northeast from the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城), crossing mountains and traversing valleys, and heading upstream along the Indus River (信度河), the path is perilous and the valleys are dark and gloomy. One must tread on rope bridges or cling to iron chains; plank paths are suspended over voids, bridges are built precariously high, and one must step on wooden pegs driven into the rock. After traveling over a thousand *li*, one reaches the valley of Darada (達麗羅川), which is the old capital of the kingdom of Udyāna (烏仗那國). It produces much gold and saffron.  Beside a great monastery in the Darada valley, there is a carved wooden statue of the Bodhisattva Maitreya (慈氏菩薩). Its golden color shines brightly, and its spiritual efficacy is subtly pervasive. It is over a hundred feet tall and was created by the Arhat Madhyāntika (末田底迦) (Original note: formerly called Madhyandina, which is an incorrect abbreviation). The Arhat used his supernatural powers to transport a craftsman up to the Tuṣita Heaven (覩史多天) (Original note: formerly called Duoshita, and also Doushuta, which are incorrect) to personally observe the Bodhisattva's exquisite features. After three such visits, the work was finally completed. Ever since this statue came into existence, the Dharma has flowed toward the eastern regions.

Traveling east from here, crossing ridges and traversing valleys, going upstream along the Sindhu (信度) River, and passing over flying bridges and plank paths, one treads through danger and peril for over five hundred li to reach the country of Balūra (鉢露羅國) (within the borders of North India). The country of Balūra is over four thousand li in circuit, situated amidst the Great Snow Mountains; it is long from east to west and narrow from south to north. It produces much wheat and beans, and yields gold and silver; due to the profit from this gold, the state is wealthy and prosperous. The climate is consistently cold and harsh. The people are fierce and violent by nature, lacking in benevolence and righteousness, and have no knowledge of etiquette or propriety. Their appearance is coarse and unrefined, and they wear garments of wool and hair. Their writing is largely the same as that of India, but their language differs from that of other countries. There are several hundred sanghārāmas (伽藍) and several thousand monks; they have no specialized studies, and their observance of the precepts is largely lax.

From here I returned to the city of Udakhanda (烏鐸迦漢荼城) and crossed the Indus River (信度河) to the south. The river is three or four li wide and flows southward; it is clear and bright as a mirror, yet its currents are surging and rapid. Venomous dragons and evil beasts dwell within it, and if those who carry precious gems, rare flowers, fruit seeds, or Buddha relics attempt to cross, their boats are often overturned and lost. After crossing the river, I arrived at the country of Takṣaśilā (呾叉始羅國) (within the borders of North India). The country of Takṣaśilā is over two thousand li in circuit. The capital city is over ten li in circuit. The local chieftains contend for power, and the royal lineage has died out; in the past, it was subject to the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國), and recently it has become a vassal to the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國). The land is known for its fertile soil; agriculture is flourishing, springs are numerous, and flowers and plants grow luxuriantly. The climate is mild and pleasant, the customs of the people are light and courageous, and they revere the Three Jewels. Although there are many monasteries, they are mostly in a state of great ruin, and the number of monks is small; they all study the Great Vehicle.

Twelve or thirteen li to the north of the city is a stupa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). On days of fasting, it sometimes emits a divine light, and there are many accounts of people seeing and hearing divine flowers and celestial music. I have heard from the records of former sages that recently a woman suffering from malignant leprosy came secretly to the stupa to reproach herself and perform repentance. Seeing that the courtyard was covered in filth, she cleared it away, swept and sprinkled the ground, smeared it with incense, scattered flowers, and gathered blue lotuses to spread over the ground again. Her malignant disease was cured, her appearance became more beautiful, and her body emitted a famous fragrance, as fragrant as the blue lotus. This is a sacred site where the Tathāgata, in the past while practicing the bodhisattva path, was a great king named Candraprabha (戰達羅鉢剌婆; in Tang language, "Moonlight"). With a determined quest for bodhi, he severed his head as an act of charity. He underwent such sacrifices for a thousand lifetimes. Beside the Śīrṣa-stūpa (捨頭窣堵波; "Stupa of the Severed Head") is a monastery with a desolate courtyard and few monks. In the past, the Sautrāntika master Kumāralāta (拘摩羅邏多; in Tang language, "Child-Received") composed various treatises here.

To the southeast of the city, on the northern side of the South Hill, there is a stūpa over a hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王) at the place where his son, Prince Kuṇāla (拘浪拏), had his eyes gouged out after being falsely accused by his stepmother. Blind people who pray here often have their sight restored. This prince was the son of the first queen; he was elegant in appearance and had long been renowned for his kindness and benevolence. After the first queen passed away, the stepmother, who was arrogant and lewd, gave free rein to her muddled stupidity and privately attempted to seduce the prince. The prince wept, took the blame upon himself, and withdrew to apologize for his perceived offense. Seeing her advances rejected, the stepmother’s fury intensified. Waiting for a moment when the king was at leisure, she said composedly, "Takṣaśilā (呾叉始羅) is a strategic key to the kingdom; can it be entrusted to anyone other than a close royal scion? Now, the prince is known for his benevolence and filial piety, and because he is both a relative and a man of virtue, public opinion favors him." The king, hearing this, was pleased by the treacherous scheme; he immediately summoned the prince and admonished him, saying, "I have inherited the legacy of my ancestors to continue their rule, and I live in constant fear of losing it and thereby bringing shame upon the late kings. Takṣaśilā is the throat and belt of the kingdom, and I now appoint you to govern that country. The affairs of the state are heavy and complex, and the sentiments of the people are devious and mixed; do not act rashly or carelessly, lest you damage the foundation of our inheritance. Whenever there is a summons, verify it with my tooth-seal. The seal is in my mouth; how could there be any error?" Thereupon, the prince accepted the command and came to govern. As time passed, the stepmother’s anger grew; she forged a royal decree, sealed it with purple clay, and while the king was sleeping, she stole his teeth to make the impression, then dispatched a messenger to deliver the letter of condemnation. The assisting ministers knelt to read it, looking at one another in dismay. The prince asked, "Why are you so sorrowful?" They replied, "The Great King has issued a command, a written decree reprimanding the prince, ordering that your two eyes be gouged out and that you be exiled and abandoned in the mountain valleys, leaving you and your wife to live or die as fate decides. Although this command exists, we have not yet been able to act upon it. We should now request a confirmation, and you should present yourself bound to await your punishment." The prince said, "If a father grants death to his son, how can it be refused? The tooth-seal serves as the signet; truly, there can be no error." He ordered a Caṇḍāla to gouge out his eyes. Once his eyes were blinded, he begged for alms to sustain himself, wandering from place to place until he reached his father’s capital city. His wife said to him, "This is the royal city. Alas, the suffering of hunger and cold is truly bitter! Once a prince, now a beggar! I wish for us to make this known and have the previous charge re-examined." Thereupon, they devised a plan to enter the king’s inner stables. In the final watch of the night, weeping as he faced the clear breeze, he sang out in a long, mournful wail, accompanying himself on the konghou (harp). From his high pavilion, the king heard the elegant singing, the lyrics of which were deeply resentful and sorrowful; wondering at it, he asked, "The sound of the singing to the konghou seems to be that of my son; for what reason has he come here?" He immediately asked the inner stables, "Who is singing and wailing?" They then brought the blind man before the king. Seeing the prince, the king asked with suppressed grief, "Who has harmed your body and brought this calamity upon you? My beloved son has lost his sight, yet I remained unaware; how then can I investigate the affairs of all the common people? O Heaven, O Heaven! How has my virtue declined!" The prince wept piteously and replied in apology, "It is truly because of my lack of filial piety that I have incurred the blame of Heaven. On a certain day of a certain month, I suddenly received your compassionate edict; having no way to voice my plea, I did not dare to evade my responsibility." The king, in his heart, knew that his new queen had acted wickedly, but without further investigation, he immediately imposed a severe punishment.  At that time, in the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) monastery, there was a great Arhat named Ghoṣa (瞿沙; Tang language: "Sublime Sound"), who possessed unobstructed mastery of the four analytical knowledges and was fully endowed with the three insights. The king brought his blind son to him, explained the situation, and prayed only for his compassion to restore the prince's sight. Having accepted the king's request, the Arhat immediately announced to the people of the country on that very day, "The day after tomorrow, I wish to preach the sublime truth. Let each person bring a vessel and come here to listen to the Dharma, so as to collect your tears."  Thereupon, people from near and far hastened to the site, and men and women gathered like clouds. At that time, the Arhat preached on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. Among all those who heard the Dharma, there was none who was not moved to deep sorrow, and they used the vessels they carried to collect their falling tears. When the preaching was finished, he collected all the tears and placed them in a golden basin, then made a vow, saying, "All that I have spoken is the ultimate truth of the Buddhas. If this truth is not genuine and my teaching contains errors, then so be it; but if it is not so, I wish to wash these blind eyes with the tears of the multitude, so that his sight may be restored and he may see as clearly as before."  Having spoken these words, he took the tears and washed the eyes, and the eyes were immediately restored to sight. The king then rebuked his ministers and interrogated his officials; some were dismissed, some were banished, some were demoted, and some were put to death. The powerful and wealthy families were moved to the sandy desert to the northeast of the Snow Mountains (Himālaya).

From here, traveling southeast across various mountains and valleys for more than seven hundred li, one arrives at the country of Siṃhapura (僧訶補羅國) (in the territory of Northern India). The country of Siṃhapura is three thousand five or six hundred li in circuit and borders the Indus River (信度河) to the west. The capital city of the country is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit; it relies on the mountains and occupies the ridges, making it firm, steep, and impregnable. Agriculture requires little labor, yet the land yields abundant harvests. The climate is cold, the people are fierce by nature, their customs prize bravery, and they are also often deceitful. The country has no sovereign ruler and is subject to the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國).

From here, I returned to the northern border of the country of Takṣaśilā (呾叉始羅國), crossed the Indus River (信度河), and traveled southeast for more than two hundred li, passing through a great stone gate. This is the place where, in the past, Prince Mahāsattva sacrificed his body to feed a starving tigress (Original note: The sound is *tú*). About one hundred and forty or fifty paces to the south is a stone stūpa. Pitying the starving beast for its lack of strength, the Mahāsattva had come to this spot, pierced himself with a dry bamboo splinter, and fed it his blood, whereupon the beast devoured him. The soil of this place, as well as the plants and trees, is slightly reddish in color, as if stained with blood. When people tread upon this ground, they feel as if they are carrying thorns on their backs; regardless of whether they are skeptical or faithful, none can help but feel a sense of profound grief.

From here, traveling southeast for more than five hundred li, one reaches the country of Uraśā (烏剌尸國) (within the borders of North India). The country of Uraśā is more than two thousand li in circuit; the mountains and hills are connected, and the fields are narrow. The capital city of the country is seven or eight li in circuit; it has no great sovereign ruler and is a dependency of the country of Kaśmīra (迦隰彌羅國). It is suitable for agriculture, but there are few flowers or fruits. The climate is mild, with slight frost and snow. The customs lack propriety and righteousness; the people’s nature is fierce and violent, they often practice deceit, and they do not believe in the Buddha’s Dharma. Four or five li to the southwest of the great city is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). Beside it is a saṃghārāma (伽藍) with few monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna.

From here, traveling southeast, climbing mountains and traversing dangerous paths, crossing an iron bridge, and journeying more than one thousand li, one arrives at the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國) (formerly called Jibin [罽賓], which is a corruption; it is in the territory of Northern India). The country of Kaśmīra is over seven thousand li in circumference. Its four borders are backed by mountains; the mountains are extremely steep and precipitous. Although there are gateways and paths, they are narrow and constricted, and since ancient times, neighboring enemies have been unable to attack or conquer it. The capital city of the country faces a great river to the west, measuring twelve or thirteen li from north to south and four or five li from east to west. It is suitable for agriculture, abounds in flowers and fruits, and produces dragon-breed horses, saffron (鬱金香), fire pearls, and medicinal herbs. The climate is cold and harsh, with much snow and little wind. The people wear woolen garments and white cotton (白㲲) clothing. The local customs are frivolous, and the people are mostly timid and cowardly. The country is protected by a dragon, and thus it has become powerful among its neighbors. The people are beautiful in appearance but deceitful in nature. They are fond of learning and are well-informed, believing in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are over one hundred saṃghārāmas and more than five thousand monks. There are four stūpas, all built by King Aśoka (無憂王), each containing over a pint of the Tathāgata’s relics. The *Country Records* (國志) state: "The land of this country was originally a dragon lake. In the past, when the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had subdued an evil spirit in the country of Uḍḍiyāna (烏仗那國) and wished to return to the Middle Kingdom, he rode through the air and, upon reaching the space above this country, said to Ānanda: 'After my parinirvāṇa, there will be an arhat named Madhyāntika (末田底迦) who will establish a kingdom in this land, settle the people, and propagate the Buddha-dharma.'" In the fiftieth year after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the arhat Madhyāntika (末田底迦), a disciple of Ānanda, having attained the six supernatural powers and possessing the eight liberations, heard the Buddha’s prediction and felt great joy in his heart. He then came to this place, sat in meditation within the woods of the great mountain range (大山), and manifested great supernatural transformations. The dragon saw this and, having developed deep faith, asked what he desired. The arhat said, "I wish for you to grant me enough space within this lake to accommodate my knees." The dragon king thereupon caused the water to recede and offered the land to him. The arhat used his supernatural power to expand his body, and the dragon king exerted his strength to shrink the water; when the lake was empty and the water exhausted, the dragon turned and asked for the land back. The arhat left one pool for him in the northwest of this place, measuring one hundred and more li in circumference; the rest of his kin and dependents were to dwell in smaller pools separately. The dragon king said, "I have bestowed the entire lake and land upon you; I wish to provide offerings perpetually." Madhyāntika replied, "I shall soon enter parinirvāṇa without remainder; though I wish to accept your invitation, how would that be possible?" The dragon king requested again, "May five hundred arhats always receive my offerings until the Dharma comes to an end; after the Dharma has ended, I shall take back this country to serve as my dwelling pool." Madhyāntika acceded to his request. Once the arhat had obtained the land, he employed his great supernatural power to establish five hundred monasteries (伽藍). He purchased people of low status from various other countries to serve as laborers and provide for the monastic community. After Madhyāntika entered parinirvāṇa, those low-status people established their own leader. The neighboring countries despised their lowly caste and would not intermarry with them, calling them Kṛta (translated into Chinese as "bought"). At the present time, the spring water has already overflowed in many places.  In the hundredth year after the Tathāgata’s nirvana, King Aśoka (無憂王) of the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) ascended the throne and ruled the world; his majesty extended to distant lands. He had deep faith in the Three Jewels and cherished and nurtured the four types of living beings. At that time, there were five hundred arhat monks and five hundred ordinary monks, all of whom the king revered and supported without distinction. There was an ordinary monk named Mahādeva (摩訶提婆; translated into Chinese as "Great Heaven" [大天]), who was broad-minded and highly intelligent. He sought deeply into name and reality and composed a treatise through profound reflection that contradicted the holy teachings; those who heard of it followed his heterodox views. King Aśoka, unable to distinguish between the ordinary and the holy, sympathized with those he liked and sided with those close to him; he summoned the monks to the Ganges River (殑伽河), intending to drown them in the deep current and execute them all.  When the arhats were faced with this mortal danger, they all exercised their supernatural powers, ascended into the void, and walked through the air, coming to this country to dwell in the mountains and hide in the valleys. When King Aśoka heard of this, he was afraid; he came in person to apologize and requested them to return to their own country. The arhats firmly refused to comply. King Aśoka built five hundred monasteries (伽藍) for the arhats and bestowed this entire country upon the community of monks.  In the four-hundredth year after the Tathāgata’s nirvana, King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王) of the country of Gandhāra (健馱邏國) ascended the throne in accordance with the prophesied time; his royal influence spread far and wide, and people of diverse customs came to submit to his rule. In his leisure time from state affairs, he would study the Buddhist scriptures, daily inviting a monk to the palace to expound the Dharma. However, the various schools held divergent views, and the king was deeply perplexed, finding no way to resolve his doubts. At that time, the Venerable Pārśva (脇尊者) said: "Since the Tathāgata passed away, the years have grown distant; the disciples have formed different schools, and teachers have held divergent views, each relying on what they have heard and seen, and all contradicting one another." When the king heard this, he was deeply moved and grieved; after sighing in lamentation for a long while, he said to the Venerable: "By my humble remaining merit, I have followed in the footsteps of my predecessors; though far removed from the Sage, I am still fortunate. I dare not forget my own unworthiness and wish to promote and exalt the Dharma, explaining the Tripiṭaka in full according to the tenets of the various schools." The Venerable Pārśva said: "Your Majesty has planted roots of goodness in past lives and is richly endowed with blessings; that you should devote your mind to the Buddha-dharma is exactly what I desire."  The king then issued a decree to near and far, summoning the sages and philosophers. Thereupon, they gathered from the four directions, traveling like stars across ten thousand miles; the brilliant and the wise all assembled. For seven days, he provided the four requisites as offerings. Wishing to hold a doctrinal discussion, he feared it would be noisy and chaotic. The king then expressed his thoughts to the monks, saying: "Those who have attained the fruits of sainthood may stay; those who are still bound by worldly fetters shall return." Even so, the number remained large. He issued another order: "Those who are 'without learning' (aśaikṣa) may stay; those who are 'still learning' (śaikṣa) shall return." Still, they were numerous. He issued yet another order: "Those who possess the three insights and are equipped with the six supernatural powers may stay; all others shall return." Yet, they were still numerous. He issued another order: "Those who have internally mastered the Three Baskets (Tripiṭaka) and externally attained the Five Sciences (pañcavidyā) may stay; all others shall return." Thereupon, four hundred and ninety-nine people were obtained. The king wished to hold the assembly in his own country, but he was troubled by its heat and humidity; he also wished to go to the stone cave in Rājagṛha where Mahākāśyapa had conducted the council. The Venerable Pārśva and the others deliberated, saying: "That is not possible. There are many non-Buddhists there, and their divergent views are tangled and confusing; one would be too busy responding to them to have any energy to compose the treatise. The hearts of the assembly are set on this country. This country is surrounded by solid mountains, guarded by yakṣas, its land is fertile, and its products are abundant; it is a place where sages and saints gather, and where spiritual immortals roam and dwell." The assembly deliberated on this, and all said: "This is appropriate." At that time, the king and the arhats arrived from there, established a monastery, and compiled the Tripiṭaka, intending to compose the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*. At that time, the Venerable Vasumitra was outside the door mending his robes. The arhats said to Vasumitra: "Your fetters (kleśa) are not yet removed, and your pure deliberations are erroneous; you should go far away and not stay here." Vasumitra replied: "You worthies have no doubts regarding the Dharma; you act on behalf of the Buddha to transform others, and are now gathering the great meaning, wishing to compose a correct treatise. Although I am not clever, I have a rough understanding of the subtle words; I have also studied deeply the profound texts of the Tripiṭaka and the ultimate principles of the Five Sciences, and have grasped their essence." The arhats said: "Words cannot be like this. You should withdraw and dwell apart, quickly attain the state of 'no-learning' (aśaikṣa), and then join us; it will not be too late." Vasumitra said, "I regard the state of 'no-learning' (aśaikṣa) as I would spit or mucus; my aspiration is to seek the fruit of Buddhahood, not to pursue the lesser path. I shall throw this ball of thread, and before it falls to the ground, I shall certainly attain the holy fruit of 'no-learning'." At that time, the arhats rebuked him again, saying, "This is what is called a person of excessive pride. The fruit of 'no-learning' is praised by all Buddhas; you should attain it quickly to resolve the doubts of the assembly." Thereupon, Vasumitra threw the ball of thread. The devas in the air caught the ball of thread and pleaded, "You are about to realize the fruit of Buddhahood and will next succeed Maitreya (慈氏); as the most honored one in the three realms and the one upon whom all beings of the four births depend, why do you wish to realize the lesser fruit here?" When the arhats saw this event, they apologized for their fault, acknowledged his virtue, and invited him to be the chairperson; whenever there were doubts or discussions, they all took his decision as final. These five hundred sages first composed the *Upadeśa-śāstra* (鄔波第鑠論) (Original note: The old name, *Upadeśa-śāstra* (優波提舍論), is a corruption) in one hundred thousand stanzas, explaining the *Sūtra-piṭaka* (素呾纜藏) (Original note: The old name, *Sūtra-piṭaka* (修多羅藏), is a corruption). Next, they composed the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (毘柰耶毘婆沙論) in one hundred thousand stanzas, explaining the *Vinaya-piṭaka* (毘奈耶藏) (Original note: The old name, *Vinaya-piṭaka* (毘那耶藏), is a corruption). Finally, they composed the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (阿毘達磨毘婆沙論) in one hundred thousand stanzas, explaining the *Abhidharma-piṭaka* (阿毘達磨藏) (Original note: Or it is called *Abhidharma-piṭaka* (阿毘曇藏), which is an abbreviation). In total, there are three hundred thousand stanzas and nine million six hundred thousand words, providing a complete explanation of the Tripiṭaka to be preserved for all eternity; they exhaustively explore every branch and detail, investigating both the shallow and the deep, so that the great principles are clarified once more, the subtle words are again revealed, and through their wide circulation, later students may rely upon them. King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王) then had the treatises incised on red copper plates, sealed them in stone cases, and erected a stūpa to store them inside. He commanded Yakṣa deities to guard the country, not allowing those of other schools to take these treatises out; those who wished to study them were to receive instruction within the country. When this work was completed, he returned his army to his capital. He went outside the western gate of this country, knelt facing east, and once again bestowed this entire country upon the community of monks. After King Kaniṣka passed away, the Kṛta (訖利多) tribe again claimed the kingship, expelled the monks, and destroyed the Buddha-dharma. The King of Himatala (呬摩呾羅國) (Original note: In the language of the Tang, "under the snow mountains") in the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國) was a descendant of the Śākya clan. Six hundred years after the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa, he came to possess vast territories and inherited the royal enterprise; he planted his heart in the soil of the Buddha and poured his sentiments into the sea of the Dharma. Hearing that the Kṛta had destroyed the Buddha-dharma, he gathered three thousand brave warriors from his country, disguised them as merchants, and, carrying many precious goods while concealing weapons, entered this country. The king of this country treated them with special courtesy. From among the merchants, he further selected five hundred men who were fierce and resourceful; each hid a sharp blade in his sleeve and carried heavy treasures, personally bearing their offerings to present them to the king. At that moment, the King of Himatala (雪山下王) removed his cap and took the throne. The King of the Kṛta (訖利多王) was paralyzed with terror, whereupon the king beheaded him and commanded the subordinates, saying: "I am the King of Himatala in the country of Tukhāra (覩邏國). I am enraged by this base race’s public practice of tyrannical government, and therefore I have executed the guilty one today. As for all you common people, this is not your crime." However, he relocated the country’s ministers and officials to a foreign territory. Having pacified this country, he summoned the monks, established monasteries, and restored peace and order as before. Furthermore, outside the western gate of this country, he knelt facing east and offered alms to the assembly of monks. Because the Kṛta tribe had frequently caused the ruin of clans and the extinction of sacrifices on account of the monks, they had accumulated resentment for generations and detested the Buddha-dharma. As time passed, they again proclaimed themselves kings. Therefore, this country does not hold the faith in high esteem today, and they pay special attention to the temples of the non-Buddhist gods.

Traveling over thirty li southeast from the small monastery, one reaches the great mountain (Pravaragiri), where there is an old monastery. Its design was once magnificent, but it is now largely overgrown and in ruins, with only a small multi-storied pavilion remaining in one corner. There are over thirty monks, all of whom study the Mahāyāna teachings. Formerly, the śāstra-master Saṃghabhadra (in the language of Tang, "Zhongxian" [Mass of the Virtuous]) composed the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (順正理論) here. In the various stūpas around the monastery, the relics of great arhats are preserved. Wild beasts and mountain apes gather flowers to offer them, never failing throughout the seasons, as if following a command. There are many miraculous traces in these mountains; for instance, stone walls are split horizontally, and horse tracks remain upon the peaks. All such phenomena, with their strange and unusual forms, are said to be the result of arhats and novices playing in groups, pointing and gesturing, or riding horses to and fro. Such remaining traces are too numerous to describe in detail.

Traveling over two hundred li to the northwest of the royal city, one arrives at the Vikrītavana Monastery (商林伽藍), where the śāstra master Pūrṇa (布剌拏; in the language of the Tang, "Complete") composed the *Exposition of the Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (*釋毘婆沙論*).

From here, traveling southwest for over seven hundred li across mountains and through dangerous terrain, one arrives at the kingdom of Parṇotsa (半笯嗟國) (within the borders of North India). The kingdom of Parṇotsa is over two thousand li in circuit. There are many mountains and rivers, and the arable land is narrow; crops are sown in their proper seasons, and flowers and fruits grow in abundance. There is much sugarcane but no grapes; fruit trees such as the āmra (mango), udumbara (cluster fig), and moca (plantain) are planted in groves by every household, as their flavors are highly prized. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs of the people are fierce and valiant. Regarding their clothing, they mostly wear cotton cloth. The people are honest and straightforward by nature, and they have pure faith in the Three Jewels. There are five monasteries, all of which are mostly ruined and desolate. There is no great sovereign, and the country is subject to the kingdom of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國). In the monastery to the north of the city, there are few monks. To the north of the monastery is a stone stūpa, which manifests many spiritual miracles.

From here, traveling southeast for over four hundred li, one reaches the country of Rājapura (within the borders of North India). The country of Rājapura is over four thousand li in circuit. The capital city is over ten li in circuit. It is extremely steep and secure, with many mountains and hills; the rivers and plains are narrow and confined, and the land is not fertile. The soil, crops, and climate are the same as in the country of Parṇotsa. The customs are fierce, and the people are brave and valiant. The country has no sovereign and is subject to the country of Kaśmīra. There are ten saṃghārāmas, with few monks. There is one Deva temple, and there are many followers of non-Buddhist paths. From the country of Lampā to this land, the people’s appearance is coarse and ugly, their nature is vulgar and violent, their language is crude and base, and their sense of courtesy and righteousness is slight; this is not the proper territory of India, but a remote frontier with rustic customs. From here, traveling southeast, descending mountains and crossing rivers for over seven hundred li, one reaches the country of Ṭakka (within the borders of North India).

Fourteen or fifteen *li* to the southwest of the great city, one reaches the old city of Śākala (奢羯羅故城). Although the walls are ruined, the foundations remain solid. It is over twenty *li* in circumference. Within it, a smaller city has been built, six or seven *li* in circumference, where the inhabitants are wealthy; this is the former capital of this country. Several hundred years ago, there was a king named Mihirakula (摩醯邏矩羅) (translated as "Great Clan" in Chinese), who made this city his capital and ruled over all of India. He possessed talent and wisdom, and his nature was brave and fierce; there was no neighboring country that did not submit to him. During his leisure from state affairs, he wished to study the Buddha-dharma and ordered the monks to recommend a person of outstanding virtue. At that time, the monks dared not respond to the order, for they were few in desire and practiced non-action, not seeking fame or status; those who were learned and brilliant feared his majesty. At that time, there was a former servant of the royal household who had long worn the dyed robes (i.e., was a monk), whose rhetoric was refined and elegant, and whose speech was eloquent and quick; the assembly collectively recommended him to respond to the order. The King said, "I respect the Buddha-dharma and have sought out famous monks from afar, yet the assembly recommends this menial to engage in discussion with me. I always thought that among the monks, the wise and brilliant were comparable; now that I know this, what is there to respect?" Thereupon, he issued a decree throughout the five regions of India that from then on, the Buddha-dharma was to be utterly destroyed, and all monks were to be expelled until not a single one remained. King Bālāditya (婆羅阿迭多) of the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) (translated as "Young Sun" in Chinese) revered the Buddha-dharma and loved his people; because of King Mihirakula’s excessive punishments and tyrannical rule, he guarded his own borders and did not offer the customary tribute. At that time, King Mihirakula mobilized his troops, intending to punish him. When King Bālāditya (幼日王) learned of this news, he told his ministers, "I hear the invaders are coming, but I cannot bear to let my soldiers engage in battle. I hope my officials and the common people will forgive me for this, and I shall take this humble body and hide in the marshes and wilderness." Having finished speaking, he left the palace and took refuge in the mountains and forests. More than ten thousand people in the country, moved by gratitude and admiration, followed him and hid on islands in the sea. King Mihirakula (大族王) entrusted his troops to his younger brother and sailed across the sea to attack him. King Bālāditya guarded the strategic passes and sent light cavalry to lure the enemy into battle; at the first sound of the gongs and drums, ambushers rose from all sides, capturing Mihirakula alive and leading him forward with his hands tied behind his back. King Mihirakula, ashamed of his failure, covered his face with his garment. King Bālāditya sat upon his lion throne, surrounded by his officials, and ordered his attendants to say to Mihirakula, "Uncover your face, for I have words for you." Mihirakula replied, "The positions of subject and master have been reversed, and we look upon each other as enemies; since we are not on friendly terms, what is the use of speaking face to face?" Though they urged him again and again, he would not comply. Thereupon, the King issued a proclamation enumerating his crimes, saying, "The Three Jewels are a field of merit upon which the four forms of birth depend. You have acted like a jackal or wolf, destroying these noble works. Fortune has not protected you, and you have been captured by me. Your crimes are unpardonable, and you must face the penalty of the law." At that time, the mother of King Bālāditya was widely learned and possessed a keen memory, and she was highly skilled in physiognomy. Hearing that he was about to execute Mihirakula, she hurriedly told King Bālāditya, "I have heard that Mihirakula possesses an extraordinary appearance and great wisdom; I wish to see him once." King Bālāditya ordered that Mihirakula be led into his mother's palace. The mother of Bālāditya (幼日王) said, "Alas, Mahirakula (大族), I pray you do not feel ashamed! The world is impermanent, and honor and disgrace alternate. I am like a mother to you, and you are like a son to me; you should remove the cloth covering your face and speak to me face to face."  Mahirakula said, "Formerly the ruler of a hostile state, I am now a captive prisoner. Having ruined the royal enterprise and extinguished the ancestral sacrifices, I am ashamed before the spirits of my ancestors above and the common people below; I am truly disgraced to show my face. Looking up and down between heaven and earth, I cannot bear the loss of myself, and that is why I cover my face."  The king's mother said, "Rise and fall follow the times; existence and extinction have their destiny. If you use the mind to equalize things, then gain and loss are both forgotten; if you use things to equalize the mind, then praise and blame arise in turn. You should believe in karmic retribution and move along with the times. Remove your covering and speak; perhaps you may preserve your life."  Mahirakula thanked her, saying, "Being a man of no talent, I inherited the royal throne, yet my governance strayed from the Way, leading to the ruin of my kingdom. Although I am now in bonds, I still cling to the hope of living for a little longer. I dare to accept your great kindness and will uncover my face to thank you for your profound grace."  Thereupon, he removed the cloth and revealed his face. The king's mother said, "Take care of yourself, for you shall live out your natural lifespan."  Soon after, she told King Bālāditya, "The ancient scriptures contain the teaching to forgive transgressions and cherish life. Although King Mahirakula has accumulated evil for a long time, his remaining merit is not yet exhausted. If you kill this man, for twelve years there will be famine and suffering. However, he possesses the energy of a restoration; he will not ultimately be a king of a great country, but he shall occupy the north and possess a small territory." King Bālāditya, obeying his compassionate mother's command and pitying the sovereign who had lost his kingdom, gave him a young daughter in marriage and treated him with extraordinary courtesy; he assembled the king's remaining troops and provided additional guards before they had even left the island. The younger brother of King Mahirakula returned to his country and established himself as ruler; having lost his throne, Mahirakula fled to hide in the mountains and wilderness, eventually seeking refuge in the north in the kingdom of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國). The King of Kaśmīra treated him with great courtesy and, pitying him for the loss of his kingdom, granted him a territory as a fief. After some time had passed, he led his townspeople, treacherously killed the King of Kaśmīra, and established himself as ruler. Taking advantage of the prestige of his victory, he attacked the kingdom of Gandhāra (健馱邏國) to the west; by deploying hidden troops and an ambush, he killed its king and completely exterminated the royal clan and the high ministers. He destroyed one thousand six hundred stūpas and sanghārāmas. Beyond those killed in battle, there were nine hundred million people whom he intended to execute, leaving no survivors. At that time, his assistants all remonstrated, saying, "The Great King has intimidated powerful enemies and, without engaging in battle, has executed the chief culprits. What fault have the common people committed? We wish to offer our own humble bodies to die in their stead." The King replied, "You believe in the Buddha-dharma, value merit in the afterlife, aspire to attain the fruit of Buddhahood, and speak extensively on the Jātakas; do you wish to transmit my evil deeds to future generations? You should return to your positions and speak no more of this." Thereupon, he took three hundred million of the upper-class families and had them killed at the bank of the Sindhu (信度) River; three hundred million of the middle-class families were drowned and killed in the Sindhu River; and three hundred million of the lower-class families were distributed among the soldiers. Having seized the wealth of the ruined state, he gathered his troops and returned. Before a year had passed, he suddenly died. At that time, clouds and fog grew dark and gloomy, the great earth shook, and violent winds raged. A person who had attained the fruit (of the path) felt pity and sighed, saying, "By unjustly killing the innocent and destroying the Buddha-dharma, he has fallen into the Avīci hell, to transmigrate without end."  In the old city of Śākala (奢羯羅故城), there is a monastery (saṃghārāma) with more than one hundred monks, all of whom study the Hīnayāna teachings. The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (世親) formerly composed the *Paramārthasaptati* (勝義諦論) here. Beside it is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, where the four past Buddhas preached the Dharma. There is also a site with traces of the four Buddhas walking in meditation. Five or six li to the northwest of the monastery is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which is the place where the four past Buddhas preached the Dharma. More than ten li to the northeast of the new capital city, one reaches a stone stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka, which is the place where the Tathāgata halted midway while traveling north to spread his teachings. The *Account of India* (印度記) says, "There are many relics within the stūpa, and on days of fasting, it sometimes emits light."

Traveling eastward from here for more than five hundred li, one arrives at the country of Cīnabhukti (至那僕底國) (within the borders of North India). The country of Cīnabhukti is more than two thousand li in circuit. The capital city is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit. The crops are lush and abundant, but fruit trees are sparse. The households are settled in their occupations, and the national resources are plentiful. The climate is warm and hot; the customs of the people are timid and weak. Their studies encompass both the true and the conventional, and their faith includes both the heterodox and the orthodox. There are ten saṃghārāmas and eight deva temples.  In the past, during the reign of King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王), his reputation shook neighboring countries and his might extended to distant lands; the border tribes west of the river feared his power and sent hostages. Once King Kaniṣka had obtained the hostages, he treated them with great generosity and favor, changing their residences according to the three seasons and providing guards from the four branches of the military. This country was his winter residence, and therefore it is called Cīnabhukti (which in the language of the Tang means "Han Fief"). Because it was the place where the hostages resided, it became the name of the country.  Before this time, throughout the various parts of India, the land had no pears or peaches. They were planted by the hostages, and thus peaches are called *cīnānī* (至那爾) (which in the language of the Tang means "brought from Han"), and pears are called *cīnarājaputra* (至那羅闍弗呾邏) (which in the language of the Tang means "Han Prince"). Therefore, the people of this country deeply revere the eastern lands, and they point to one another and say, "These are the people from the original country of our former king."

Traveling more than five hundred *li* to the southeast of the great city, one arrives at the Tamasavana Monastery (Tamasavana; in Chinese: Dark Forest). There are more than three hundred monks who study the Sarvāstivāda school; their deportment is solemn and their moral conduct is lofty, and they are particularly well-versed in the studies of the Lesser Vehicle. The thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa all gathered assemblies of gods and humans in this place to preach the profound and wonderful Dharma. In the three-hundredth year after the Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the master Kātyāyana (formerly called Kātyāyana, which is incorrect) composed the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* here. Within the Tamasavana Monastery, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. Small stūpas and various large stone chambers (dakṣiṇa-giri) stand facing one another like the scales of a fish, in numbers too many to detail; these are all places where the various sages who have attained fruition since the beginning of the *kalpa* have entered into extinction, and it is difficult to enumerate them all, though their teeth and bones still remain. The monasteries surrounding the mountain cover a circuit of twenty *li*, and there are hundreds of thousands of stūpas containing the Buddha’s relics, with their corners connected and their shadows touching.

From here, traveling northeast for one hundred forty or fifty li, one arrives at the country of Jālaṃdhara (闍爛達羅國) (in the territory of North India). The country of Jālaṃdhara is over one thousand li from east to west and over eight hundred li from north to south. The capital city of the country is twelve or thirteen li in circumference. It is suitable for grain crops, with an abundance of non-glutinous rice; the forests and trees are lush and spreading, and flowers and fruits are abundant. The climate is warm and hot; the customs of the people are fierce and unyielding, their appearance is coarse and ugly, and their households are wealthy and prosperous. There are more than fifty saṃghārāmas and over two thousand monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles. There are three Deva temples, and more than five hundred followers of non-Buddhist paths, all of whom are of the sect that smears themselves with ash.  A former king of this country revered non-Buddhist paths, but later he met an arhat, heard the Dharma, and attained faith and enlightenment. Therefore, the king of Mid-India, emulating his pure faith, took overall charge of the affairs of the Three Jewels throughout the five Indias. He made no distinction between this and that, forgot preferences and aversions, supervised the monks, and thoroughly discerned the virtuous and the wicked. Thus, those whose moral character was renowned were honored with utmost sincerity, while those who violated the precepts were severely punished. At all sites of sacred traces, he erected memorials, whether stūpas or saṃghārāmas, and there is no place within the territory of India where these are not found.

From here, traveling northeast, crossing steep ridges, traversing deep valleys, passing over perilous routes, and wading through dangerous paths for more than seven hundred *li*, one reaches the country of Kulūta (屈露多國) (within the borders of North India). The country of Kulūta is more than three thousand *li* in circuit, with mountains surrounding its four borders. The capital city of the country is fourteen or fifteen *li* in circuit. The land is fertile, grain is sown in its season, flowers and fruits are abundant, and plants and trees flourish. As it borders the Snow Mountains (Himālaya), it is rich in precious medicinal herbs and produces gold, silver, red copper, as well as fire-pearls and rain-stones. The climate is extremely cold, and frost and snow fall lightly. The people are coarse and ugly in appearance, and are prone to goiters and swollen feet; their nature is fierce and impetuous, and they value spirit and courage. There are more than twenty *saṃghārāmas* (伽藍) with over one thousand monks, most of whom study the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), while few practice the various schools (Hīnayāna). There are fifteen *deva* temples, where followers of different paths live together. Relying on cliffs and occupying ridges, stone chambers are situated at intervals, some being dwellings of *arhats* and others being places where *ṛṣis* (仙人) have stayed. In the country there is a *stūpa* built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata came to this country, preached the Dharma to save people, and this record remains of his traces.

More than two thousand li to the north of this place, the route is difficult and obstructed, with cold winds and flying snow, until one reaches the country of Marasā (秣邏娑國) (also called the country of Sampaha (三波訶國)).

Traveling south from the country of Kulūta (屈露多國) for over seven hundred li, crossing a great mountain and fording a large river, one arrives at the country of Śatadru (設多圖盧國) (within the borders of North India). The country of Śatadru is over two thousand li in circuit and borders a large river to the west. The capital city of the country is seventeen or eighteen li in circuit. The grain crops are abundant, fruits and produce are plentiful, and there is much gold, silver, and precious pearls. The people’s clothing is fresh and plain, though their garments are elegant and fine. The climate is hot, the customs are honest and harmonious, the people are naturally kind and compliant, and there is order between those of high and low status. They are devoted to the Buddha-Dharma and are sincere and respectful in their faith. Inside and outside the royal city, there are ten saṃghārāmas, but the courtyards and buildings are desolate, and the number of monks is small. Three or four li to the southeast of the city, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas.

From here, traveling southwest for more than eight hundred li, one arrives at the country of Pāriyātra (波理夜呾羅國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Pāriyātra is more than three thousand li in circuit. The capital city is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit. The land is suitable for grain crops and is abundant in winter wheat; there is a unique variety of rice that is harvested in sixty days. There are many cattle and sheep, but few flowers or fruits. The climate is hot, and the customs of the people are fierce and impetuous. They do not value learning or the arts, and they believe in and practice non-Buddhist paths. The king is of the Vaiśya (吠奢) caste; his nature is brave and fierce, and he possesses much martial strategy. There are eight sanghārāmas, which are in a state of great ruin, and the number of monks is small; they study the Hīnayāna. There are more than ten deva temples, and over one thousand followers of non-Buddhist paths.

From here, traveling east more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Mathurā (秣菟羅國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Mathurā is more than five thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty *li* in circuit. The land is fertile and rich, and the people are devoted to agriculture. Every household plants mango trees to form groves; although they share the same name, there are two varieties: the small ones are green when raw and yellow when ripe, while the large ones remain green from beginning to end. The country produces fine striped cotton cloth and gold. The climate is hot, and the customs are honest and compliant; the people delight in cultivating merit for the afterlife, and they revere virtue and value learning. There are more than twenty monasteries and over two thousand monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles with equal diligence. There are five *deva* temples, where followers of various heterodox sects live together. There are three *stūpas* that were all built by King Aśoka. There are many traces of the four past Buddhas. There are *stūpas* containing the relics of the holy disciples of the Śākya Tathāgata, namely: Śāriputra (formerly called Shelizi or Shelifu, which are erroneous abbreviations), Maudgalyāyana (formerly called Mujianlian, which is erroneous), Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra (called Manci Zi in the Tang language; formerly called Miduoluonizi, which is an erroneous abbreviation), Upāli, Ānanda, Rāhula (formerly called Luohou or Luoyun, both of which are erroneous abbreviations), and Mañjuśrī (called Miaojixiang in the Tang language). (The former name was Rushou, also called Mañjuśrī, or sometimes Mañjuśrī [曼殊尸利], translated as 'Wonderful Virtue' [妙德], which is erroneous) and the stūpas of the various Bodhisattvas. During the three long fast months of every year and the six fast days of every month, the members of the Saṅgha compete with one another, leading those of like mind to bring offerings and prepare many rare curiosities, presenting them before the images of their respective patrons. Those who study the Abhidharma make offerings to Śāriputra; those who practice meditation make offerings to Maudgalyāyana; those who recite and uphold the Sūtras make offerings to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra; those who study the Vinaya make offerings to Upāli; the various bhikṣuṇīs make offerings to Ānanda; those who have not yet received the full ordination make offerings to Rāhula; and those who study the Mahāyāna make offerings to the various Bodhisattvas. On these days, the various stūpas compete in performing offerings; pearl-adorned banners are arrayed in rows, precious canopies are lined up, smoke from incense is like clouds, and flowers are scattered like rain, obscuring the sun and moon and shaking the valleys. The king and his ministers make the cultivation of merit their primary duty.

Traveling five or six *li* to the east of the city, one arrives at a mountain monastery where the cliffs were hollowed out to form chambers and the valleys were utilized as gateways; it was built by the Venerable Upagupta (in the language of the Tang, "Close Protector" [Jinhu]). Within it is a *stūpa* containing the finger-nails of the Tathāgata. In the cliffs to the north of the monastery, there is a stone chamber over twenty *chi* high and thirty *chi* wide, filled with fine bamboo tallies four *cun* in length. When the Venerable Close Protector preached the Dharma and provided guidance, whenever a husband and wife both attained the fruit of an Arhat, he would place one tally inside; those from different households or different clans, even if they attained the fruit, were not recorded. Twenty-four or twenty-five *li* to the southeast of the stone chamber, one reaches a large dried-up pond, beside which stands a *stūpa*. In the past, when the Tathāgata was traveling through this place, there was a monkey who brought honey to offer to the Buddha. The Buddha instructed him to mix it with water and distribute it to the great assembly. The monkey, leaping with joy, fell into a pit and died; by the power of this merit, he was reborn among humans. Not far to the north of the pond, in a large forest, are the remains of the places where the four Buddhas of the past walked in meditation. Beside them is the place where Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and one thousand two hundred and fifty great Arhats practiced meditation; *stūpas* have been built at all these sites to mark the remains. While the Tathāgata was in the world, he frequently traveled through this country, and at the places where he preached the Dharma, mounds and trees have been established.

From here, traveling northeast for more than five hundred li, one reaches the country of Sthāneśvara (薩他泥濕伐羅國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Sthāneśvara is more than seven thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty li in circuit. The land is fertile and rich, and the crops are abundant. The climate is warm and hot. The customs are degenerate; the households are wealthy and prosperous, and they compete in being extravagant. They are deeply skilled in magical arts and highly esteem extraordinary abilities. They mostly pursue profit and pay little attention to farming; rare goods from various regions are mostly gathered in this country. There are three saṃghārāmas (伽藍) with more than seven hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Hīnayāna. There are more than one hundred deva temples (天祠), and there are many heterodox sects.

Traveling more than one hundred li to the south of the city, one arrives at the Gukhunda (俱昏荼) monastery. Multi-storied pavilions have connected roof ridges, and terraced platforms stand interspersed between them. The community of monks is pure and disciplined, and their deportment is calm and elegant.

From here, traveling northeast for more than four hundred li, one arrives at the country of Srughna (窣祿勤那國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Srughna is over six thousand li in circuit; it borders the Ganges (gaṅgā) river to the east, rests against great mountains (pravaragiri) to the north, and the Yamunā river flows through the middle of its territory. The capital city of the country is over twenty li in circuit; it borders the Yamunā river to the east. Although it is very desolate, its foundations remain firm. The produce of the land and the suitability of the climate are the same as in the country of Sthāneśvara (薩他泥濕伐羅國). The people are honest and simple by nature, and they revere and believe in non-Buddhist paths. They value the arts and sciences, and esteem both merit and wisdom. There are five monasteries with over one thousand monks, most of whom study the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), while few study other schools. They deliberate on subtle doctrines and engage in pure, profound discussions; talented scholars from distant regions come here to investigate doctrines and resolve doubts. There are one hundred Deva temples, and the non-Buddhist sects are very numerous. To the southeast of the great city, on the west bank of the Yamunā river and outside the eastern gate of a large monastery, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. In the past, the Tathāgata once preached the Dharma here to save people. Beside it is another stūpa, which contains the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. Surrounding it on the left and right are several dozen stūpas containing the hair and nails of the arhats Śāriputra (舍利子) and Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅). After the Tathāgata entered extinction, this country was misled by various non-Buddhists; they accepted and followed erroneous teachings and abandoned correct views. The five monasteries that exist today were built at the sites where masters from other countries held debates and emerged victorious over various non-Buddhists and Brahmins.

Crossing the river to the east bank, one arrives at the country of Matipura (秣底補羅國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Matipura is over six thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is over twenty li in circuit. It is suitable for grain and wheat, and there are many flowers and fruits. The climate is harmonious and pleasant, and the customs are simple and honest. The people esteem learning and the arts, and are deeply skilled in magical incantations. Those who believe in heterodox paths and those who believe in the orthodox path are about equal in number. The king is of the Śūdra caste; he does not believe in the Buddha-Dharma and reverently serves the heavenly deities.
