There are more than ten monasteries with over eight hundred monks, most of whom study the Sarvāstivāda school of the Lesser Vehicle teachings. There are more than fifty temples to the heavenly deities, where followers of different paths live together. Four or five li to the south of the great city, one reaches a small monastery with over fifty monks. In the past, the master of treatises Guṇaprabha (唐言德光 - Tang language: "Virtue-Light") composed the *Tattvavibhaṅga* (辯真) and other treatises here, totaling over one hundred works. The master of treatises was heroic and outstanding in his youth, and broad-minded and quick-witted in his maturity; he was widely learned and possessed a retentive memory, being a scholar of great erudition. Originally, he studied the Mahayana, but not having exhausted its profound mysteries, he read the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* and subsequently abandoned his former studies to learn the Lesser Vehicle. He composed several dozen treatises, refuting the principles of the Mahayana and establishing the attachments of the Lesser Vehicle. He also produced several dozen secular books, criticizing and rejecting the canonical treatises composed by his predecessors. He pondered the Buddhist scriptures deeply, but there were over ten points he could not resolve; though he studied them with refinement for a long time, his doubts remained. At that time, there was an arhat named Devasena (唐言天軍 - Tang language: "Heavenly-Army") who traveled back and forth to the Tuṣita Heaven. Guṇaprabha wished to see Maitreya to resolve his doubts and request further instruction. Devasena, using his supernatural powers, took him up to the heavenly palace. Upon seeing Maitreya (慈氏 - *Maitreya*), he merely made a long bow and did not prostrate. Devasena said to him, "Maitreya Bodhisattva is the next to succeed to the Buddha’s throne; why are you so arrogant that you dare not show him respect? You are seeking to receive instruction, so how can you not humble yourself?" Guṇaprabha (德光 - *Guṇaprabha*) replied, "Venerable one, your words are indeed a guide. However, I am a fully ordained bhikṣu and a monastic disciple, while Maitreya Bodhisattva enjoys the bliss of heavenly rewards and is not a member of the monastic order; I fear it would be inappropriate for me to pay him homage." The Bodhisattva, knowing that his pride was deeply rooted and that he was not a vessel fit to hear the Dharma, allowed him to travel back and forth three times without resolving his doubts. Guṇaprabha asked Devasena again, wishing to pay homage once more, but Devasena, disgusted by his pride, ignored him and did not reply. Since Guṇaprabha did not have his wish fulfilled, he harbored resentment and went into the mountain forests to practice meditation for the attainment of supernatural powers; however, because his pride was not eliminated, he did not realize the fruits of the Path.  Three or four *li* to the north of the Guṇaprabha monastery, there is a large monastery with over two hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). This is the place where the master of treatises Saṃghabhadra (眾賢 - *Saṃghabhadra*) passed away. The master of treatises was a man from the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國 - *Kaśmīra*); he was intelligent and erudite, and from his youth he was renowned for his elegance, having studied the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (說一切有部毘婆沙論) with particular depth. At that time, there was the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (世親 - *Vasubandhu*), who was single-mindedly devoted to the profound Path and sought to understand the meaning beyond the words. He refuted the positions held by the masters of the *Vibhāṣā* and composed the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (阿毘達磨俱舍論), in which the language and meaning were skillful and the principles were lofty and refined. Saṃghabhadra (眾賢) read it and was moved to action. Thereupon, he delved deeply into study and research for twelve years, composing the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (俱舍雹論) in twenty-five thousand verses, totaling eight hundred thousand words. It was said that his words were profound and his reach far, exhausting the hidden and penetrating the subtle. He told his disciples, "With my outstanding talent and by upholding my correct arguments, go and refute Vasubandhu (世親 - *Vasubandhu*), to blunt his sharp edge, so that the old man may no longer enjoy a monopoly on pre-eminent fame." Thereupon, three or four of his most talented disciples took the treatise he had written and went to seek out Vasubandhu. At that time, Vasubandhu was in the city of Sākala (奢羯羅城) in the country of Takka (磔迦國). Word was sent from afar that Saṃghabhadra was arriving. Upon hearing this, Vasubandhu immediately began to pack his belongings. His disciples, filled with doubt, came forward to remonstrate, saying, "Great Master, your virtue surpasses that of former sages and your fame is unrivaled in the present age; among students near and far, there are none who do not defer to you. Now, hearing of Saṃghabhadra, why are you so flustered? If you must yield to him, we will be deeply ashamed." Vasubandhu replied, "I am traveling far away now, not to avoid this man. It is just that in this country, there are no longer any discerning scholars. Saṃghabhadra is a younger scholar whose sophistry flows like a river; I am old and frail and cannot engage in debate. I wish to defeat his heterodox views with a single word and lead him to Central India to face the eminent and learned scholars, so that they may discern truth from falsehood and examine right and wrong." He immediately ordered his companions to pack their book-satchels and set out on the long journey. The Master of Treatises Saṃghabhadra (眾賢) arrived at this monastery one day later, when he suddenly felt his vitality failing. He then composed a letter to apologize to Vasubandhu (世親), saying: "Since the Thus-Come One passed into extinction, the disciples have held to their own sectarian views, each transmitting their own school's learning, each specializing in their own field, favoring those who share their path and disparaging those of different schools. In my ignorance and dullness, I rashly received these traditions. Upon reading the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (阿毘達磨俱舍論) that you composed, which refutes the great principles of the Vaibhāṣika masters, I—without measuring my own strength—spent years in deep study and composed this treatise to uphold the orthodox school. My wisdom was small but my ambition was great, and now death is approaching. You, Bodhisattva, expound the subtle words and propagate the supreme truth; if you do not disparage my convictions and allow my writings to be preserved, I shall be fortunate indeed, and what regret could I have in death?" He then selected from among his disciples those who were eloquent and told them: "I am truly a junior scholar who has rashly insulted a senior master; such is my fate, what can be done? I am about to pass away. You must take this letter and the treatise I have composed, apologize to that Bodhisattva, and repent on my behalf." No sooner had he finished dictating these words than he suddenly passed away. The disciples took the letter to Vasubandhu and delivered the message, saying: "Our master Saṃghabhadra has already abandoned his life. He left a final letter to reproach himself and apologize for his faults. That his name not be forgotten is not something we would dare to hope for." Bodhisattva Vasubandhu read the letter and examined the treatise, and after pondering for a long time, he said to the disciples: "The Master of Treatises Saṃghabhadra was a clever junior; although his reasoning was insufficient, his rhetoric was more than enough. I now wish to refute Saṃghabhadra’s treatise, and it will be as easy as pointing to the palm of my hand." "However, considering his dying request and valuing his challenging words, if it serves the great principles, I shall preserve his original intention; furthermore, this treatise clarifies my own school." He then changed the title to the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise Following the Correct Principles). His disciples remonstrated, saying: "Saṃghabhadra is not yet dead, and the Master is far away; having obtained his treatise, you are now changing its title—how can all the students face the shame of this?" Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, wishing to remove their doubts, spoke a verse: "Like a lion king, avoiding a boar and going far away, the wise should know the victory or defeat of the two powers." After Saṃghabhadra died, they cremated his body and collected his bones. In the Āmra (mango) grove, two hundred paces northwest of the monastery, they erected a stūpa, which still exists today. Beside the Āmra grove is a stūpa containing the remains of the master Vimalamitra (in Tang language, "Stainless Friend"). The master was a man of the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國) and had renounced the household life in the Sarvāstivāda school. He extensively studied the various scriptures and researched heterodox treatises. He traveled through the five Indias, studied the profound texts of the Tripiṭaka, and having established his reputation and completed his work, he was about to return to his home country. Passing by the stūpa of the master Saṃghabhadra, he patted it and sighed, saying: "The master possessed such noble magnanimity and refined character, expounding the great principles; just as he was about to defeat the heterodox sects and establish the legacy of his own school, how is it that his years were not prolonged! I, Vimalamitra, humbly follow in his footsteps; I have long admired his righteousness and have cherished his virtue across the ages." "Although Vasubandhu (世親) has passed away, his school's teachings are still transmitted. I shall exhaust all my knowledge to compose various treatises, causing the scholars of Jambudvīpa (贍部洲) to abandon the name of the Mahāyāna and to efface the fame of Vasubandhu; this shall be my immortal achievement, fulfilling my long-held ambition." Having spoken these words, his mind became deranged, five tongues emerged from his mouth, and hot blood gushed forth. Knowing that his life was surely coming to an end, he composed a letter of repentance, saying: "The Mahāyāna teachings are the ultimate discourse within the Buddha-dharma. Their names and meanings are profound and absolute, and their principles are subtle and mysterious. Because of my ignorance, I lightly refuted these advanced teachings; the karmic retribution is clear, and it is fitting that my body should be destroyed. I dare to warn all students: take this as a lesson, guard your intentions, and do not harbor doubts." The great earth shook, and his life then ended. At the place where he died, the ground sank into a pit. His traveling companions cremated his corpse, collected the remains, and built a memorial over them. At that time, an Arhat (羅漢) saw this and sighed, saying: "Alas! How painful! This master of treatises, following his own emotions and holding to his views, slandered and disparaged the Mahāyāna, and has fallen into the Avīci (無間) hell."

From here, traveling north for over three hundred li, one reaches the country of Brahmapura (婆羅吸摩補羅國) (within the borders of North India). The country of Brahmapura is over four thousand li in circuit, and mountains surround its four borders. The capital city of the country is over twenty li in circuit. The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, and the households are wealthy. The soil is fertile, crops are sown in their proper seasons, and it produces brass and rock crystal. The climate is slightly cold, and the customs are fierce and unyielding. The people have little interest in the arts and are mostly driven by profit. Their nature is wild and violent, and they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are five sanghārāmas, with few monks. There are more than ten deva temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together.

In the Great Snow Mountains to the north of this country lies the kingdom of Suvarṇagotra (translated into Chinese as the "Gold Clan"). It produces superior gold, and is named accordingly. It is long from east to west and narrow from north to south; this is the Eastern Women's Kingdom. For generations, it has been ruled by women. The husband is also called king, but he does not manage state affairs; the men's only duties are warfare and farming. The soil is suitable for winter wheat, and there is an abundance of sheep and horses. The climate is cold and harsh, and the people are impetuous and violent. To the east it borders the kingdom of Tubo, to the north it borders the kingdom of Khotan, and to the west it borders the kingdom of Sampaha.

Traveling southeast from Matipura (末底補羅國) for more than four hundred li, one arrives at the country of Goviṣāṇa (瞿毘霜那國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Goviṣāṇa is over two thousand li in circuit. The capital city is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit; it is high, precipitous, and strategically secure, with a dense and prosperous population, and flowery groves and ponds are interspersed throughout. The climate and soil are the same as in the country of Matipura. The customs are simple and honest, and the people are diligent in learning and fond of merit. Many believe in non-Buddhist paths and seek present-day happiness. There are two saṃghārāmas with over one hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). There are more than thirty Deva temples, where followers of various paths live together. Beside the old saṃghārāma near the great city, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王) that is over two hundred feet high. In the past, the Tathāgata stayed here for one month to preach the essential Dharma; nearby are the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. Beside these are two stūpas containing the hair and nail clippings of the Tathāgata, each over one zhang high.

From here, traveling southeast for more than four hundred li, one reaches the country of Ahicchattra (堊醯掣呾邏國) (in the region of Central India). The country of Ahicchattra is more than three thousand li in circuit. The capital city is seventeen or eighteen li in circuit; it is situated in a secure and rugged position, is suitable for grain and wheat, and has many forests and springs. The climate is temperate and pleasant, and the customs of the people are honest and simple. They delight in the Way and are diligent in their studies, being talented and widely learned. There are more than ten sanghārāmas (伽藍) and over one thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Sammatiya school (正量部) of the Lesser Vehicle. There are nine deva temples, and more than three hundred sectarians who serve Īśvara (自在天) and are followers of the ash-smearing ascetics. Outside the city, beside a dragon pool, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). It was here that the Tathāgata, in a former life when he was a dragon king, preached the Dharma for seven days. Beside it are four small stūpas, which are the sites of the remains of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas.

From here, traveling east for two hundred sixty or seventy li and crossing the Ganges (Gaṅgā) River, one arrives south at the country of Vilaśāṇa (毘羅那拏國), which is within the borders of Central India. The country of Vilaśāṇa is over two thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is over ten li in circuit. The climate and soil conditions are the same as those of the country of Ahicchatrā (堊醯掣呾邏國). The customs of the people are fierce and violent, yet they are knowledgeable in the arts. They revere and believe in non-Buddhist paths and have little respect for the Buddha-Dharma. There are two monasteries with three hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Great Vehicle. There are five Deva temples where followers of various non-Buddhist paths live together. Inside an old monastery in the great city, there is the base of a stūpa which, although dilapidated, is still over one hundred feet high; it was built by King Aśoka. This is the place where the Tathāgata in the past spent seven days preaching the *Skandhadhātvāyatana-sūtra* (蘊界處經). Beside it are the seats and traces of the walking paths of the four past Buddhas.

From here, traveling southeast for more than two hundred li, one reaches the country of Kapitha (劫比他國) (the old name is the country of Saṃkāśya; it is within the borders of Central India). The country of Kapitha is more than two thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty li in circuit. The climate and soil conditions are the same as those of the country of Viraṇāṇa (毘羅那拏國). The customs are honest and harmonious, and the people are mostly devoted to learning and the arts. There are four saṃghārāmas with more than one thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Hīnayāna Saṃmitīya school. There are ten deva temples where followers of different paths live together, all of whom jointly worship Maheśvara.

More than twenty *li* west of the city is a large monastery, its construction magnificent and its craftsmanship exquisite; the sacred forms and venerable images are adorned with the utmost solemnity. There are several hundred monks who study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school, and tens of thousands of laypeople reside in its vicinity. Within the great wall of the monastery are the Devāvatāra (三寶階), arranged from north to south and facing east, where the Tathāgata returned from the Trāyastriṃśa heaven. In the past, the Tathāgata rose from the Jetavana (勝林) and ascended to the heavenly palace, where he resided in the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā-sabhā) to preach the Dharma for his mother. After three months had passed, he intended to descend. Śakra, the Lord of Devas, then exercised his divine power to establish a precious stairway: the middle step was of gold, the left of crystal, and the right of silver. The Tathāgata rose from the Hall of Good Dharma and, followed by a host of deities, stepped down the middle stairway; the Great Brahmā King, holding a white whisk, walked on the silver stairway to attend on the right; Śakra, the Lord of Devas, holding a precious canopy, stepped on the crystal stairway to attend on the left; the heavenly host hovered in the void, scattering flowers and praising his virtues. Several hundred years ago, the stairs still existed, but by the present time, they have completely sunk into the earth. The kings of various countries, lamenting that they could not see them, stacked bricks and stones and decorated them with precious gems upon the original foundation to imitate the ancient precious stairway. It is over seventy feet high, and a *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) is built upon it. Inside is a stone Buddha image, and on the stairs to the left and right are images of Śakra and Brahmā, modeled after the original appearance, still in a descending posture. Beside it is a stone pillar, over seventy feet high, erected by King Aśoka (無憂王). Its color is dark blue and lustrous, its substance hard and fine-grained. At the top is a lion, crouching and facing the stairway, with strange forms carved and engraved around its four sides; according to the merit or demerit of the person, shadows appear within the pillar. Not far from the precious stairway is a stūpa, which is the site of the traces where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation. Beside it is a stūpa where the Tathāgata formerly bathed. Beside that is a *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍), which is the place where the Tathāgata entered into meditation. Beside the *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* is a large stone, fifty paces long and seven feet high, which is the place where the Tathāgata performed walking meditation. The footprints he trod upon all have lotus patterns. To the left and right of the base are small stūpas, built by Śakra (帝釋) and Brahmā (梵王). In front of the stūpas of Śakra and Brahmā is the place where the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā (蓮華色), wishing to be the first to see the Buddha, transformed herself into a wheel-turning king. When the Tathāgata returned from the heavenly palace to Jambudvīpa, at that time Subhūti (Original note: In Tang language, 'Subhūti' means 'Good Manifestation'. The old translations 'Xufuti' or 'Subuti', or the translation 'Good Auspicious', are all erroneous.) was sitting in meditation in a stone chamber and thought to himself: "Now the Buddha is descending, guided and followed by humans and devas. As for someone like me, what is appropriate to do? I have heard the Buddha say that to know all phenomena are empty and to realize the nature of all phenomena is to behold the Dharma-body with the eye of wisdom." At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, wishing to be the first to see the Buddha, transformed herself into a wheel-turning king, guided by the seven treasures and guarded by the fourfold army, and upon arriving at the place of the World-Honored One, she returned to her form as a bhikṣuṇī. The Tathāgata replied, "You are not seeing me for the first time. One who truly manifests is one who perceives that all phenomena are empty; this is to behold the Dharma-body." Within the enclosure of the sacred traces, miraculous signs occurred one after another. To the southeast of the great stūpa, there is a dragon pond, and the dragon constantly protects the sacred traces. Because there is this unseen protection, they are difficult to violate lightly; though they have decayed naturally over the long years, no person has been able to destroy them. Traveling southeast from here for less than two hundred li, one arrives at the country of Kanyakubja (羯若鞠闍國) (in the language of Tang, the Kingdom of the Hunchbacked Maiden City; it is within the borders of Central India).

The country of Kanyākubja (羯若鞠闍國) is over four thousand li in circumference. The capital city borders the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) to the west; it is over twenty li in length and four to five li in breadth. The city moats and ramparts are solid and steep, with towers and pavilions facing one another, and flower groves and ponds that are bright and clear as mirrors. Rare goods from distant regions are mostly gathered here. The inhabitants are prosperous and happy, and their households are wealthy and abundant. Flowers and fruits are plentiful, and crops are sown in their proper seasons. The climate is harmonious and mild, and the customs are honest and simple. The people are refined in appearance and wear bright and elegant clothing. They are devoted to learning and skilled in the arts, and their discourse is clear and profound. Regarding the two paths of the heterodox and the orthodox, the number of believers is about equal. There are over one hundred saṅghārāmas and more than ten thousand monks, who study both the Great and Small Vehicles with equal diligence. There are over two hundred deva temples, and several thousand followers of heterodox paths.  In the age when the people of the country of Kanyākubja enjoyed long lives, the old capital city was called Kusumapura (拘蘇磨補羅) (Original note: In the language of the Tang, this means "Flowery Palace"). The king was named Brahmadatta (梵授); he possessed the accumulated merits of wisdom and virtue, was fully accomplished in both civil and military affairs, his power intimidated Jambudvīpa, and his fame shook neighboring countries. He had a full thousand sons, who were wise, brave, magnanimous, and resolute; he also had one hundred daughters, who were beautiful in appearance and refined in manner.  At that time, there was a rishi living by the side of the Gaṅgā who concentrated his spirit in meditative absorption for tens of thousands of years until his form resembled a withered tree. Migratory birds perched and gathered there, dropping a nyagrodha fruit upon the rishi's shoulder; as summers went and winters came, it cast a shade and grew to the size of an arch. After many years had passed, he rose from his meditation and wished to remove the tree, but fearing he might overturn the birds' nests, he desisted. The people of the time praised his virtue and called him the "Rishi of the Big Tree." The rishi cast his eyes along the riverbank and wandered through the thickets, where he saw the king’s daughters playing together. Desire for the world of the senses arose, and a heart of attachment was born; he then went to the magnificent palace, wishing to make a formal request. When the king heard the rishi had arrived, he went to welcome him in person and greeted him, saying, "The great rishi dwells in spirit beyond the material world; what has prompted this sudden visit?" The rishi said, "I have dwelt in the forest and marshes for many years. Emerging from meditation to wander, I saw the king’s daughters, and a heart of attachment was born; I have come from afar to make a request." Hearing these words, the king was at a loss for a plan and said to the rishi, "Return now to your dwelling; please wait for an auspicious day." The rishi heard this command and returned to the forest and marshes. The king then asked each of his daughters in turn, but none would consent to the marriage. Fearing the rishi’s power, the king became sorrowful and haggard. His youngest daughter, waiting for a break in the king’s affairs, calmly asked, "Father, you have a full thousand sons and ten thousand nations admire your transformation; for what reason are you so sorrowful, as if you are in fear?" The king said, "The Rishi of the Big Tree (Mahāvṛkṣa-ṛṣi) has deigned to seek a marriage alliance, yet none of you sisters are willing to obey. An immortal possesses great power and can bring about either disaster or fortune; if his heart’s desire is not met, he will surely fall into a rage, destroying the kingdom, ending our ancestral sacrifices, and bringing shame upon the late kings. Deeply contemplating this calamity, I am truly afraid." The youngest daughter replied, "To have caused this deep sorrow is our fault. I am willing to offer my humble self to preserve the prosperity of the state." Hearing this, the king was overjoyed; he ordered a carriage to be prepared and sent her to him. Upon arriving at the hermit’s hut, the king thanked the hermit, saying, "The great hermit has condescended from his transcendent state to show concern for worldly affairs; I dare to offer my young daughter to serve you by sweeping and cleaning." The hermit saw her and was displeased, saying to the king, "You slight this old man by matching me with one so unattractive." The king replied, "I have asked all my daughters, and none were willing to obey. Only this young one is willing to serve as a maid." The hermit, harboring anger, uttered a wicked curse: "May the ninety-nine daughters all have their waists bent at once; their forms being thus ruined and spoiled, they shall have no marriage for their entire lives." The king sent someone to verify this, and indeed, their backs were already hunched. From that time on, it has been called the City of the Hunchbacked Maidens (Kanyakubja).  The present king is of the Vaiśya caste, and his name is Harṣavardhana (translated into Chinese as "Increment of Happiness"). He rules over the land, the third king of two generations. His father’s name was Prabhākaravardhana (translated into Chinese as "Increment of Light"), and his elder brother’s name was Rājyavardhana (translated into Chinese as "Increment of the Kingdom"). Rājyavardhana succeeded to the throne as the eldest and governed with virtue. At that time, King Śaśāṅka (translated into Chinese as "Moon") of the kingdom of Karṇasuvarṇa (translated into Chinese as "Golden Ear") in East India often said to his ministers, "To have a virtuous ruler in a neighboring state is a misfortune for one's own country." Thereupon, he lured and invited him, and at the meeting, he killed him. Once the people had lost their ruler, the country fell into chaos. At that time, the high minister Bhaṇi (translated into Chinese as "Eloquent and Wise"), whose position and reputation were of great weight, said to the officials and the populace, "The great plan for the country must be decided this day." "The son of the former king and younger brother of the deceased monarch is benevolent by nature and filial by heart; he is truly close to the virtuous, and I wish for him to succeed to the throne. What do you think of this matter? Each of you, speak your mind." The assembly all looked up to his virtue, and there was never any dissenting opinion. Thereupon, the assistant ministers and officials all exhorted him to take the throne, saying: "May the prince listen to us; the late king accumulated merits and cultivated virtues, gloriously possessing the mandate of the state. The succession reached the king, and we expected him to live out his full span of years; but his assistants were not good, and he abandoned his life at the hands of an enemy—this is a great shame for the country and the fault of us, your humble servants. Public opinion and the rumors of the time truly point to your brilliant virtue. If you were to grace the land and the territory, recover the debt from the enemy, wash away the shame of the country, and glorify the legacy of your father, what merit could be greater than this? We hope you will not decline!"  The prince said, "The matter of national succession has been a difficult one from ancient times to the present; the establishment of one in the position of a sovereign must be considered with great prudence. I am truly lacking in virtue, and now that my father and elder brother have been taken from me, if I were to be pushed to succeed to the great throne, would I be able to succeed in my duties? Although public opinion deems it appropriate, how could I forget my own insignificance? Now, on the bank of the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) river, there is an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩) which is highly responsive; I wish to go there to seek guidance."   He immediately went before the Bodhisattva's image and fasted to make his request. The Bodhisattva, moved by his sincerity, manifested his form and asked, "What do you seek, that you are so diligent and earnest?" The prince said, "I have only accumulated disasters; my benevolent father has passed away, and to add to this cruel punishment, my virtuous elder brother has been murdered. Reflecting on myself, I am lacking in virtue, yet the people of the country honor me and urge me to succeed to the great throne to glorify my father's legacy." "I am foolish and ignorant; how dare I hope for the holy decree!" The Bodhisattva replied, "In your former life, you were an āraṇyaka-bhikṣu (練若苾芻) in this forest, and you were diligent and unremitting. By the power of that merit, you have become this prince. Since the King of Karṇasuvarṇa (金耳國王) has destroyed the Buddha-dharma, you, in succeeding to the throne, should revive it; let compassion be your aim and sympathy dwell in your heart, and you will soon be the ruler of the five regions of India. If you wish to extend the prosperity of the state, you must follow my instructions; then, through hidden blessings, you will have no powerful enemies in the neighboring lands. Do not ascend the lion throne, and do not assume the title of Great King."  Thereupon, having received these instructions, he withdrew and assumed the throne, calling himself "The Prince" and taking the title Śīlāditya (尸羅阿迭多) (in the language of Tang, this means "Sun of Precepts"). He then said to his ministers, "The vengeance for my brother has not been requited, and the neighboring countries have not submitted; I shall not have a moment to eat with my right hand. Let all you officials be of one mind and exert your strength." He then gathered the national troops and trained his soldiers. He had 5,000 elephant troops, 20,000 cavalry, and 50,000 infantry, and from the west to the east, he campaigned against those who would not submit. Without the elephants being unsaddled or the men removing their armor, he brought the five regions of India into submission within six years. Having expanded his territory, he further increased his military forces, reaching 60,000 elephant troops and 100,000 cavalry. For nearly thirty years, the weapons of war were not raised, and the government and teachings were peaceful. He devoted himself to frugality, cultivated merit and goodness, and forgot both sleep and food. He ordered that no meat be eaten throughout the five regions of India, and if anyone took a life, they would be executed without pardon. Along the banks of the Ganges (gaṅgā), he erected several thousand stūpas, each over one hundred feet high. In the cities, villages, thoroughfares, and crossroads of the five regions of India, he established hospices (精廬) stocked with food, drink, and medicine to be distributed to travelers and the poor, providing for them without ceasing. At every site of a sacred relic, he built a monastery (saṅghārāma). Every five years, he held a great pan-charity assembly (pañcavārṣika), emptying the royal treasury to bestow gifts upon all beings, withholding only the weaponry from his charitable offerings. Every year, he gathered śramaṇas from various countries for a meeting lasting twenty-one days, during which he provided them with the four requisites, grandly decorated the Dharma seats and discussion halls, and had them engage in debate to assess their relative merits, praise the virtuous and criticize the evil, and demote the ignorant while promoting the enlightened. Those whose observance of the precepts was steadfast and whose moral character was profound were invited to ascend the lion seat, and the king would receive the Dharma from them in person. Those whose precepts were pure but whose learning was not grounded in the classics were merely treated with respect to show his veneration. Those who had no discipline and whose corrupt conduct was manifest were driven out of the country, as he did not wish to see or hear of them. If the minor rulers and assistant ministers of neighboring countries cultivated merit without ceasing and sought goodness without weariness, the king would take them by the hand to sit together and call them his "virtuous friends." If they were otherwise, he would not meet them face-to-face, and if there were matters to discuss, he would communicate only through the exchange of envoys. He toured the regions to inspect the customs of the people and did not have a fixed residence, building temporary huts wherever he stopped. Only during the three months of the rainy season did he cease traveling due to the heavy rains. At his temporary palaces, he would daily prepare fine meals to feed one thousand monks and five hundred Brahmins of various schools. He divided each day into three periods: one period for managing affairs and governing, and two periods for cultivating merit and practicing virtue. He was diligent and tireless, feeling that the day was never long enough. Initially, I had accepted an invitation from King Kumāra to travel from the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) to the country of Kāmarūpa (迦摩縷波國). At that time, King Śīlāditya (戒日王) was on a tour of inspection in the country of Kajuṅghira (羯朱嗢祇羅國) and commanded King Kumāra, saying: "You should come quickly with the guest śramaṇa from Nālandā (那爛陀) to attend the assembly." Thereupon, I went with King Kumāra to meet him. After King Śīlāditya had offered greetings, he asked: "From what country have you come, and what is it that you seek?" I replied: "I have come from the Great Tang (大唐國) to seek the Buddha-Dharma." The king asked: "In what direction does the Great Tang lie? What is the extent of the route, and how far is it from here?" I replied: "It lies more than several tens of thousands of *li* to the northeast of here; it is what you in India call the country of Mahācīna (摩訶至那國)." The king said: "I have heard that in the country of Mahācīna there is a Son of Heaven, the Prince of Qin (秦王天子), who was perceptive and wise in his youth and has become divinely martial in his maturity. In the past, when the previous dynasty fell into chaos, the land was divided and collapsed, weapons of war arose on all sides, and the masses were poisoned by suffering. The Prince of Qin, however, early on cherished far-reaching strategies, aroused great compassion, rescued all sentient beings, and pacified the world. His civilizing influence reached far and wide, and his virtuous grace extended to distant places; strange lands and foreign regions admired his transformation and declared themselves his subjects. The people, having received his protection and nurturing, all sing the 'Music of the Prince of Qin Breaking the Ranks' (秦王破陣樂). I have heard these elegant hymns for a long time now. Is the reputation of his magnificent virtue truly as it is said?" 'Is this the country of the Great Tang?' I replied, 'It is. Cīna (至那) was the name of the country under former kings; Great Tang is the title of my sovereign's realm. Before he ascended the throne, he was called the Prince of Qin; now that he has assumed the succession, he is titled the Son of Heaven. When the fortune of the previous dynasty ended, the masses were without a master, weapons of war arose in chaos, and living beings were cruelly harmed. The Prince of Qin, endowed by Heaven with vast magnanimity, felt compassion in his heart; his majestic influence stirred and spread, the various violent factions were exterminated, the eight directions were pacified, and ten thousand nations came to pay tribute. He loves and nurtures the four forms of birth, reveres and honors the Three Jewels, lightens taxes and levies, and reduces punishments; yet the state’s resources are abundant, and the common people have no need for hidden shelters. His civilizing influence and great transformation are difficult to fully describe.' King Śīlāditya (戒日王) said, 'Magnificent! The living beings of that land are blessed to be moved by such a holy lord.'  At that time, King Śīlāditya was about to return to the city of Kanyākubja (曲女城) to hold a religious assembly, followed by hundreds of thousands of people on the southern bank of the Ganges (殑伽河). King Kumāra (拘摩羅王) followed with tens of thousands of people, residing on the northern bank. They divided the river between them and advanced by both land and water. The two kings led the way, escorted by the four divisions of the army; some sailed in boats, others rode elephants, beating drums, blowing conches, and playing string and wind instruments. After ninety days, they reached the city of Kanyākubja, located in the Great Flower Wood to the west of the Ganges. At that time, more than twenty kings of various countries, having previously received the summons, arrived with the eminent śramaṇas, brahmans, officials, and soldiers of their respective kingdoms to gather for the great assembly. The King had previously built a large monastery (saṃghārāma) on the west side of the river. To the east of the monastery, he erected a precious terrace over one hundred feet high, in which was a golden Buddha image equal in size to the King’s own body. To the south of the terrace, he built a precious altar as a place to bathe the Buddha image. Fourteen or fifteen li to the northeast of this, he constructed a separate temporary palace. It was then the month of the middle of spring. From the first day of the month until the twenty-first, he provided delicious food to all the śramaṇas and brahmans. From the temporary palace to the monastery, pavilions were built along the sides of the road, exhausted of all adornments, where musicians remained stationed, playing elegant music in succession.  The King brought out a golden image from the temporary palace, hollow and embossed, over three feet in height; it was loaded onto a large elephant and covered with a precious canopy. King Śīlāditya (戒日王), dressed in the attire of Indra (帝釋), held a precious canopy and attended on the left, while King Kumāra (拘摩羅王) assumed the guise of Brahmā (梵王), holding a white fly-whisk and attending on the right. Five hundred elephant-mounted soldiers on each side, clad in armor, provided a protective escort, while a hundred great elephants preceded and followed the Buddha image, carrying musicians who played music and beat drums. King Śīlāditya scattered pearls, various jewels, and gold and silver flowers at every step as an offering to the Three Jewels. First, they proceeded to the precious altar to bathe the image with perfumed water; then the King personally carried the image and escorted it to the western terrace, offering tens of hundreds of thousands of jewels and kauśeya garments as offerings. At that time, only twenty-some śramaṇas were permitted to follow, while the various kings served as guards. Once the meal was finished, he gathered the various heterodox scholars to discuss subtle doctrines and clarify profound principles. As the sun approached dusk, the King returned to his temporary palace. In this manner, he escorted the golden image daily, with the procession following as before, until the day of the dispersal. Suddenly, a fire broke out on the great terrace, and smoke and flames began to rage at the gatehouse of the monastery. The King said: "I have exhausted the treasures of the nation to build this monastery in honor of my late father, so as to manifest his magnificent achievements; yet my lack of virtue has left me without protection, resulting in such a disaster—with such an omen of calamity, what is the use of living!" He then burned incense, made a respectful petition, and took a vow, saying: "By the grace of my past good deeds, I have become a king over all India; may the power of my merit extinguish this fire, and if there is no spiritual response, I shall lose my life from this moment forth!" He immediately exerted himself, leaped across the threshold of the gate, and as if by some force extinguishing it, the fire died out and the smoke vanished. The various kings witnessed this miracle and their awe and reverence increased. Afterward, the King’s expression remained unchanged and his speech was as usual; he asked the various kings: "Suddenly this disaster has occurred, burning and destroying the finished work; what is in your hearts, and what are your thoughts?" The various kings prostrated themselves, weeping in sorrow, and replied: "This magnificent achievement was hoped to be passed on to future generations; now that it is reduced to ashes in an instant, how can we not be grieved? Furthermore, the various heterodox scholars are rejoicing in their hearts!" The King said: "Viewing it from this perspective, what the Tathāgata said is true. The heterodox scholars and those of different doctrines cling to the view of permanence, whereas only our Great Master teaches impermanence. However, my giving and renunciation have already been completed, and my heart’s desire has been fulfilled. Encountering this destruction, I have come to know once again the truthful teaching of the Tathāgata; this is a great good, and there is no reason for deep sorrow." Thereupon, he followed the various kings to the east to ascend the great stūpa to view the surroundings. Just as he was descending the steps, a strange man suddenly appeared holding a blade to confront the King. The King, in that moment of peril, retreated up the steps, bent down to seize the man, and handed him over to his officials. At that time, the officials were in a state of panic and did not know how to advance to rescue him. The various kings all requested that this man be executed, but King Śīlāditya (戒日王) showed no sign of anger and merely ordered that he not be killed. The King personally asked, "What have I done to wrong you that you would commit such a violent and evil act?" He replied, "Your Majesty’s virtuous grace is impartial, and both within and without the realm, all are indebted to you. However, I am mad and foolish; without considering the grander scheme, I was moved by a single word from the heretics to become an assassin and plot this treasonous murder." The King asked, "For what reason did the heretics harbor such evil intentions?" He replied, "Your Majesty has assembled the various nations and emptied the treasury to provide offerings to the śramaṇas and to cast Buddha images, yet the heretics, who were summoned from afar, have not been granted an audience; they truly feel ashamed and humiliated. This led me, in my madness and folly, to dare to commit this violent deception." Thereupon, the King investigated the followers of the heretics. There were five hundred Brahmins, all of them men of high talent, who had assembled by royal command; envious of the śramaṇas receiving the King's respect and honors, they shot fire-arrows to burn the precious terrace, hoping that in the ensuing chaos as people rushed to put out the fire, they could kill the Great King. Having found no other opportunity, they hired this man to rush into the narrow passage and carry out the assassination. At that time, the various kings and ministers requested that the heretics be executed, but the King only punished the ringleaders, left the remaining partisans unpunished, and banished the five hundred Brahmins from the borders of India. Thereupon, he returned to the capital.  To the northwest of the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata spent seven days here preaching various wonderful Dharmas. Beside it are the traces of where the four past Buddhas sat and walked. There are also small stūpas containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata.  To the south of the preaching stūpa, overlooking the Ganges (殑伽河) river, there are three monasteries (saṃghārāma) sharing the same wall but having separate gates; the Buddha images are magnificent and beautiful, the monastic community is solemn and respectful, and they employ over a thousand households of pure servants (karmadāna). In the precious casket of the mūla-gandha-kuṭī (精舍) is a tooth of the Buddha, over an inch and a half long, of extraordinary luster and changing colors, shifting from morning to evening. People from near and far flock there, and the gentry and commoners gather in great numbers, daily numbering a hundred thousand, to perform acts of veneration. Because the overseers were troubled by the noise and confusion, they provisionally established a heavy tax, announcing to those near and far: "Those who wish to see the Buddha's tooth must pay a large sum of gold." Nevertheless, the number of those coming to pay homage remained vast, and they were happy to compete in their hearts to pay the gold tax. On every fast day, it is brought out and placed on a high seat; hundreds of thousands of people burn incense and scatter flowers, and although the flowers pile up, the tooth casket is never submerged.  To the left and right in front of the monasteries, there is a mūla-gandha-kuṭī, each over a hundred feet high, with stone foundations and brick chambers; the Buddha images within are adorned with various jewels, some cast in gold or silver, others smelted from brass (鍮石). In front of each of the two mūla-gandha-kuṭī is a small monastery. Not far to the southeast of the monastery, there is a large mūla-gandha-kuṭī (精舍) with stone foundations and brick chambers, over two hundred feet in height. Inside is a standing image of the Tathāgata, over thirty feet high, cast in brass (鍮石) and adorned with various wonderful jewels. On the stone walls surrounding the mūla-gandha-kuṭī, the deeds experienced by the Tathāgata while practicing the bodhisattva path are carved and painted, fully and exhaustively engraved. Not far to the south of the stone mūla-gandha-kuṭī, there is a temple to the Sun God (Āditya-deva). Not far to the south of that temple, there is a temple to Maheśvara (大自在天). Both are polished with blue stone and are equally exhaustive in their carvings; their scale and dimensions are the same as the Buddha’s mūla-gandha-kuṭī. Each has a thousand households assigned to sweep and clean them, with drums, music, and singing continuing day and night without cessation. Six or seven li to the southeast of the great city, on the south bank of the Gaṅgā (殑伽河), there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata spent six months here speaking on the impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and impurity of the body. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. There are also small stūpas containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata; when people are afflicted with illness, if they circumambulate them with utmost sincerity, they will certainly be cured and receive their blessings.

From here, traveling southeast for more than six hundred li and crossing the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) River, one arrives south at the country of Ayodhyā (阿踰陀國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Ayodhyā is more than five thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty li in circuit. The crops are abundant, and flowers and fruits are lush. The climate is temperate and pleasant, the customs are virtuous and compliant, and the people are fond of performing meritorious deeds and are diligent in studying the arts. There are more than one hundred monasteries and over three thousand monks, who study both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings with equal effort. There are ten Deva temples, and there are few followers of heterodox paths. Within the great city is an old monastery; this is where the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (伐蘇畔度) (in the language of Tang, *Shiqin* [世親]; formerly called *Posoupandou* [婆藪盤豆], translated as *Tianqin* [天親]; this is erroneous) spent several decades composing various treatises on the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Beside it are the old foundations of the hall where the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu lectured on the meaning of the teachings and expounded the Dharma for kings, talented scholars from the four quarters, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas. Four or five li to the north of the city, on the bank of the Gaṅgā River, within a large monastery, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka. It was here that the Tathāgata preached the various wonderful teachings for three months to an assembly of gods and men. Beside it is a stūpa marking the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. Four or five li to the west of the monastery, there is a stūpa containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. To the north of the hair and nail stūpa are the remains of a monastery where the Sautrāntika master Śrīlabdha (translated into Chinese as Shengshou, "Victorious Reception") formerly composed the Sautrāntika *Vibhāṣā Śāstra*. In a large mango grove five or six li to the southwest of the city, there is an old monastery, which is the place where the Bodhisattva Asaṅga (translated into Chinese as Wuzhuo, "Unattached") sought instruction and guided the common people. At night, the Bodhisattva Asaṅga would ascend to the heavenly palace and receive the *Yogācārabhūmi Śāstra*, the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra Śāstra*, the *Madhyāntavibhāga Śāstra*, and others from the Bodhisattva Maitreya, while by day he would lecture and proclaim these profound principles to the great assembly. More than one hundred paces to the northwest of the mango grove, there is a stūpa containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. The old foundation beside it is the place where the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu descended from the Tuṣita Heaven to see the Bodhisattva Asaṅga.  The Bodhisattva Asaṅga was a man from the country of Gandhāra (健馱邏國). One thousand years after the Buddha passed away, he was born with spiritual insight and keen faculties; following the tradition, he awakened to the Way. He left the household life to study in the Mahīśāsaka school, but after a short time, he turned his faith to the Mahāyāna. His younger brother, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, left the household life and received his training in the Sarvāstivāda school; he was widely learned and possessed a strong memory, having mastered the teachings and investigated their underlying mechanisms. Asaṅga’s disciple Buddhasimha (translated into Chinese as Shizijue, "Lion-Awakened") had a hidden practice that was unfathomable, and he was renowned for his high talent. These two or three sages would often say to one another: "In all our cultivation of practice, we vow to behold Maitreya. If one of us should pass away first, he must return to report and let the other know where he has gone." Afterward, Buddhasimha (Shizijue) passed away first, but for three years he sent no report. Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (Shiqin) also passed away shortly thereafter, and six months went by without any report. At that time, various heterodox practitioners all mocked them, believing that Bodhisattva Vasubandhu and Buddhasimha had been reborn in the evil realms and thus possessed no spiritual insight.  Later, in the first watch of the night, as Bodhisattva Asaṅga (Wuzhuo) was instructing his disciples in the methods of meditation, the lamp light suddenly dimmed and the air became brilliantly illuminated. A celestial being descended through the void, approached the courtyard, and paid homage to Asaṅga. Asaṅga asked, "Why have you come so late? What is your name now?"  He replied, "Upon departing this life, I was reborn in the inner assembly of Maitreya (Cishi) in the Tuṣita (Dushiduo) heaven, within a lotus flower. The moment the lotus opened, Maitreya praised me, saying, 'Welcome, Vast-Wisdom (Guanghui), welcome, Vast-Wisdom.' I had only just finished circling him once when I came to report."  Bodhisattva Asaṅga asked, "Where is Buddhasimha now?"  He replied, "When I was circling, I saw Buddhasimha in the outer assembly, indulging in sensual pleasures. He had no time to look at me, so how could he have come to report?"  Bodhisattva Asaṅga said, "That matter is finished. What is Maitreya’s appearance like, and what Dharma does he expound?"  He replied, "Maitreya’s physical marks and excellence are beyond the power of words to describe. The wonderful Dharma he expounds is not different in meaning from this [Dharma here], yet the Bodhisattva’s wonderful voice is clear, smooth, and harmonious; those who hear it forget their fatigue, and those who receive it are never satiated." More than forty li to the northwest of the old foundations of the lecture hall of Asaṅga (無著), one reaches an old monastery. It faces the Ganges (gaṅgā) River to the north and contains a brick stupa over a hundred feet high, marking the place where Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (世親) first conceived the aspiration for the Mahayana. When Bodhisattva Vasubandhu arrived here from northern India, Bodhisattva Asaṅga ordered his disciples to go and welcome him. Upon arriving at this monastery, they met and gathered. A disciple of Asaṅga stopped outside the window and, after the middle of the night, recited the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* (十地經). Having heard this, Vasubandhu became enlightened and filled with remorse, thinking, "This profound and wonderful Dharma is something I have never heard before. The fault of my slander originated from my tongue; since the tongue is the root of my offense, I should now cut it off." He immediately took up a sharp knife, intending to cut off his own tongue. Then he saw Asaṅga standing there, who told him, "The Mahayana teaching is the ultimate truth, praised by all Buddhas and revered by all sages. I wished to instruct you, and now you have realized it yourself. Since you have realized it at this time, what could be better? According to the holy teachings of the Buddhas, cutting off one's tongue is not repentance. In the past you used your tongue to revile the Mahayana, so now you should use your tongue to praise the Mahayana; to make amends and start anew is still a virtuous deed, but what benefit is there in remaining silent and speechless?" Having spoken these words, he suddenly disappeared. Vasubandhu followed the instruction and did not cut off his tongue. At dawn, he went to Asaṅga to consult him and receive the Mahayana. Thereupon, he refined his essence and pondered deeply, composing over a hundred Mahayana treatises, all of which were widely propagated and practiced.

From here, traveling east for more than three hundred li and crossing the Ganges River (gaṅgā), one arrives north at the kingdom of Ayamukha (阿耶穆佉國) (within the borders of Central India). The kingdom of Ayamukha is two thousand four or five hundred li in circuit. The capital city of the kingdom borders the Ganges River and is more than twenty li in circuit. Its climate and soil conditions are the same as those of the kingdom of Ayodhyā (阿踰陀國). The people are honest and simple in their customs, diligent in study, and fond of meritorious deeds. There are five monasteries with over one thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Sāmmitīya school of the Lesser Vehicle. There are more than ten Deva temples, where followers of various sects live together. Not far to the southeast of the city, on the bank of the Ganges River, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, over two hundred feet high, which is the place where the Tathāgata formerly preached the Dharma for three months. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. There is also a stūpa of blue stone containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. Beside it is a monastery with over two hundred monks; the Buddha images are adorned and majestic, as if he were still present. The towers and pavilions are magnificent, with unique structures rising high; this is where the master of treatises Buddhadeva (唐言覺使 - Original note: In the language of the Tang, "Messenger of Awakening") formerly composed the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* of the Sarvāstivāda school.

From here, traveling southeast for more than seven hundred li, crossing to the south of the Ganges (Gaṅgā) and the north of the Yamunā, one reaches the country of Prayāga (鉢邏耶伽國) (in the territory of Central India). The country of Prayāga is more than five thousand li in circuit. The great capital city of the country is situated at the confluence of the two rivers and is more than twenty li in circuit. The crops are abundant and lush, and the fruit trees are thick and spreading. The climate is harmonious and pleasant, and the customs are virtuous and compliant. The people are fond of learning the arts and believe in non-Buddhist paths. There are two monasteries with few monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). There are several hundred deva temples, and the followers of non-Buddhist paths are very numerous.  To the southwest of the great city, in a forest of Campaka (瞻博迦) flowers, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). Although the base has collapsed and sunk, it is still more than one hundred feet high. In the past, the Tathāgata subdued non-Buddhists at this place. Beside it are the stūpas of the hair and nails, as well as traces of his walking meditation. Beside the hair and nail stūpas is an old monastery; this is the place where the Bodhisattva Deva (提婆) (in the language of the Tang, "Heaven-Received") composed the *Śataśāstra-vaipulya* (廣百論) to frustrate the Lesser Vehicle and subdue the non-Buddhists.  Formerly, when the Bodhisattva Deva came to this monastery from South India, there was a non-Buddhist Brahmin in the city who was renowned for his lofty arguments and possessed unimpeded eloquence; he would scrutinize names to demand their reality and use counter-interrogations to exhaust his opponents' words. Knowing that Deva was widely versed in profound mysteries and wishing to blunt his edge, he followed the name and asked, "What is your name?" Deva replied, "My name is Heaven (Deva)." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who is Heaven?" Deva replied, "Me." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who am I?" Deva replied, "A dog." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who is the dog?" Deva replied, "You." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who are you?" Deva replied, "Heaven (Deva)." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who is Heaven?" Deva replied, "Me." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who am I?" Deva replied, "A dog." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who is the dog?" Deva replied, "You." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who are you?" Deva replied, "Heaven." Through this cycle, the non-Buddhist finally attained realization. From that time forward, he deeply respected his noble conduct.

From here, traveling southwest into a great forest, one encounters ferocious beasts and wild elephants that attack travelers in herds; unless one has a large party, it is difficult to pass through. After traveling more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Kauśāmbī (憍賞彌國) (formerly called the country of Kausāmbi, which is incorrect; it is within the borders of Central India). The country of Kauśāmbī is over six thousand *li* in circumference. The capital city is over thirty *li* in circumference. The soil is described as fertile, the land is rich in produce, and there is much *śāli* rice and abundant sugarcane. The climate is hot, and the customs of the people are fierce and impetuous. They are fond of learning and the arts, and they esteem and cultivate merit and goodness. There are more than ten *saṃghārāmas*, which are dilapidated and overgrown, with over three hundred monks who study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle. There are more than fifty *deva* temples, and the followers of non-Buddhist paths are very numerous. Within the old palace in the city, there is a large *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) over sixty feet high, housing a sandalwood Buddha image with a stone canopy suspended above it, which was made by King Udayana (唐言出愛; formerly inaccurately called King Youtian). Miraculous signs appear from time to time, and divine light shines forth occasionally. Kings of various countries, relying on their strength, have wished to move it, but although they brought many people, none could shift it. Consequently, they have sought to make offerings to it, all claiming to have obtained the true image; when speaking of its origin and history, it is indeed this very image. Initially, after the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment, he ascended to the heavenly palace to preach the Dharma for his mother, and for three months he did not return. The king, longing for him, wished to have his likeness made. He then requested the Venerable Maudgalyāyana to use his supernatural powers to transport an artisan to the heavenly palace to personally observe the Buddha's marvelous features and carve an image from sandalwood. When the Tathāgata returned from the heavenly palace, the sandalwood image (mūla-gandha-kuṭī) rose to greet the World-Honored One, who consoled it, saying: "Have you been weary from the work of converting and guiding others? You are truly the hope for guiding those in the final age." More than one hundred paces to the east of the monastery are the sites containing the traces of where the four past Buddhas sat and walked. Not far to the side are a well and a bathhouse used by the Tathāgata; the well still provides water for drawing, but the bathhouse has fallen into ruin.

In the southeast corner of the city are the remaining foundations of an old residence, which was the former home of the elder Ghoṣila (formerly transcribed as Jushiluo, which is incorrect). Within it are a Buddhist temple (mūla-gandha-kuṭī) and a stupa containing hair and nail relics. There are also old foundations that were the bathroom of the Tathāgata. Not far to the southeast of the city is an old monastery, which was the former garden of the elder Ghoṣila. Within it is a stupa built by King Aśoka, over two hundred feet high. The Tathāgata preached the Dharma here for several years. Beside it are the seats of the four past Buddhas and the sites of their walking meditation, as well as another stupa containing the hair and nail relics of the Tathāgata. In a brick chamber on an upper story to the southeast of the monastery, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu once resided and composed the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* to refute the Lesser Vehicle and challenge various non-Buddhist schools. In an Āmra (mango) grove to the east of the monastery are old foundations where the Bodhisattva Asaṅga composed the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-śāstra*. Eight or nine *li* to the southwest of the city is the stone cavern of a poisonous dragon. In the past, the Tathāgata subdued this poisonous dragon and left his shadow within it; although this is recorded in the chronicles, it cannot be seen today. Beside it is a stupa built by King Aśoka, over two hundred feet high. Nearby are the sites of the Tathāgata’s walking meditation and a stupa containing his hair and nail relics; those suffering from illnesses who pray there are often healed. When the Dharma of Śākyamuni reaches its end, this country will be the last to remain; therefore, from the sovereign above down to the common people, all who enter the borders of this country naturally feel a sense of sorrow, and there is no one who does not weep and return home with sighs of lamentation.

Traveling northward from here for one hundred and seventy or eighty li, one arrives at the country of Viśākhā (鞞索迦國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Viśākhā is over four thousand li in circuit. The capital city is sixteen li in circuit. The crops are abundant, and flowers and fruits are plentiful. The climate is temperate and pleasant, and the customs are honest and simple. The people are fond of learning without fatigue and are unswerving in their pursuit of merit. There are more than twenty saṃghārāmas and over three thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Sāṃmitīya school of the Lesser Vehicle. There are more than fifty deva temples, and there are many followers of non-Buddhist paths. To the left of the road south of the city, there is a large saṃghārāma. In the past, the Arhat Devaśarman (提婆設摩) composed the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra* (識身論) here, which argues that there is no self or person; the Arhat Gopa (瞿波) composed the *Śrī-śāstra-sāra* (聖教要實論), which argues that there is a self and a person. Because of this difference in doctrinal adherence, they engaged in deep debate. Furthermore, it was here that the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla (護法) defeated one hundred masters of the Lesser Vehicle in seven days. Beside the saṃghārāma is a stūpa, over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka. In the past, the Tathāgata spent six years here preaching the Dharma and guiding the people. Beside the place where he preached is a marvelous tree, six or seven feet high; as spring and autumn succeed one another, it remains constant, neither increasing nor decreasing. It is said that the Tathāgata once cleaned his teeth here and discarded the twig, which then took root and has remained lush to this day. Various people of wrong views and followers of non-Buddhist paths have vied to cut it down, but it immediately grows back as it was before. Not far from there is the site of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. There is also a stūpa containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. The spiritual foundations are connected at the corners, and the woods and ponds reflect one another. Traveling northeast from here for more than five hundred li, one arrives at the country of Śrāvastī (室羅伐悉底國) (formerly called Shewei, which is an error; it is within the borders of Central India).

The country of Śrāvastī (室羅伐悉底國) is over 6,000 li in circuit. The capital city is desolate and ruined, and its boundaries are not clearly defined. The old foundations of the palace city are over 20 li in circuit; although it is largely ruined and overgrown, there are still inhabitants. The grain crops are abundant, and the climate is temperate. The customs are honest and simple, and the people are devoted to learning and fond of merit. There are several hundred monasteries, most of which are in ruins, and the number of monks is small; they study the Sammatiya (正量部) school. There are one hundred deva temples, and there are many followers of non-Buddhist paths.  This was the capital city governed by King Prasenajit (鉢邏犀那恃多王; in Chinese, Shengjun [Victorious Army]; the old term, Posinì, is a corruption and abbreviation) during the time the Tathāgata was in the world. Within the old palace city, there are old foundations, which are the remaining traces of the palace of King Prasenajit. Not far to the east, there is an old foundation upon which a small stupa is built; this was the Great Dharma Hall that King Prasenajit formerly built for the Tathāgata. Not far from the side of the Dharma Hall, there is a stupa on old foundations; this is the nunnery of the Buddha’s maternal aunt, Prajāpatī (鉢邏闍鉢底; in Chinese, Shengzhu [Lord of Life]; the old term, Bojeboti, is a corruption), which was built by King Prasenajit. To the east of this is a stupa, which is the former residence of Sudatta (蘇達多; in Chinese, Shanshi [Well-Bestowing]; the old term, Xuda, is a corruption). Beside the residence of the elder Sudatta, there is a large stupa; this is the place where Aṅgulimāla (鴦窶利摩羅; in Chinese, Zhiman [Finger-Garland]; the old term, Yangjumolu, is a corruption) abandoned his evil ways. Aṅgulimāla was a violent man of Śrāvastī. He harmed living beings and committed atrocities in the city and the country, killing people to take their fingers and wearing them on his head as a garland. He was about to kill his mother to complete the count of his fingers. The World-honored One, moved by compassion, set out to guide and transform him. Seeing the World-honored One from afar, he secretly rejoiced and said, "I am now certain to be reborn in heaven. My former teacher gave me instructions, and his legacy is here: by killing a Buddha and killing one's mother, one shall be reborn in the Brahmā heaven." He said to his mother, "Old lady, stay here for now; I must first kill that great śramaṇa." He immediately took up his sword and went to intercept the World-honored One. The Tathāgata then retreated at a slow pace, yet the wicked Aṅgulimāla could not catch up even though he ran fast. The World-honored One said to him, "Why do you persist in your base intentions, abandoning the root of goodness and stirring up the source of evil?" At that time, Aṅgulimāla heard this instruction and realized that his actions were wrong; he then took refuge, sought to enter the Dharma, practiced diligently without slackening, and attained the fruit of an Arhat.

Five or six *li* south of the city is the Jetavana (逝多林; in the language of the Tang, "Victory Grove"; the old term "Jeta" is a corruption), which is the Anāthapiṇḍada-ārāma (給孤獨園). The minister Sudatta (善施) of King Prasenajit (勝軍王) built a *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) for the Buddha; it was formerly a monastery, but now it lies in ruins. To the left and right of the east gate stand stone pillars over seventy feet high; the left pillar is topped with a carved wheel, and the right pillar is surmounted by the figure of a bull, both of which were erected by King Aśoka (無憂王). The buildings have collapsed, leaving only the old foundations, save for a single brick chamber that stands alone and intact, containing an image of the Buddha. Formerly, after the Tathāgata had ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother, King Prasenajit heard that King Udayana (出愛王) had carved a sandalwood image of the Buddha, and he thereupon had this image made. The Elder Sudatta was benevolent and intelligent; he accumulated wealth only to distribute it, rescuing the needy, relieving the poor, and showing compassion to the orphaned and the aged. People of the time praised his virtues and called him Anāthapiṇḍada ("the Giver to the Orphaned and Solitary"). Having heard of the Buddha’s merits, he developed a deep sense of reverence and wished to build a *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* and invite the Buddha to descend. The World-Honored One commanded Śāriputra to accompany him to survey the land, and they found that only the garden of Prince Jeta (逝多太子) was high and dry. He immediately went to the Prince and explained his intentions in full. The Prince jokingly said, "If you cover the ground with gold, I will sell it." Upon hearing this, Sudatta’s heart was filled with joy; he immediately brought out his hidden gold and covered the ground as he had said. There was a small portion left uncovered, and the Prince requested to keep it, saying, "The Buddha is truly a fertile field; it is fitting to plant good seeds there." He then built the *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* on the vacant land. The World-Honored One went there and said to Ānanda, "The garden ground was purchased by Sudatta (善施), and the trees were donated by Jeta (逝多); the two men were of one mind, and thus they jointly established this meritorious work. From now on, this place shall be called the Jetavana-anāthapiṇḍikārāma (逝多林給孤獨園)."  To the northeast of the Jetavana-anāthapiṇḍikārāma is a stūpa, which is the place where the Tathāgata washed a sick bhikṣu. Formerly, when the Tathāgata was in the world, there was a sick bhikṣu who was suffering and living alone. The World-Honored One saw him and asked, "What is your suffering? Why do you live alone?" He replied, "I am by nature lazy and cannot endure nursing the sick; therefore, I am now afflicted with illness, and there is no one to look after me." At that time, the Tathāgata felt compassion and said to him, "Good man, I will now nurse you." He stroked him with his hand, and his illness and suffering were all healed. He helped him out of the room, changed his bedding, personally washed him, and put new clothes on him. The Buddha said to the bhikṣu, "You should be diligent and exert yourself." Hearing this instruction, he felt gratitude, and his heart was joyful and his body at ease.  To the northwest of the Jetavana-anāthapiṇḍikārāma is a small stūpa, which is the place where Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅) exercised his supernatural power to lift Śāriputra’s (舍利子) robe and belt, but could not move them. Formerly, when the Buddha was at Lake Anavatapta (無熱惱池), humans and devas had all gathered, but only Śāriputra did not arrive at the assembly in time. The Buddha ordered Maudgalyāyana to go and summon him to join the gathering. Maudgalyāyana accepted the command and went; Śāriputra was mending his dharma-robe. Maudgalyāyana said, "The World-Honored One is now at Lake Anavatapta and has ordered me to summon you." Śāriputra (舍利子) said, "Wait a moment; I must finish mending this, and then I will go with you." Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅) said, "If you do not go quickly, I shall use my supernatural power to lift your stone chamber and take it to the great assembly." Śāriputra then untied his robe and belt, placed them on the ground, and said, "If you can lift this belt, my body might move." At that time, Maudgalyāyana exerted his great supernatural power, but he could not lift the belt, and the earth shook because of it. He then used his supernatural foot-power to return to the place of the Buddha, where he saw that Śāriputra was already seated in the assembly. Maudgalyāyana bowed his head and sighed, saying, "Only now do I know that the power of supernatural abilities is not equal to the power of wisdom."  Not far from the stupa of the belt, there is a well. When the Tathāgata (如來) was in the world, water was drawn from it for the Buddha’s use. Beside it is a stupa built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which contains relics of the Tathāgata. The sites of his walking meditation and the places where he preached the Dharma are all marked with signs and have stupas built upon them. Dark spirits guard and protect them, and miraculous signs appear from time to time; sometimes heavenly music is played, and sometimes divine incense is smelled. The auspicious omens of these blessings are difficult to describe in full.  Not far behind the monastery is the place where the non-Buddhist ascetics (外道梵志) murdered a courtesan to slander the Buddha. The Tathāgata possesses the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the omniscience of all modes; he is revered by humans and devas, and honored by sages and worthies. At that time, the various non-Buddhists consulted together, saying, "We should employ deceit and slander him in the midst of the assembly." They then enticed and hired a courtesan, pretending she was coming to listen to the Dharma, and once this was known to the assembly, they secretly murdered her, buried her corpse beside a tree, and complained to the king, claiming injury. The king ordered a search, and her body was found in the Jetavana (逝多園). At that time, the non-Buddhists loudly proclaimed: "The great śramaṇa Gautama (喬答摩) always praises precepts and patience; now he has had illicit relations with this woman and killed her to silence her. Having committed both lechery and murder, where are his precepts and where is his patience?" The devas in the sky responded in unison, saying: "The wicked non-Buddhists have fabricated this slander."  More than one hundred paces to the east of the monastery is a large, deep pit; this is the place where Devadatta (提婆達多), intending to harm the Buddha with poison, fell alive into hell. Devadatta (in Chinese, "Heaven-bestowed") was the son of King Droṇodana (斛飯王). He practiced diligently for twelve years and had already memorized the eighty thousand sections of the Dharma-store. Later, for the sake of profit, he sought to learn supernatural powers and associated with evil friends, consulting with them: "My physical marks are thirty; they are not much less than the Buddha's. With the great assembly surrounding me, how am I different from the Tathāgata?" Having thought this, he proceeded to cause a schism in the Sangha. Śāriputra (舍利子) and Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子), following the Buddha’s instructions and relying on the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, preached and admonished them, and the Sangha was reconciled. Devadatta did not abandon his evil heart; he placed a deadly poison under his fingernails, intending to harm the Buddha while performing an act of homage. As he was carrying out this plot, coming from afar and arriving at this spot, the earth suddenly split open, and he fell alive into hell. To the south of this, there is another large pit where the Bhikṣu Kokālika (瞿伽梨) fell alive into hell for slandering the Tathāgata. More than eight hundred paces to the south of the pit of Kokālika, there is a large, deep pit, which is the place where the Brahmin woman Ciñcā (戰遮) fell alive into hell for slandering the Tathāgata. When the Buddha was preaching the essentials of the Dharma to humans and devas, a disciple of an external path saw from afar the great assembly paying homage to the World-Honored One and thought to herself, "I must humiliate Gautama (喬答摩) today and ruin his good reputation, so that my teacher alone may possess a fragrant name." She then concealed a wooden basin tied to her body and went to the Jetavana (給孤獨園), where she cried out in a loud voice amidst the great assembly, "This preacher has had illicit relations with me, and the child in my womb is of the Śākya clan." Those of evil views all believed it to be true, while those who were steadfast knew it to be a slander. At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra (天帝釋), wishing to dispel the doubt, transformed into a white mouse and gnawed through the cord holding the basin. The sound of the cord snapping startled the great assembly, and all who saw and heard it felt their joy increase. One person in the assembly stood up, held the wooden basin, and showed it to the woman, saying, "Is this your child?" At that moment, the earth split open of its own accord, and she fell into it, her whole body sinking into the Avīci (無間) hell to suffer the full consequences of her actions. These three pits are bottomless; during the heavy rains of autumn and summer, when ditches and pools overflow, no water ever remains in these deep hollows.
