When eloquence is granted by demons, one cannot speak face-to-face with others, and once their words are heard, they can never be repeated. I shall now go there to observe his conduct."  He then went to the Brahman’s hut and said to him, "I have long admired your great virtue. I hope you will be willing to raise the curtain, as I dare to express a long-held wish." Yet the Brahman remained arrogant and haughty, responding from behind the lowered curtain and refusing to speak face-to-face. Aśvaghoṣa (馬鳴) knew in his heart that it was a demon, yet he was very confident. After taking his leave and withdrawing, he said to the people, "I have already understood it; I shall certainly defeat him." He then went to inform the king, "I only hope you will grant me permission to engage that householder in a rigorous debate." Hearing this, the king was alarmed and said, "What kind of person is this! If one has not realized the three knowledges (三明) and possesses the six supernatural powers (六通), how can one debate with him?" The king ordered his carriage to attend in person to observe the debate in detail. At that time, Aśvaghoṣa discussed the subtle words of the Tripitaka (三藏) and expounded the great principles of the five sciences (五明); his marvelous eloquence was unrestrained, and his lofty arguments were profound and far-reaching. After the Brahman had finished stating his case, Aśvaghoṣa spoke again, saying, "You have missed the gist of my argument; you should state it again." At that moment, the Brahman remained silent and kept his mouth shut. Aśvaghoṣa scolded him, saying, "Why do you not resolve the difficulty? The demon you serve should quickly provide you with words!" He then swiftly lifted the curtain to look at and observe the strange creature. The Brahman was terrified and said, "Stop! Stop!" Aśvaghoṣa withdrew and said, "This fellow’s reputation has collapsed this morning; a false name does not last long—this is what is meant by that." The king said, "If not for a man of great virtue, who could discern the heterodox path? Such wisdom in knowing men is unparalleled in the past and future; the country has established laws, and we should honor such genuine substance."

More than thirty *li* to the northwest of the mountain, in a mountain recess, there is a monastery. It rests against a ridge with a lofty foundation, and its pavilions stand upon sparse cliffs. There are more than fifty monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. This is the place where the Bodhisattva Guṇamati (in the language of the Tang, "Virtue-Wisdom") defeated a non-Buddhist.  Formerly, there was a non-Buddhist in this mountain named Mādhava, who took the Sāṃkhya (僧佉) school as his ancestor and practiced its path. His learning exhausted both internal and external doctrines, his words reached the limits of emptiness and existence, his reputation stood above his contemporaries, and his virtue was esteemed at the time. The king cherished and respected him, calling him the "treasure of the country," and the ministers and commoners revered him, all calling him their "family teacher." Scholars from neighboring countries, hearing of his influence and admiring his virtue, ranked him among the foremost, truly a man of broad attainment. He was supported by the income of two cities, which surrounded his residence as a fief.  At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇamati of South India was quick-witted from his youth; he excelled early in the subtle and profound, his learning mastered the Tripiṭaka, and his reasoning exhausted the Four Noble Truths. Hearing that Mādhava’s theories were extremely profound and subtle, he harbored the intent to blunt his sharp edge. He ordered a disciple to write a letter saying: "I respectfully inquire whether Mādhava is well and at peace. You should forget your weariness and toil, and diligently study your old learning; three years from now, I shall destroy your fine reputation."  In the second and third years, he sent messengers to notify him in this manner. When he was about to set out, he wrote another letter saying: "The time limit has expired; how is your study progressing? I am arriving now; you should be aware of this." Mādhava was filled with great fear and warned his disciples and the inhabitants of his town: "From this day forward, you must not provide lodging to any śramaṇas or followers of heterodox paths; spread this word among yourselves and do not violate this command." At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇamati (德慧) came carrying his staff and arrived at the town of Mādhava. The people kept their agreement, and no one would offer him lodging. The Brahmins further reviled him, saying, "With your shaven head and strange robes, how are you different from a non-human? You should leave quickly; do not stay here!" The Bodhisattva Guṇamati, wishing to defeat the heterodox teachings and hoping to lodge in the town, spoke with a compassionate heart and humble words, saying, "You all practice the pure conduct of worldly truth, while I practice the pure conduct of the ultimate truth; since our pure conduct is the same, why do you reject me?" The Brahmins would not speak to him, but only sought to drive him away. They drove him out of the town and into a great forest. In the forest, packs of fierce beasts acted with violence. A man of pure faith, fearing he might be harmed by the beasts, bound together a torch and took up a staff, saying to the Bodhisattva, "There is a Bodhisattva Guṇamati of South India whose reputation has spread far and wide, and who intends to come here for a debate; therefore, the lord of this town, fearing the loss of his good name, has strictly decreed that no śramaṇa be allowed to stay. Fearing you might be harmed by the creatures, I have come to assist you. Go now and be at peace; have no other worries." Guṇamati said, "I must tell you, pure believer, that I am Guṇamati." Having heard this, the pure believer showed even deeper respect and said to Guṇamati, "Since it is as you say, you should depart quickly." He then left the deep forest and rested in an empty marsh. The pure believer lit a fire and held his bow, patrolling around him; when the night had ended, he said to Guṇamati, "You may go now, for I fear people may hear of this and come to harm you." Guṇamati thanked him, saying, "I shall not forget your kindness." Thereupon he departed. Arriving at the royal palace, he said to the gatekeeper, "There is a śramaṇa who has come from afar; he requests the king's gracious permission to debate with Mādhava (摩沓婆)." Hearing this, the king was surprised and said, "This is a delusional man." He immediately ordered an envoy to go to Mādhava’s residence to proclaim the royal decree, saying, "An extraordinary śramaṇa has come seeking a debate; the debate hall has now been cleansed and prepared, and an announcement has been sent out far and near; we await your arrival and hope you will grace us with your presence." Mādhava asked the king's envoy, "Is it not the Śāstra Master Guṇamati (德慧) of South India?" The envoy replied, "It is." Upon hearing this, Mādhava was very displeased, but as the matter was difficult to decline, he proceeded to the debate hall. The king, ministers, scholars, commoners, and noble families all gathered to listen to the profound discourse. Guṇamati first established his thesis, and by the time the sun had set, Mādhava excused himself on the grounds of his advanced age and the dullness of his wit in responding quickly, requesting to return home to reflect so that he might respond to the challenge later. Every point was met with a request to return home, and when he ascended the seat the next morning, he ultimately offered no counter-arguments. On the sixth day, he vomited blood and died. As he was about to expire, he looked at his wife and commanded, "You possess great talent; do not forget this shame!" After Mādhava died, his death was concealed and not announced; his wife changed into his fine, colorful robes and came to the debate hall. The crowd broke into a hubbub, saying to one another, "Mādhava is conceited about his own talent and is ashamed to face Guṇamati, so he has sent his wife instead; the difference in their caliber is now clear." Guṇamati Bodhisattva (德慧菩薩) said to his wife, "The one who could control you, I have already subdued." Mādhava’s wife, realizing the difficulty, withdrew. The King asked, "What was that secret conversation, that she became silent?" Guṇamati replied, "Alas, Mādhava is dead! His wife intended to come and debate with me." The King asked, "How did you know this? I wish you would explain it to me." Guṇamati said, "When his wife came, her face bore the look of mourning and her voice was filled with grief and resentment; therefore, I knew that Mādhava was dead. 'The one who could control you' referred to her husband." The King ordered an envoy to go and observe, and it was indeed as discussed. The King then apologized, saying, "The Buddha-Dharma is profound and mysterious; brilliant sages follow in succession. By practicing the Way through non-action, all sentient beings are moistened by its transformation. According to the ancient laws of the state, there is a constant practice of praising virtue." Guṇamati said, "Though I am ignorant, I embody the Way and dwell in purity. If one maintains integrity and seeks to benefit others, then to promote and guide them, one must first crush their arrogance. As for using expedient means to gather and transform them, now is the time. I only wish that Your Majesty would assign the descendants of the households in Mādhava’s fief to serve the monastery (saṃghārāma) for a thousand generations, so as to leave a warning for future ages and spread this beauty boundlessly. May those with pure faith who provide protection have their merit extended throughout the world, and may their food and provisions be the same as the monks, so as to encourage the pure-hearted and praise profound virtue." Thereupon, this monastery was built to commemorate this remarkable event. Initially, after Mādhava was defeated in debate, more than ten pure-practitioners (brahmacārins) fled to a neighboring country to escape the disaster. They reported the humiliation to various heretics (tīrthikas) and recruited talented individuals to come and wash away their previous shame. Since the king esteemed and respected Guṇamati (德慧), he went in person to request him, saying: "Now these heretics, overestimating their own strength, have formed a clique and dared to sound the drum of debate; I only wish that the Great Master would crush these heterodox sects." Guṇamati said: "It is appropriate to assemble the debaters." Thereupon, the heretical scholars comforted one another with joy, saying: "Today, we are certain to be victorious over him." When the heretics began to expound their doctrines, Guṇamati Bodhisattva said: "These heretics have fled from afar to take refuge here; according to the king's prior decree, they are all outcasts, so how can I engage in a debate with them?" Guṇamati had a seat-carrier (a servant who carried his portable seat) who had long listened to his debates and was quite familiar with the subtle meanings; he stood by his side, listening to their lofty discourse. Guṇamati patted his seat and said: "Seat, you may debate with them." The assembly was entirely shocked and found his command strange. At that time, the seat-carrier immediately launched his challenge; profound meanings gushed forth like a spring, and his clear eloquence responded to every point. After three rounds, the heretics lost their tenets; their sharpness was severely blunted, and their wings were broken. Ever since they were defeated in debate, they were established as the households of the monastery (saṃghārāma).

More than twenty *li* southwest of the Guṇamati (德慧) monastery, one arrives at the Vyāsa (孤山) mountain. There is a monastery here that was built by the master Śīlabhadra (唐言戒賢; Skt. Śīlabhadra) after he won a debate; he donated his village to establish it. A single precipitous peak rises up like a stūpa, and within it are placed relics of the Buddha. The master was of the royal lineage of the country of Samataṭa (三摩呾吒國) and of the Brāhmaṇa caste. In his youth, he was fond of learning and possessed a noble character; he traveled throughout the various regions of India, inquiring after the wise and sagacious. Upon arriving at the Nālandā (那爛陀) monastery in this country, he met the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla (護法), and upon hearing the Dharma, he developed faith and understanding. He requested to don the dyed robes, consulted him on the ultimate goal, and asked about the path to liberation. Having exhausted the highest truths and investigated the subtle words, his fame dominated the era and his reputation was high in foreign lands.  In South India, there was a non-Buddhist who explored the obscure and searched for the hidden, exhausting the profound and penetrating the subtle. Hearing of Dharmapāla’s high fame, he conceived deep arrogance and jealousy, and undeterred by mountains or rivers, he beat the drum to demand a debate, saying: "I am a man of South India. I have heard that there is a great master of debate within this kingdom; although I am not clever, I wish to discuss matters with him in detail." The king said: "It is so; it is truly as you say." He then ordered an envoy to invite Dharmapāla, saying: "A non-Buddhist from South India has come from a distance of a thousand *li* to seek a debate; I only hope you will condescend to attend the assembly at the debate ground." Having heard this, Dharmapāla gathered his robes and prepared to go. His disciple Śīlabhadra, who was the most outstanding among the younger generation, stepped forward and requested: "Why must you go so hastily?" Dharmapāla (護法) said: "Since the Sun of Wisdom has withdrawn its light and the Lamp of the Dharma has ceased its illumination, heretics have gathered like ants and heterodox schools have swarmed like wasps; therefore, I now intend to demolish their arguments." Śīlabhadra (戒賢) said: "I have respectfully heard your arguments; I dare to demolish the heterodox path." Dharmapāla knew that he was a man of outstanding talent and therefore granted his consent. At that time, Śīlabhadra was just thirty years old, and the assembly slighted his youth, fearing he would be unable to shoulder the task alone. Dharmapāla, knowing the dissatisfaction of the assembly, explained to them: "What is valued is brilliance and wisdom, not one's age; from what I see now, he is certain to defeat them."  When the day of the debate arrived, people from far and near flocked to the scene, and both young and old gathered together. The heretic expounded his great principles, exhausting their profound subtleties; Śīlabhadra followed reason to demand the truth, reaching the depths of the abstruse. The heretic’s arguments were exhausted, and he retreated in shame. The king, wishing to reward his virtue, bestowed this city upon him. The Master of Shastras declined, saying: "A man in dyed robes finds his support in contentment and maintains himself in purity; what use has he for a city?" The king said: "The Dharma King has hidden his traces and the Boat of Wisdom has sunk; if there is no recognition, there is nothing to encourage future students. For the sake of propagating the True Dharma, I hope you will compassionately accept it." The Master of Shastras, unable to refuse, accepted the city. He then built a monastery (saṃghārāma), exhausting all the rules of construction, and dedicated the households of the city to provide for its maintenance.

Five or six *li* to the southwest of the city, one arrives at Mount Gayā (伽耶山; Gayā-śīrṣa). The ravines and valleys are dark and deep, and the peaks and cliffs are precipitous. In the customs of the country of India, it is commonly called the Spirit Mountain (靈山). Since ancient times, monarchs who have governed the universe and inherited the succession, whose civilizing influence has reached distant peoples, and whose virtues have surpassed those of previous generations, have all ascended this mountain to perform the *feng* sacrifice and announce their successes. On the summit of the mountain is a stone *stūpa* over one hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). Its spiritual efficacy is secretly felt, and divine light occasionally illuminates it; in the past, the Tathāgata expounded the *Ratnamegha* (寶雲) and other sutras here. To the southeast of Mount Gayā is a *stūpa* that marks the native village of Kāśyapa. To its south are two *stūpas*, which are the places where Gayā-Kāśyapa and Nadī-Kāśyapa (formerly called Nadi-Kāśyapa, which is an error; as for all the Kāśyapas, the omission of the 'pa' character is a simplification) practiced fire worship.

East of the place where Gayā-Kāśyapa worshiped fire, crossing a great river, one reaches the mountain of Prāgbodhi (鉢羅笈菩提山; in the language of Tang, this means "Mountain Prior to Enlightenment"; as the Tathāgata was about to realize perfect enlightenment, he first ascended this mountain, hence it is called "Prior to Enlightenment"). The Tathāgata had sought diligently for six years without attaining perfect enlightenment; he later abandoned austerities and accepted milk gruel. Traveling from the northeast, he gazed upon this mountain and, cherishing its secluded tranquility, desired to realize perfect enlightenment here. He ascended from the northeast ridge to the summit, whereupon the earth quaked and the mountain shook. The mountain god was terrified and told the Bodhisattva, "This mountain is not a blessed place for attaining perfect enlightenment. If you remain here to enter the diamond-like concentration, the earth will quake and collapse, and the mountain will overturn." The Bodhisattva descended from the southwest; halfway down the mountain cliff, with its back to the crags and facing a stream, there was a large stone chamber. The Bodhisattva entered it and sat down cross-legged, whereupon the earth quaked again and the mountain shook once more. At that time, the Pure Abode gods (Śuddhāvāsa-deva) called out from the sky, "This is not the place where the Tathāgata will attain perfect enlightenment. Fourteen or fifteen li to the southwest of here, not far from the place of your austerities, there is a Pippala tree (卑鉢羅樹) with a Diamond Throne beneath it; all Buddhas of the past and future attain perfect enlightenment upon this seat, so we pray you proceed there." Just as the Bodhisattva rose, the dragon of the chamber said, "This chamber is pure and excellent, suitable for realizing the holy state; I only pray that out of compassion, you will not abandon it." The Bodhisattva, knowing that this was not the place to realize enlightenment, in order to fulfill the dragon’s wish, left his shadow behind and departed (Original note: The shadow was seen in former days by both the wise and the ignorant; down to the present time, some may still see it). The devas led the way, proceeding to the Mahā-bodhi tree (菩提樹). When King Aśoka (無憂王) rose to power, he erected markers and built stūpas at every spot where the Bodhisattva had ascended or descended the mountain; although these monuments differ in size, their spiritual manifestations are equally remarkable, with celestial flowers sometimes raining from the sky or light illuminating the deep valleys. Every year on the day the summer retreat ends, monks and laypeople from different regions climb the mountain to present offerings, staying for two nights before returning.

Traveling fourteen or fifteen *li* southwest from the mountain of the Previous Enlightenment (Pūrvaśilā), one arrives at the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹). A surrounding wall of piled bricks is high, steep, and secure. It is long from east to west and narrow from north to south, measuring over five hundred paces in circumference. Rare trees and famous flowers interweave their shade and shadows; fine sand and exotic grasses form a lush, spreading carpet. The main gate opens to the east, facing the Nairañjanā River; the south gate connects to a large flower pond; the west side is narrow and secure; and the north gate leads to a great monastery. Within the enclosure, sacred sites are adjacent to one another, some being stūpas and others being *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍). Kings, ministers, and noble families from all the countries of Jambudvīpa, reverently upholding the Buddha’s legacy, have built them as memorials.  In the center of the Mahā-bodhi enclosure is the Vajra Seat (金剛座). Long ago, when the Bhadrakalpa was first formed, it arose together with the great earth. It is situated in the center of the three-thousand great chiliocosm, reaching down to the golden wheel and up to the surface of the ground. It is composed of diamond and measures over a hundred paces in circumference. Because the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa sit upon it to enter the diamond samādhi, it is called the Vajra Seat. It is the place where the holy path is realized, also called the *bodhimaṇḍa* (道場). When the great earth shakes, this place alone does not tremble or sway. For this reason, when the Tathāgata was about to realize perfect enlightenment, he traversed these four corners, and the ground shook everywhere; but when he later arrived at this spot, it was peaceful and did not tilt. Since entering the final age, the True Dharma has gradually faded, and it has become covered with sand and earth, no longer to be seen. After the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*, kings of various countries, having heard of the dimensions of the Vajra Seat as described by the Buddha, used two statues of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva to mark the northern and southern boundaries, facing toward the east. I have heard from the elders: "When the bodies of these Bodhisattva statues sink and disappear, the Buddha-Dharma will come to an end." Today, the Bodhisattva at the southern corner has sunk past its chest. The Mahā-bodhi tree (菩提樹) on the Vajra Seat is the pippala tree. When the Buddha was in the world, it was several hundred feet high; though it has been repeatedly cut down, it is still four or five zhang high. The Buddha sat beneath it and attained Perfect Enlightenment, and for this reason, it is called the Bodhi tree. Its trunk is yellowish-white, and its branches and leaves are emerald green; they do not wither in winter or summer, and their luster remains unchanged. Every year on the day of the Tathāgata’s *nirvāṇa*, the leaves all wither and fall, but after a short while, they return to their former state. On that day, the monarchs of various countries, along with monks and laypeople of different traditions, numbering in the tens of millions, gather without being summoned to water and wash the tree with scented water and milk; they then play music, arrange fragrant flowers, and keep lamps and torches burning day and night, vying with one another to present offerings.  After the Tathāgata’s *nirvāṇa*, when King Aśoka (無憂王) first ascended the throne, he believed in heretical doctrines and destroyed the sacred sites left by the Buddha, mobilizing troops and coming in person to cut the tree down. The roots, stems, branches, and leaves were chopped into small pieces and piled up several dozen paces to the west, where fire-worshiping Brahmins were ordered to burn them as a sacrifice to heaven; yet before the smoke and flames had subsided, two trees suddenly grew out from the midst of the fierce fire with luxuriant, verdant leaves, and were thus called the "Ash Bodhi Trees." King Aśoka witnessed this miracle and repented; he watered the remaining roots with scented milk, and by the time dawn approached, the tree had grown back as it was before. The king witnessed this miracle and was deeply overjoyed; he personally performed offerings, finding such delight that he forgot to return home. The queen, who had long believed in heretical teachings, secretly dispatched messengers after midnight to cut down the tree again. When King Aśoka (無憂王) went to pay his respects at dawn, he saw only a stump; deeply moved by grief, he prayed with utmost sincerity and irrigated it with fragrant milk, and within a few days it grew back to life. The king, deeply respecting this marvel, built a stone wall around it over ten feet high, which can still be seen today.  Recently, King Śaśāṅka (設賞迦王), a believer in heretical teachings who slandered and envied the Buddha-dharma, destroyed monasteries and cut down the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree; he dug down to the springs but could not exhaust the roots, so he set it on fire and soaked it with sugarcane juice, wishing to rot it and utterly destroy any remaining sprouts. Several months later, King Pūrṇavarman (補剌拏伐摩王; in Tang language, "Full Armor" [滿胄]) of the kingdom of Magadha (摩揭陀國), a descendant of King Aśoka, heard of this and sighed, saying: "The sun of wisdom has already set, and only the Buddha-tree remains; now that it has been destroyed again, what will living beings look upon!" He threw his entire body to the ground, his sorrow moving all who saw him. He had the milk of several thousand cows collected to irrigate it, and within a night the tree grew back to a height of over one zhang. Fearing it might be cut down again in the future, he surrounded it with a stone wall twenty-four feet high. Therefore, the Mahā-bodhi tree is now hidden within a stone enclosure, rising more than one zhang above it.

To the east of the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) is a vihāra (精舍), one hundred and sixty or seventy feet high, with a base more than twenty paces wide, built of blue bricks and plastered with lime. The tiered niches all contain golden images, and the four walls are carved with exquisite designs, some in the form of linked pearls, others as celestial beings. At the top is placed a golden-copper āmalaka fruit (亦謂寶瓶，又稱寶臺; Original note: also called a treasure vase, or a treasure terrace). The eastern side is connected to a multi-storied pavilion with eaves and roofs rising in three distinct tiers; the rafters, pillars, beams, doors, and windows are decorated with gold and silver carvings and inlaid with pearls and jade. The inner chambers and deep halls have three sets of connecting doors. On the left and right of the outer gate are niche chambers; on the left is an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva (觀自在菩薩), and on the right is an image of Maitreya Bodhisattva (慈氏菩薩), both cast in white silver and over ten feet high. On the original site of the vihāra, King Aśoka (無憂王) first built a small vihāra, which was later expanded by a Brahmin. Initially, there was a Brahmin who did not believe in the Buddha’s teachings and worshipped Maheśvara (大自在天). Hearing that the deity resided in the Snow Mountains, he went there with his younger brother to seek the fulfillment of his vows. The deity said, "All wishes and prayers are fulfilled only when one has merit. What you pray for is not something I can grant." The Brahmin asked, "What merit should I cultivate to fulfill my heart's desire?" The deity replied, "If you wish to plant good seeds and seek a superior field of merit, the Mahā-bodhi is the place where the Buddha attained the fruit of enlightenment. You should return quickly, go to the Mahā-bodhi, build a great vihāra, dig a large water pond, and perform various offerings; then your wishes shall be fulfilled." The Brahmin, having received the divine command, conceived great faith and returned together; the elder brother built a vihāra (精舍) and the younger brother excavated a water pond. Thereupon, they performed grand offerings and diligently sought the fulfillment of their heart’s desires, which were eventually realized as they became high ministers to the king, and all the emoluments and rewards they received were given away as alms. Once the vihāra was completed, they sought to recruit craftsmen to fashion an image of the Tathāgata as he first attained Buddhahood. A long time passed, and no one responded to the call. After a while, a Brahmin came and told the assembly, "I am skilled at depicting the wondrous form of the Tathāgata." The assembly asked, "Now that we are to create the image, what do you require?" He replied, "Only scented clay. It should be placed inside the vihāra, along with a single lamp for illumination. Once I have entered, seal the door firmly; it may only be opened after six months." The monastic assembly followed his instructions. With four days still remaining before the six months were up, the assembly became alarmed and curious, and they opened the door to look inside. They saw the Buddha image inside the vihāra looking majestic, sitting cross-legged with the right foot on top, the left hand withdrawn, and the right hand hanging down, facing east and appearing as solemn as if it were alive. The pedestal was four feet two inches high and twelve feet five inches wide; the image was eleven feet five inches tall, with a distance of eight feet eight inches between the knees and six feet two inches between the shoulders. Its auspicious marks were complete and its compassionate face seemed real, except that the polishing above the right breast was not yet finished. Since the man was nowhere to be seen, they realized it was a divine manifestation, and the assembly sighed with sorrow and earnestly prayed to understand. There was a śramaṇa of simple and honest character who had a dream in which the former brahmin appeared and said to him, "I am Maitreya Bodhisattva (慈氏菩薩); fearing that the thoughts of craftsmen could not fathom the holy countenance, I came in person to depict the Buddha's image. As for the lowered right hand, formerly when the Tathāgata was about to realize the fruit of Buddhahood, the celestial Māra came to harass him, and the earth deities announced their arrival. One of them emerged first to help the Buddha subjugate the demon, but the Tathāgata told him, 'Do not be worried or afraid; I shall surely subjugate him through the power of forbearance.' The demon king asked, 'Who will be the clear witness?' The Tathāgata then lowered his hand and pointed to the ground, saying, 'This is the witness.' At that time, the second earth deity emerged to bear witness; therefore, the hand of the present image imitates that former posture of lowering." The assembly, knowing of this spiritual manifestation, was filled with sorrow and reverence. Consequently, where the area above the breast was not yet finished, they filled it with various precious substances, and adorned it with pearl necklaces, jeweled crowns, and rare treasures.  After King Śaśāṅka (設賞迦王) had felled the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree, he wished to destroy this image; however, once he beheld its compassionate countenance, his heart could not bear it, and as he turned his carriage to return, he commanded a high minister, saying, "You should remove this Buddha image and install a figure of Maheśvara (大自在天)." Having received the decree, the minister was afraid and sighed, saying, "If I destroy the Buddha image, I shall incur calamity for kalpas to come; yet if I disobey the King's command, I shall lose my life and have my clan exterminated. In such a dilemma, what is the proper course of action!" He then summoned men of faith to serve as laborers and built a brick wall across the front of the image; feeling ashamed that it would be in total darkness, he also placed a bright lamp inside, and on the front of the brick wall, he painted a picture of Maheśvara. When the work was completed, he reported back to the King. Upon hearing this, the King was terrified; his entire body broke out in pustules, his skin and flesh cracked and split, and before long, he died. The minister hurried back and destroyed the wall that had served as a barrier. Although many days had passed, the lamp was still not extinguished. The image remains to this day, and the divine craftsmanship is unimpaired. Since it is situated in a secluded chamber where lamps are kept burning in succession, one who wishes to behold the compassionate countenance cannot examine it clearly; one must hold a large, bright mirror in the morning to reflect light inside, and only then can the sacred image be seen. Those who see it naturally feel an increase in sorrow and reverence.  The Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment on the eighth day of the second half of the Indian month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the eighth day of the third month in our calendar. According to the Sthavira school, however, he attained perfect enlightenment on the fifteenth day of the second half of the month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the third month. At that time, the Tathāgata was thirty years old; others say he was thirty-five.  To the north of the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) is the place where the Buddha walked in meditation. After the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment, he did not rise from his seat for seven days, remaining in silent meditation. When he arose, he went to the north of the Mahā-bodhi and walked in meditation for seven days, pacing back and forth from east to west for more than ten paces. Extraordinary flowers appeared in his footprints, numbering eighteen in total. Later generations built a brick foundation here, more than three feet high. I have heard from ancient records that this sacred foundation indicates the length of a person's life: if one first makes a sincere vow and then measures it, the number will increase or decrease according to the length of one's lifespan. To the north of the meditation foundation, on the right side of the path, upon a large rock, there is a great shrine (精舍) containing a Buddha image that is looking upward with its eyes raised. In the past, the Tathāgata spent seven days here gazing at the Mahā-bodhi tree (菩提樹) without once averting his eyes. He did this to repay the tree for its kindness, and thus he kept it in his view. Not far to the west of the Mahā-bodhi tree, in a great shrine (精舍), there is a brass Buddha image adorned with rare jewels, standing and facing east. In front of it is a blue stone with wonderful patterns and extraordinary colors; this is where, when the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment, the Brahma King (Brahmā) built a hall of seven treasures and Lord Indra (Śakra) constructed a throne of seven treasures, upon which the Buddha meditated for seven days, emitting a wondrous light that illuminated the Mahā-bodhi tree. As the time since the Sage’s passing is long, the treasures have turned into stone.  Not far to the south of the Mahā-bodhi tree, there is a stūpa over a hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). When the Bodhisattva had bathed in the Nairañjanā River and was about to proceed to the Mahā-bodhi tree, he secretly pondered what he should use for a seat. He soon realized that he required clean grass. Lord Indra (天帝釋) transformed himself into a grass-cutter, carrying grass and following the path. The Bodhisattva said to him, "Could you bestow upon me some of the grass you are carrying?" The transformed being, hearing this request, respectfully offered the grass, which the Bodhisattva accepted, holding it as he proceeded forward.  Not far to the northeast of where he received the grass, there is a stūpa, which marks the place where bluebirds and herds of deer presented auspicious omens when the Bodhisattva was about to attain the fruit of Buddhahood. In India, such signs are considered favorable omens; therefore, the gods of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsa-deva) conformed to the ways of the world, and the flocks followed, flying and circling to manifest their spiritual power and reveal the holiness of the site. To the east of the Mahā-bodhi tree, on either side of the main road, there is a stūpa; these are the places where the King of Māras disturbed the Bodhisattva. When the Bodhisattva was about to attain the fruit of Buddhahood, the King of Māras urged him to accept the position of a Wheel-Turning King; when his entreaties failed, he returned in deep sorrow. The daughters of the King of Māras requested to go and seduce him, but through the Bodhisattva’s divine power, their beautiful appearances withered and changed; they withdrew supporting one another, frail and leaning on staves. To the northwest of the Mahā-bodhi tree (菩提樹), inside a shrine (精舍), there is an image of Kāśyapa Buddha; it is renowned for its spiritual efficacy and frequently emits a brilliant light. According to ancient records, if a person with utmost sincerity circumambulates it seven times, they will attain the knowledge of past lives in whatever place they are reborn. To the northwest of the Kāśyapa Buddha shrine are two brick chambers, each containing an image of an earth deity. In the past, when the Tathāgata was about to attain perfect enlightenment, one reported the arrival of Māra, and the other served as a witness for the Buddha. Later generations, mindful of their service, depicted their forms to honor their virtue. Not far to the west of the Mahā-bodhi tree enclosure, there is a stūpa called the Saffron (郁金香) Stūpa, over forty feet high, which was built by a merchant lord of the country of Jāguḍa (漕炬吒國). Formerly, in the country of Jāguḍa, there was a great merchant lord who worshiped heavenly deities and offered sacrifices to seek blessings, while holding the Buddha’s teachings in contempt and disbelieving in cause and effect. Later, he led a group of merchants to trade goods, sailing on the southern sea, when they encountered a storm and lost their way. Drifting on the waves for three years, their provisions were exhausted and they could not even secure enough food to survive. The people on the ship, unable to plan for the next day, joined their efforts and shared their resolve, calling upon the deities they served; yet, though their minds were weary with anxiety, their secret prayers were not answered. Suddenly, they saw a great mountain (pravaragiri) with towering cliffs and steep ridges, where two suns shone together, casting a brilliant, double light. At that time, the merchants comforted one another, saying, "We are fortunate; having passed this great mountain, we should stop here and find peace and happiness." The merchant leader said, "It is not a mountain, but a makara-fish. The towering cliffs and steep ridges are its whiskers and mane, and the two suns shining together are the light of its eyes." Before his voice had faded, the ship drifted toward it. Thereupon, the merchant leader told his companions, "I have heard that the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara can bestow peace and happiness in the midst of all dangers and difficulties; we should each, with utmost sincerity, call upon his name." They immediately joined their voices in unison, taking refuge and reciting his name. The towering mountain then vanished, and the two suns also disappeared. Suddenly, they saw a śramaṇa, dignified and composed, holding a staff and walking through the void, who came to rescue them from drowning; before long, they arrived at their own country.  Because of this, their faith became firm and steadfast, and they sought merit without wavering. They built a stūpa and performed offerings, coating it from top to bottom with saffron-scented mud. Having developed this faith, they led their companions to personally pay homage to the sacred sites and view the Mahā-bodhi tree. Before they had time to return home, a month had already passed. As the merchants traveled together, they said to one another, "The mountains and rivers are vast and our homeland is far away; since we are here, who is there to sweep and clean the stūpa we previously built?" Having said this, they circled around to this spot and suddenly saw the stūpa. Astonished at how this could be, they went forward to examine it and found it was the very stūpa built by their own country. Therefore, in India today, it is known by the name of Saffron. At the southeast corner of the wall surrounding the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹), beside a banyan tree (nyagrodha), there is a vihāra (精舍) next to a stūpa, containing a statue of the Buddha in a seated posture. In the past, when the Tathāgata first attained the fruit of Buddhahood, the Great Brahmā King (Mahābrahmā-devarāja) here entreated him to turn the wheel of the wonderful Dharma. Within the enclosure of the Mahā-bodhi, there are large stūpas at each of the four corners. In the past, after the Tathāgata had received the auspicious grass (kuśa), he proceeded toward the Mahā-bodhi; he first passed by the four corners, and the great earth shook, only becoming still when he reached the Vajrāsana (金剛座). Within the enclosure of the tree, sacred sites are arranged like the scales of a fish, and it is difficult to enumerate them all.  Outside the enclosure of the Mahā-bodhi, to the southwest, there is a stūpa marking the former residence of the two milkmaids who offered the milk gruel. Beside it is a stūpa where the milkmaids boiled the gruel. Next to this stūpa is the place where the Tathāgata received the gruel. Outside the south gate of the Mahā-bodhi enclosure is a large pond, over seven hundred paces in circumference, with clear, mirror-like waves where dragons and fish dwell; it was excavated by two Brahmin brothers acting under the command of Maheśvara (大自在天). To the south of this is another pond; in the past, when the Tathāgata had first attained perfect enlightenment and wished to bathe, Śakra-devānām-indra (天帝釋) manifested this pond for the Buddha. To the west is a large stone; after the Buddha had washed his robes and wished to dry them, Śakra-devānām-indra brought it from the Great Snow Mountains (Himālaya). Beside it is a stūpa where the Tathāgata accepted an old garment. Further to the south, in the forest, is a stūpa marking the place where the Tathāgata accepted the offering of an old garment from a poor elderly woman.

Outside the north gate of the Bodhi tree is the Mahābodhi Monastery (摩訶菩提僧伽藍), which was built by a former king of the country of Siṃhala (僧伽羅國). It has six courtyards and three-storied pavilions, surrounded by walls thirty to forty feet high; the workmanship is of the utmost ingenuity, and the painted decorations are exquisite. As for the Buddha images, they are cast in gold and silver, and all their adornments are inlaid with precious gems. The various stupas are lofty, spacious, and exquisitely decorated, containing the relics of the Tathāgata; the bone relics are as large as a finger joint, lustrous, pure white, and translucent inside and out. The flesh relics are like large pearls, with a color tinged with reddish-blue. Every year, on the full moon day of the month of the Tathāgata’s great spiritual manifestations, they are displayed to the public (Original note: This is the thirtieth day of the twelfth month in India, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the first month here). At this time, they sometimes emit light or rain down flowers. The community of monks numbers nearly one thousand; they study the teachings of the Mahāyāna and the Sthavira school, their monastic discipline is pure and strict, and their conduct is upright and bright. Formerly, in the southern sea, there was the country of Siṃhala, whose king was purely devoted to the Buddha-dharma, a faith arising from his own nature. He had a younger cousin who became a monk and, longing to see the sacred sites of the Buddha, traveled far to India. He stayed in various monasteries, but all of them treated him with contempt as a border-dweller. He then returned to his own country, and the king personally went out to welcome him. The śramaṇa was sorrowful and distressed, as if he were unable to speak. The king said, "What burden do you carry that causes such deep melancholy?" The śramaṇa said, "Relying on the prestige of the state, I traveled to distant lands to inquire after the Way. Living as a stranger in foreign territories, I endured the cold and the heat, and at every turn I encountered humiliation and was mocked for my speech. Bearing such sorrow and shame, how could I be happy?" The king asked, "What do you mean by this?" He replied, "I sincerely wish that Your Majesty would take the field of merit to heart and establish a monastery (saṃghārāma) in India. This would both honor the holy sites and bring you great fame, while the resulting merit would support the late king and its blessings would reach your descendants." The king said, "This is a wonderful idea; why did I not hear of it sooner?" He then sent the treasures of his country as an offering to the King of India.  Having accepted the tribute and wishing to show kindness to those from afar, the King of India said to the envoy, "What should I now give as a return gift for your mission?" The envoy said, "The King of Siṃhala (僧伽羅) bows his head to the Great Auspicious King of India! Your majesty’s prestige and virtue extend far, and your benevolent grace reaches to distant places. The śramaṇas of our lowly land, admiring your influence and transformation, dared to travel to your superior kingdom to pay their respects at the holy sites. Yet, when they stayed in the monasteries, they were not provided with lodging; they suffered extreme hardship and returned home having endured shame. I humbly propose a far-reaching plan to set an example for future generations: to build this monastery in India so that traveling mendicants may have a place to rest, the two countries may enjoy friendly relations, and travelers may pass between them without end." The king said, "The Tathāgata’s subtle influence has passed, but his legacy remains; you may choose any one of the holy sites." The envoy accepted the command and returned to report the mission. The ministers offered their congratulations, and the king then gathered the śramaṇas to deliberate on the construction. The śramaṇas said, "The Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) is the place where all Buddhas of the past and future attain holiness; having examined the various opinions, there is no better plan than this." Thereupon, the king gave up the treasures of his country and built this monastery, assigning monks from his own country to perform the offerings, and he engraved a copper plate as a record, which stated: "To provide for all without partiality is the supreme teaching of the Buddhas; to aid those with affinity through wisdom is the clear instruction of the ancient sages. Now I, this humble person, having inherited the great royal undertaking, have built this monastery to commemorate the holy site, so that the resulting merit may benefit my ancestors and its grace may extend to the common people. Only monks from my own country shall have authority here, and any of my countrymen who are present shall also be treated according to the monastic regulations. May this be passed down to descendants, forever and ever without end." For this reason, this monastery is mostly occupied by monks from the country of Siṃhala (師子國).  More than ten li south of the Mahā-bodhi, holy sites are adjacent to one another, and it is difficult to list them all. Every year, when the bhikṣus conclude the rains retreat (vārṣika), hundreds of thousands of laypeople from the four directions, for seven days and seven nights, carry incense and flowers, play music, and travel throughout the forest to pay homage and make offerings. According to the holy teachings of the Buddha, the monks of India all enter the two-part rains retreat on the first day of the first half of the month of Śrāvaṇa, which corresponds to the sixteenth day of the fifth month here; they conclude the two-part rains retreat on the fifteenth day of the second half of the month of Aśvayuja, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the eighth month here. The names of the Indian months are based on the stars and have remained unchanged from ancient times to the present; among all the schools, there is no discrepancy. It is because the local dialects were not fully reconciled and there were errors in translation regarding the division of time and the calculation of months that these discrepancies have arisen; therefore, the retreat is entered on the sixteenth day of the fourth month and concluded on the fifteenth day of the seventh month.

Going east from the Mahā River, one enters a great forest wilderness and, after traveling over a hundred li, reaches Kukkuṭapāda Mountain (translated into Chinese as Jizu, "Cock's Foot"), also called Gurupāda Mountain (translated into Chinese as Zunzu, "Venerable Foot"). The high peaks are steep and the ravines infinitely deep; the caverns are boundless, and at the foot of the mountain by the mountain streams, tall trees fill the valleys, while ridges and cliffs are covered with lush grass. Three peaks rise sharply with sheer precipices standing at their sides, their atmosphere joining with the heavens and their forms merging with the clouds. Because the Venerable Mahākāśyapa later entered nirvana in its midst, people did not dare to refer to him directly by name, and thus it is called "Venerable Foot."  Mahākāśyapa (摩訶迦葉波) is a disciple of the Śrāvaka vehicle who attained the six supernatural powers and possesses the eight liberations. When the Tathāgata had finished his work of transformation and was about to enter nirvana, he told Kāśyapa: "Throughout vast eons I have diligently practiced austerities, seeking the supreme Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings. The vows I made in the past have now been fulfilled. I am now about to enter the great nirvana, and I entrust the entire treasury of the Dharma to you. Maintain and proclaim it; do not let it be lost or fall into ruin. The golden-threaded robe offered by my aunt is to be kept and passed on to Maitreya when he attains buddhahood. Among the practitioners within my bequeathed Dharma—whether they be bhikṣus, bhikṣunīs, or upāsakas (translated into Chinese as 'laymen who serve'; the old terms 'yisaisai', 'yuposai', and 'yuposai' are all incorrect), or upāsikās (translated into Chinese as 'laywomen who serve')." (Original note: The old terms 'yuposai' [upāsaka] and 'yupoyiyi' [upāsikā] are both incorrect.) All of them are to be liberated first, causing them to depart from the cycle of transmigration." Kāśyapa accepted the command to uphold the True Dharma. Once the compilation was finished, in the twentieth year, he grew weary of the world and its impermanence and was about to enter final extinction. He then went to Mount Kukkutapāda (雞足山), ascended from the northern side of the mountain, and took a winding path to the southwest ridge. The mountain peaks were steep and obstructed, and the cliff paths were rugged; he struck them with his staff, and they split open as if cut. Once the mountain path was opened, he proceeded along the way, winding and turning through crisscrossing passages until he reached the summit and emerged on the northeast side. Having entered the midst of the three peaks, he stood holding the Buddha’s robe, and by the power of his vow, the three peaks closed over him, which is why the mountain now has three protruding ridges. When the future Maitreya, the World-Honored One, appears in the world and completes his three assemblies of preaching the Dharma, there will remain countless arrogant sentient beings who shall ascend this mountain and come to the place of Kāśyapa. When Maitreya snaps his fingers, the mountain peaks will open of their own accord; yet when those sentient beings see Kāśyapa, their arrogance will increase even further. At that time, the Great Kāśyapa will present the robe and deliver a discourse; once they have finished paying their respects, he will ascend into the void, manifest various spiritual transformations, transform into fire to consume his body, and thus enter final extinction. At that time, the assembly will gaze up in reverence, their arrogant minds will be dispelled, and through this realization, they will all attain the holy fruits. Therefore, a stūpa has been built on the mountain; on quiet nights, one may see a bright torch from afar, but upon ascending the mountain, nothing can be seen.

Traveling more than thirty *li* eastward through the empty valleys of Buddhavana Mountain (Skt. *buddha-vana*), one reaches Yaṣṭivana (the *yi* and *jie* characters are reversed in pronunciation; in the language of Tang, this means "Staff Forest"). The forest’s bamboo is tall and slender, covering the mountains and filling the valleys. Long ago, there was a Brahmin who heard that the body of the Buddha Śākyamuni was sixteen feet tall; he constantly harbored doubts and, unable to believe it, took a sixteen-foot bamboo staff, intending to measure the Buddha’s body. The staff always extended beyond the sixteen-foot mark at its tip; as it continued to grow taller in this way, he could never reach the truth of it, so he threw the staff away and departed, and it subsequently took root. Within the forest is a large *stūpa* built by King Aśoka. In the past, the Tathāgata spent seven days here manifesting great supernatural powers for the sake of gods and humans, and expounding the profound and subtle Dharma.  Recently, in the Staff Forest, there was an *upāsaka* named Jayasena (in the language of Tang, this means "Victorious Army"), who belonged to the Kṣatriya caste of Western India. His aspirations were for simplicity and ease, his heart delighted in the mountains and forests, and while his physical traces remained in this illusory realm, his mind roamed the boundaries of ultimate truth. He had thoroughly investigated the subtle mysteries of both internal and external scriptures, possessing noble eloquence and elegant manners. Śramaṇas, Brahmins, followers of non-Buddhist paths, heterodox scholars, kings, ministers, elders, and the wealthy and influential all flocked to visit him, bowing their heads to request instruction. Six out of every ten students who received his teachings were his disciples. Now approaching seventy years of age, he studied with tireless devotion; having abandoned all other arts, he practiced only the Buddhist scriptures, exerting his body and mind without ceasing day or night. According to the custom of India, scented powder is mixed into clay to make small stupas five or six inches high; scriptures are written and placed inside them, which are called Dharma relics. As the number gradually accumulates, a large stupa is built to house them all within, where offerings are constantly performed. Thus, the practice of Jayasena (勝軍) was as follows: his mouth would proclaim the wonderful Dharma to guide and encourage students, while his hands would make stupas to cultivate superior merit. At night, he would practice circumambulation, chanting, and seated meditation, never finding time for sleep or food, and working day and night without slackening. He reached one hundred years of age, yet his resolve and work did not decline. Over a period of thirty years, he made a total of seven koṭis (in the Tang language, this means one hundred million) of Dharma-relic stupas. Each time he completed one koṭi, he built a large stupa to house them all, where he grandly performed offerings and invited the monastic assembly to celebrate with a religious ceremony. At those times, a divine light would shine brilliantly as a manifest miracle, and from then on, it would emit light from time to time.

Four or five li to the northeast of the Isolated Hill (Vyāsa) is the Small Isolated Hill (Asura). In the cliffside of the mountain is a stone chamber, vast and spacious, capable of seating over a thousand people; here the Tathāgata in the past preached the Dharma for three months. Above the stone chamber is a large flat rock where Śakra and Brahmā ground ox-head sandalwood to anoint the Buddha’s body; the lingering fragrance on the rock remains potent to this day. In the southwest corner of the stone chamber is a rocky grotto, which in India is called the palace of the Asura (Original note: The older terms *Asura*, *Ashulun*, and *Axiuluo* are all erroneous). In the past, there were some curious individuals deeply skilled in magical arts who gathered their companions, totaling fourteen people, and having made a pact to share the same purpose, entered this grotto. After traveling thirty or forty li, it suddenly became brightly illuminated, and they beheld cities, towers, and pavilions, all made of gold, silver, and lapis lazuli. Once these people arrived, there were various young maidens standing by the gates who joyfully welcomed them and treated them with great courtesy. Proceeding gradually to the inner city gate, there were two maidservants, each holding a golden basin filled with flowers and incense, who came to greet them. They said to the group, "It is fitting to go to the pool to bathe, to apply perfumes and wear flower garlands, and only after that to enter; this would be most excellent. Only that sorcerer should proceed quickly." The other thirteen people then bathed, but as soon as they entered the pool, they felt as if they had forgotten everything, and they found themselves sitting in a rice paddy on a level plain to the north of this place, already thirty or forty li away. Beside the stone chamber is a plank road, more than ten paces wide and four or five li long. In the past, when King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王) was about to go to the place of the Buddha, he had rocks cut to open the valley and cliffs leveled to fill the ravines; he either piled up stones or excavated the cliffs to create steps, in order to reach the place of the Buddha.

Traveling east from these great mountains for more than sixty li, one reaches the city of Kuśāgrapura (矩奢揭羅補羅城; in the language of Tang, the City of Superior Thatch Palaces). The City of Superior Thatch Palaces is located in the center of the kingdom of Magadha and was the capital of ancient kings; because it produces an abundance of excellent and auspicious fragrant thatch, it is called the City of Superior Thatch. Lofty mountains surround it, serving as an outer wall; to the west it connects to a mountain pass, and to the north a mountain gate opens. It is long from east to west and narrow from north to south, with a circumference of more than one hundred and fifty li. The remaining foundations of the inner city measure more than thirty li in circumference. *Karṇikāra* (羯尼迦) trees cover all the paths; their flowers contain a unique fragrance and their color is as brilliant as gold, so that in the month of late spring, the forests are all golden.  Outside the north gate of the palace city is a stūpa, marking the place where Devadatta, having become an intimate friend of King Ajātaśatru (未生怨王), released the intoxicated elephant Dhanapāla (護財) in an attempt to harm the Tathāgata. From the tips of the Tathāgata’s fingers, five lions emerged, and the intoxicated elephant was subdued and bowed down here. To the northeast of the place where the intoxicated elephant was subdued is a stūpa, marking the place where Śāriputra heard the bhikṣu Aśvajit (阿濕婆恃; in the language of Tang, Ma Sheng) preach the Dharma and attained the fruit of sainthood.   Formerly, when Śāriputra was a householder, he possessed high talent and elegant bearing, and was esteemed by his contemporaries; students and disciples came to him to receive instruction. At this time, he was about to enter the great city of Rājagṛha, and the bhikṣu Aśvajit was also just then begging for food. At that time, Śāriputra saw Aśvajit from afar and said to his disciples, "That person coming here is very composed and dignified; if he has not attained the holy fruit, how could he be so calm and tranquil?" "We should wait a moment and observe his demeanor." The bhikṣu Aśvajit had already attained the state of an arhat; his mind was at ease, his bearing was gentle and refined, and he approached with the ringing of his khakkhara. Śāriputra said, "Elder, are you well and at peace? Who is your teacher, and what Dharma have you realized, that you are so joyful?" Aśvajit replied, "Do you not know? The crown prince of King Śuddhodana, who renounced the position of a wheel-turning monarch, out of compassion for the six destinies, practiced austerities for six years, attained supreme enlightenment (samyaksambodhi), and possesses omniscience—he is my teacher. As for the Dharma, it is neither existent nor non-existent; it is difficult to define or explain. Only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully describe it; how could one as ignorant as I discuss it in detail?" He then recited a verse in praise of the Buddha’s Dharma. Upon hearing this, Śāriputra attained the fruit.  Not far to the north of where Śāriputra attained the fruit, there is a large, deep pit with a stūpa built beside it; this is the place where Śrīgupta (translated into Chinese as Shengmi [Victorious Secret]) attempted to harm the Buddha with a fire pit and poisoned food. This Śrīgupta followed the teachings of the non-Buddhists and was deeply attached to erroneous views. The various Brahmins said to him, "Gautama is respected by the people of the country, which has left our followers with nothing to rely on. You should now invite him to your home for a feast; dig a large pit at the gate, fill it with fire, bridge it with rotten wood, and cover it with dry earth. All the food and drink should be mixed with poison; if he escapes the fire pit, he will surely encounter the poisoned food." Śrīgupta accepted their command and prepared the poisoned feast. The people in the city all knew that Śrīgupta (勝密) harbored evil and harmful intentions toward the World-Honored One, and they all urged and pleaded with the Buddha not to go. The World-Honored One replied, "Do not harbor anxiety. The body of the Tathāgata cannot be harmed by anything." Thereupon, he accepted the invitation and went. As his foot stepped upon the threshold of the gate, the fire pit turned into a pool, its clear waters reflecting like a mirror and filled with blooming lotuses. Having seen this, Śrīgupta was filled with panic and confusion, and said to his disciples, "He used magic to escape the fire, but there is still the poisoned food." After the World-Honored One had finished his meal, he preached the wonderful Dharma for him; having heard this, Śrīgupta confessed his faults and took refuge.

To the northeast of the fire pit of Śrīgupta (勝密), at a bend in the mountain city, there is a stūpa. This is where the great physician Jīvaka (時縛迦; formerly called Qipo [耆婆], which is incorrect) built a preaching hall for the Buddha. He planted flowers and fruit trees around its surrounding walls, and the remains of the foundations and the stumps of the trees can still be seen. When the Tathāgata was in the world, he often stayed here. Beside it are the former residence of Jīvaka, the remains of the foundations, an old well, and the hollows of the ruins, which still exist.

Traveling fourteen or fifteen *li* northeast from the palace city, one reaches Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain (in the language of Tang, this means Vulture Peak, and it is also called Vulture Terrace; the old name, Qidujue Mountain, is incorrect). It adjoins the southern slope of the North Mountain and rises solitary and steep; it is a place where vultures dwell and it resembles a lofty terrace, with the verdant peaks reflecting against the sky in varying shades of color. During the fifty years that the Tathāgata presided over the world, he resided mostly on this mountain, extensively expounding the subtle Dharma. For the sake of hearing the Dharma, King Bimbisāra mobilized laborers to build a path from the foot of the mountain to the summit, spanning valleys and scaling rocks, laying stones to form steps more than ten paces wide and five or six *li* in length. Midway along the path are two small stūpas: one is called "Dismounting," marking the spot where the king would proceed on foot; the other is called "Turning Back the Ordinary," marking the spot where he would screen out ordinary people and not allow them to accompany him further. The summit of the mountain is long from east to west and narrow from north to south.

To the east of the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove (迦蘭陀竹園) is a stūpa built by King Ajātaśatru (阿闍多設咄路王; translated in the Tang language as "Unborn Enemy" [未生怨], formerly called Ajāśatru [阿闍世], which is an erroneous abbreviation). After the Tathāgata entered nirvāṇa, the various kings divided the relics among themselves. King Ajātaśatru obtained his share and brought them back, where he formally observed the rites of construction and performed offerings. When King Aśoka (無憂王) developed faith, he opened the stūpa to retrieve the relics and built [new] stūpas; there were still remnants left over, which at that time emitted a light like a candle.  In the stūpa of King Ajātaśatru, there are relics of half the body of the Venerable Ānanda. Formerly, when the Venerable One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he left the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) and headed toward the city of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐城). The two countries were in conflict and intended to raise an army. The Venerable One felt compassion and therefore divided his body; the King of Magadha received his portion and brought it back for veneration, and at this very sacred site, he formally performed the rites of construction. Beside it is a place where the Tathāgata walked in meditation. Not far from this is a stūpa, which is the place where Śāriputra (舍利子) and Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子) and others resided during the rainy season.

Traveling five or six li southwest from the Bamboo Grove (Veṇuvana), on the northern side of the South Mountain (Dakṣiṇagiri), in a great bamboo forest, there is a large stone chamber. This is where the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, together with nine hundred and ninety great arhats, compiled the Tripiṭaka after the Tathāgata’s nirvana. In front are the old foundations of a hall built by King Ajātaśatru (未生怨王) for the great arhats who were to compile the Dharma-treasury.  Initially, while Mahākāśyapa was sitting in meditation in the mountain forest, he suddenly saw a brilliant light and observed the earth quake. He said, "What omen is this, that it should be so extraordinary?" Using his heavenly eye to observe, he saw that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had entered parinirvana between the twin trees, and he immediately ordered his followers to hasten to the city of Kuśinagara (拘尸城). On the road, he met a Brahman holding a heavenly flower in his hand. Mahākāśyapa asked, "Where do you come from? Do you know where my Great Teacher is now?" The Brahman replied, "I have just come from that city of Kuśinagara; I saw that your Great Teacher has already entered nirvana, and the multitudes of gods and men are all making offerings. The flower I hold was obtained from there."  Upon hearing this, Mahākāśyapa said to his followers, "The sun of wisdom has set, the world is in darkness, the excellent guide has departed, and sentient beings will fall into ruin." Lax monks congratulated one another, saying, "The Tathāgata has attained extinction, so we are now at ease. If we commit any offense, who will be able to rebuke or restrain us?" Hearing this, Mahākāśyapa was deeply saddened and thought to compile the Dharma-treasury to govern offenses according to the teachings. He then went to the twin trees to view the transformation and pay his respects. Soon after, the Dharma King passed away, leaving humans and gods without a guide, and the great arhats also entered parinirvāṇa. At that time, Mahākāśyapa thought to himself, "In obedience to the Buddha’s teachings, it is appropriate to compile the Dharma-treasury." Thereupon, he ascended Mount Sumeru (蘇迷盧山), struck the great ghaṇṭā (大揵稚), and proclaimed: "A Dharma assembly is about to be held in the city of Rājagṛha (王舍城); all those who have realized the fruits of the path should assemble here with haste!" The sound of the ghaṇṭā carried the teaching of Kāśyapa, reaching throughout the trichiliomegachiliocosm, and all who possessed supernatural powers heard it and gathered.  At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the assembly, saying, "The Tathāgata has entered extinction, and the world is empty. We must compile the Dharma-treasury to repay the Buddha’s kindness. Now, in compiling the Dharma, we must prioritize simplicity and quietude; how could we rely on a large crowd and fail to accomplish this noble task? Those who possess the three knowledges (三明), have attained the six supernatural powers (六通), are endowed with perfect retention (聞持) without error, and possess unobstructed eloquence (辯才)—such superior persons may participate in the compilation. All others who are still in the stage of learning should return to their respective dwellings."  Thus, he obtained nine hundred and ninety people, excluding Ānanda, who was still in the stage of learning. Mahākāśyapa summoned him and said, "You have not yet exhausted the outflows (漏); you should leave the assembly of sages." Ānanda replied, "I have attended upon the Tathāgata for many years, and whenever there were discussions on the Dharma, I was never excluded. Now that the compilation is to take place, I am being expelled; the Dharma King has entered extinction, and I have lost my refuge." Kāśyapa told him, "Do not harbor sorrow or distress. Although you have personally attended upon the Buddha and are indeed learned, your attachments and delusions have not yet been exhausted, and your habitual bonds have not yet been severed." Ānanda, silenced, withdrew and went to a quiet, secluded place, desiring to attain the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), but despite his diligent efforts, he did not attain it. Having become exhausted and weary, he intended to lie down for a moment; before his head had even touched the pillow, he attained the state of an Arhat. He went to the place of the assembly and knocked on the door to announce his arrival. Kāśyapa asked, "Have you exhausted your defilements? You should employ your supernatural powers and enter without using the door." Ānanda accepted the command, entered through the keyhole, paid homage to the monks, and then withdrew to sit down. This was on the fifteenth day, the beginning of the summer retreat.  Thereupon, Kāśyapa proclaimed aloud, "Reflect and listen carefully! Ānanda, who has heard and retained the teachings, and whom the Tathāgata praised, shall compile the Sūtra-piṭaka (Original note: The old term 'Sūtra' is incorrect). Upāli, who is clear and thorough in upholding the Vinaya and is recognized by the assembly, shall compile the Vinaya-piṭaka (Original note: The old term 'Vinaya' is incorrect). I, Kāśyapa, shall compile the Abhidharma-piṭaka." After two or three months had passed, the compilation of the three piṭakas was completed. Because Mahākāśyapa was the senior elder (sthavira) among the monks, it was consequently called the Sthavira school (Sthaviravāda).  To the northwest of where Mahākāśyapa held the assembly, there is a stūpa; this is where Ānanda, having been rebuked by the monks and excluded from the assembly, came to sit in meditation and attained the fruit of Arhatship. Only after attaining this fruit was he permitted to participate.

Not far to the northeast of the stone pillar, one reaches the city of Rājagṛha (曷羅闍姞利呬城; in Chinese, Wangshe). The outer wall has already collapsed, and no remains of the ramparts are left; although the inner city is ruined, its foundations are still steep and high, measuring over twenty *li* in circumference, with one gate on each side.   Formerly, when King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王) had his capital in the Upper Palace City, the households of the registered inhabitants frequently suffered from the calamity of fire. If one family was negligent, the neighbors on all four sides would suffer the disaster; the people had no time for anything but fire prevention, their properties and livelihoods were abandoned, and the masses lived in grievance and unrest. The king said, "Because of my lack of virtue, the common people suffer; what merit can I cultivate to avert this?" The ministers replied, "Your Majesty’s virtuous transformation is harmonious and peaceful, and your governance and teachings are clear and discerning. Now, these common people are not cautious, leading to these fires. It is appropriate to establish strict regulations to prevent future offenses. If a fire breaks out, investigate thoroughly to find who started it, punish the primary culprit, and banish them to the Cold Forest (寒林)."   The Cold Forest is a place where corpses are abandoned; it is commonly called an inauspicious place, and people avoid traveling there. "Now, to banish them there is the same as treating them like a corpse. Since they will be ashamed of such a lowly dwelling, they will naturally be cautious and protective." The king said, "Good; it should be announced everywhere to the residents." Shortly after, a fire broke out in the king’s own palace first. He said to his ministers, "I shall move." He then ordered the crown prince to oversee the affairs of the capital, and wishing to clarify the laws of the state, he moved his residence there. At that time, the King of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐王), hearing that King Bimbisāra was living in the open at the Cold Forest, assembled his troops with the intent to launch a surprise attack. The border guards reported this, and he then built a city. Because the king had first taken up residence here, it was called Rājagṛha (the City of the King’s Abode). The officials, the gentry, and the common people all moved their households there. Some say that it was not until King Ajātaśatru (未生怨王) that this city was built; once the crown prince Ajātaśatru succeeded to the throne, he then made it his capital. By the time King Aśoka (無憂王) moved the capital to Pāṭaliputra (波吒釐城), he bestowed Rājagṛha upon the brahmans; therefore, there are no longer any common people in the city, only fewer than a thousand brahman families. In the southwest corner of the palace city are two small saṃghārāmas where visiting monks from various countries stay when they come and go; this is the place where the Buddha formerly expounded the Dharma. To the northwest of this is a stūpa, the former birthplace of the elder Jyotiṣka (珠底色迦; in Tang language this means "astronomy/astrological calendar"; the old translation "Śrotika" is incorrect). Outside the south gate of the city, to the left of the road, there is a stūpa where the Tathāgata expounded the Dharma and converted Rāhula.

From here, traveling north for more than thirty *li*, one arrives at the Nālandā (translated into Chinese as "Giving Without Weariness") monastery. I heard from the elders that in the mango grove to the south of this monastery there is a pond; a dragon named Nālandā lived there, and because the monastery was built beside it, it took its name from the dragon. According to the actual account, it is because the Tathāgata, in the past when practicing the bodhisattva path, was a great king who established his capital in this place. He felt compassion for sentient beings and delighted in giving generously; at the time, people praised his virtue and called him "Giving Without Weariness," and thus the monastery took this as its name. The land was originally a mango grove; five hundred merchants bought it with ten billion gold coins and offered it to the Buddha. The Buddha preached the Dharma here for three months, and the merchants all attained the fruits of sainthood. Not long after the Buddha’s nirvana, a former king of this country named Śakrāditya (translated into Chinese as "Sun of the Emperor") deeply respected the One Vehicle and honored the Triple Gem; he selected this auspicious site by divination and built this monastery. When the work first began, they pierced and injured the body of the dragon. At that time, there was a Nirgrantha outsider skilled in divination who saw this and predicted: "This is a superior site; if a monastery is built here, it will surely flourish and become the standard for the five Indias. It will grow even more prosperous after a thousand years, and later students will easily complete their studies here. However, there will be much coughing of blood, because the dragon was injured." His son, King Buddhagupta (translated into Chinese as "Protector of Awakening"), succeeded to the throne and, following the noble legacy, built another monastery to the south of this one. King Tathāgatagupta (translated into Chinese as "Thus-Come") earnestly followed the noble legacy and built another monastery to the east of this one. When King Bālāditya (translated into Chinese as "Young Sun") succeeded to the throne, he built another monastery to the northeast of this one. When the work was completed and the ceremonies finished, he held a celebratory feast of merit, expressing his sincerity to both the hidden and the manifest, and invited both the ordinary and the holy. At this assembly, monks from the five Indias gathered from ten thousand miles away. Once the assembly was seated, two monks arrived late and were led up to the third-story pavilion. Someone asked, "The King is holding this assembly and has invited the ordinary and the holy; from what place do you venerable ones come, that you arrive last?" They replied, "We came from that country; our teacher was suffering from an illness, so we departed only after he had eaten. Having received the King’s distant invitation, we have come to attend the assembly." The questioner was astonished and immediately reported this to the King. The King, knowing in his heart that they were sages, went in person to inquire of them, but when he arrived at the upper pavilion, he did not know where they had gone. The King’s faith deepened further, and he renounced his kingdom to become a monk. Once he had become a monk, he was ranked at the very end of the assembly, which left him constantly dissatisfied and uneasy, thinking: "I was once a king, occupying the highest and most honorable position; now that I have become a monk, I am ranked at the very end of the assembly." He soon went to inform the monks and recounted his situation. Thereupon, the assembly of monks reached a consensus, decreeing that those who have not yet received the full precepts shall be ranked according to their age; thus, this monastery alone possesses this rule. The King’s son, Vajra (translated into Chinese as "Diamond"), possessed a firm and steadfast faith; after succeeding to the throne, he built another monastery to the west of this site. Afterward, the King of Central India built another great monastery to the north of this one. Thereupon, the surrounding walls were raised high, and they were joined into a single gate; since successive kings have built them generation after generation, exhausting all the arts of carving and joinery, it is truly a magnificent sight. The King said that in this original great monastery, a Buddha image is now installed, and forty monks are dispatched from the assembly daily to eat here in order to repay the kindness of the donors. The number of monks is several thousand, all of whom are men of outstanding talent and high learning; those whose virtue is esteemed in the present age and whose fame has spread to foreign lands number more than several hundred. Their conduct in the precepts is pure and white, and their monastic discipline is refined and perfect; the monks have strict regulations, and the assembly is entirely upright and simple, such that all the countries of India look to them as a model. They seek instruction and discuss profound mysteries, finding the whole day insufficient; they remain vigilant and admonish one another day and night, with the old and young helping each other to perfection, and if there were any who did not discuss the subtle meanings of the Tripitaka, they would feel ashamed of their own shadows. Therefore, scholars from foreign lands who wish to spread their reputation all come here to resolve their doubts, and only then does their elegant fame flow forth.
