For this reason, those who travel here under false pretenses are all treated with respect. When those from distant regions and foreign lands wish to enter for discussion, the gatekeepers pose difficult questions, and many are forced to turn back; only those who are deeply learned in both ancient and modern studies are permitted to enter. Consequently, when visiting scholars and newcomers discuss their arts and abilities in detail, those who are forced to retreat are certainly seventeen or eighteen out of every twenty. As for the few who are broadly learned, they are questioned in turn by the assembly, and there is none whose sharpness is not blunted and whose reputation is not diminished. As for those of eminent talent and broad learning, possessing strong memories and many abilities, these virtuous and wise men join their brilliance and follow in the footsteps of their predecessors. As for Dharmapāla (護法) and Candrapāla (護月), they stirred the fragrant dust of the Buddha’s legacy; Guṇamati (德慧) and Sthiramati (堅慧) spread their elegant reputations throughout their time; there were the refined discourses of Prabhāmitra (光友) and the lofty discussions of Jinamitra (勝友); Candrakīrti (智月) was clear and keen in his discernment; and Śīlabhadra (戒賢) possessed virtue that was sublime and profound. These superior men were known to all; their virtue excelled that of their predecessors, and their learning encompassed the ancient texts; each composed more than ten treatises and commentaries, which were widely circulated and highly valued by their contemporaries. Around the monastery, there are hundreds of sacred traces; I shall cite two or three of them as a brief summary.

King Bimbisāra went to meet the Buddha and traveled more than twenty *li* to the southeast, arriving at the town of Kālapināka (迦羅臂拏迦邑). In it is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. This is the native village of the Venerable Śāriputra, and the well still exists today. Beside it is a stūpa where the Venerable entered into extinction, which contains his bodily relics. The Venerable was of a great Brahmin lineage. His father was highly talented and broadly learned, with a deep insight into the subtle and profound; there was no classic or treatise that he had not thoroughly studied. His wife had a dream and told her husband in detail, saying: "Last night in my sleep, I dreamt of a strange man clad in armor and holding a vajra, who demolished all the mountains and then stood back beneath a single mountain." Her husband said: "This is a very auspicious dream. You will give birth to a son who will be learned and peerless in the world, who will defeat all the masters of debate and shatter their doctrines, but who will be inferior to only one person, to whom he will become a disciple." She was indeed pregnant, and the mother suddenly became brilliant, engaging in high-level discussions and intense debates with speech that was never obstructed. When the Venerable was eight years old, his fame spread to the four quarters; his nature was pure and simple, his heart was compassionate, he destroyed the bonds of defilement, and he attained wisdom. He and Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子) had been friends since youth and were deeply weary of the dusty world, yet they had not found a place to turn. Thereupon, he and Maudgalyāyana went to the place of the non-Buddhist Sañjaya (珊闍耶) to study. They then said to each other: "This is not the ultimate principle, and it cannot exhaust the limits of suffering. Let us each seek a clear guide; whoever tastes the nectar first must share its flavor with the other." At that time, the great arhat Aśvajit (馬勝) held his alms bowl and entered the city to beg for food. Śāriputra (舍利子) saw his dignified and refined demeanor and immediately asked him, "Who is your teacher?" He replied, "The prince of the Śākya clan, who grew weary of the world, renounced household life, and attained equal and perfect enlightenment—he is my teacher." Śāriputra said, "What dharma does he teach? May I hear it?" He replied, "I have only recently received instruction and have not yet grasped the profound meaning." Śāriputra said, "I wish to hear what you have heard." Aśvajit then expounded it according to the occasion, and upon hearing it, Śāriputra immediately attained the first fruit. He then went with his two hundred and fifty disciples to the place of the Buddha. The World-Honored One saw them from afar and, pointing them out, told the assembly, "Among my disciples, he is the foremost in wisdom." Upon arriving, he bowed his head to the ground and wished to follow the Buddha’s dharma. The World-Honored One said, "Welcome, bhikṣu." Upon hearing these words, his precepts were fully perfected. More than half a month later, he heard the Buddha preaching to the Long-nailed Brahmacārin (長爪梵志), and upon hearing the remaining discourse, he was enlightened and attained the fruit of an arhat. Later, when Ānanda (阿難) received the Buddha’s announcement of the time of his extinction, the news was passed from one to another, and all were filled with sorrow and grief. Śāriputra’s longing and reverence deepened, and, unable to bear seeing the Buddha enter parinirvāṇa, he requested the World-Honored One to let him enter extinction first. The World-Honored One said, "You should know the time." He took leave of his disciples and went to his native village, where his attendant novice informed the entire city. King Ajātaśatru (未生怨王) and the people of his country all rushed there like the wind, gathering like clouds. Śāriputra (舍利子) preached the Dharma extensively, and having heard him, the people departed. During the last watch of the night, he focused his mind and entered the samādhi of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti); upon arising from that meditation, he entered final extinction. Four or five li to the southeast of the town of Kālapināka (迦羅臂挐迦邑), there is a stūpa at the place where the disciples of the Venerable Śāriputra entered nirvāṇa. Some say that when Kāśyapa Buddha (迦葉波佛) was in the world, three koṭis (Original note: koṭi means one hundred million in the language of Tang) of great arhats entered nirvāṇa without remainder at this same place.

Going thirty-some *li* to the east of the stupa of the disciples of Śāriputra, one arrives at the mountain of Indraśailaguhā (Indra-śaila-guhā; in the language of Tang, "Cave of Śakra"). The mountain’s rocky valleys are deep and dark, and its flowering forests are lush and dense; on the ridge are two peaks that rise prominently and steeply. Between the southern cliffs of the western peak is a large stone chamber, wide but not high, where the Tathāgata once stayed. From time to time, the Heavenly Lord Śakra would carve forty-two questions of doubt onto the stone to ask [the Buddha], and the Buddha would explain them; those traces still remain. Today, an image has been made there to emulate the sacred appearance of the past, and those who enter to pay homage are all filled with awe and trepidation. On the mountain cliffs are the sites of the sitting and walking meditation traces of the four past Buddhas. On the eastern peak is a monastery; according to local custom, the monks there sometimes see, during the night, lamps and torches shining as constant illumination before the Buddha image in the stone chamber of the western peak. In front of the monastery on the eastern peak of Indraśailaguhā Mountain is a stupa called Haṃsa (in the language of Tang, "Goose"). Formerly, this monastery practiced the Lesser Vehicle, which is the gradual teaching of the Lesser Vehicle, and therefore permitted the consumption of the three pure meats, a practice this monastery followed and did not abandon. Later, the three pure meats were not always obtainable. A monk who was walking in meditation suddenly saw a flock of geese flying by and jokingly said, "Today the midday meal for the monks is insufficient; the Mahāsattvas should know the time." Before his words had ceased, one goose flew back, landed before the monk, and cast its body down to die. After the bhikṣu saw this, he reported it fully to the assembly of monks. Those who heard were moved with grief and said to one another, "The Tathāgata established the Dharma to guide and entice according to the capacity of the individual; we have clung to our ignorance and followed the gradual teachings. The Mahāyāna is the true principle; we should change our former attachments and strive to follow the holy will. This goose has handed down a warning and is truly a bright guide; we should commemorate its great virtue and transmit this record for all eternity." Thereupon, they built a stūpa to manifest its heroic legacy, burying the dead goose beneath it.

Traveling northeast from the Indraśailaguhā (因陀羅勢羅窶訶) Mountain for one hundred and fifty or sixty li, one reaches the Kapotaka (迦布德迦; in Chinese, "pigeon") Monastery, where there are over two hundred monks who study the teachings of the Sarvāstivāda school. To the east of the monastery is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. In the past, the Buddha stayed here for one night to preach the Dharma to the great assembly. At that time, a fowler was netting birds in this forest; having caught nothing all day, he said, "I have but little merit and am always met with misfortune." He came to where the Buddha was and cried out, "Today the Tathāgata is preaching the Dharma here, causing me to catch nothing in my nets; my wife and children are starving, so what plan can I devise?" The Tathāgata replied, "You should kindle a fire, and I will provide you with food." The Tathāgata then transformed himself into a large pigeon and threw himself into the fire to die; the fowler took it home, and he and his wife and children ate it together. Afterward, he returned to the Buddha, who guided and transformed him through skillful means. The fowler heard the Dharma, repented of his faults, renewed himself, left home to study, and subsequently attained the holy fruit. For this reason, the monastery that was built there was named the Pigeon Monastery.

From here, traveling east into the mountains and forests for more than one hundred li, one reaches the village of Luobanniluo (Röhinila). In front of the monastery is a great stupa built by King Ashoka (Aśoka), where the Buddha once stayed for three months to preach the Dharma. Two or three li to the north of this place is a large pond, more than thirty li in circumference, where four-colored lotus flowers bloom in all four seasons. From here, traveling east into the great mountains and forests for more than two hundred li, one reaches the country of Yilannabafaduo (Hiraṇyaparvata) (within the borders of Central India).

The country of Īraṇaparvata (伊爛拏鉢伐多國) is over three thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city of the country borders the Gaṅgā River to the north and is over twenty *li* in circuit. The crops are lush and productive, and flowers and fruits are abundant. The climate is mild and pleasant, and the customs are honest and simple. There are more than ten monasteries with over four thousand monks, most of whom study the teachings of the Hīnayāna Saṃmitīya school. There are more than twenty deva temples where followers of various heterodox sects live together. Recently, a neighboring king deposed the ruler of this country and bestowed the capital city upon the community of monks. Within this city, two monasteries were built, each housing nearly one thousand monks, both of which study the Hīnayāna Sarvāstivāda school.  Beside the great city, overlooking the Gaṅgā River, is Mount Īraṇa, which exhales mists and clouds that obscure the sun and the moon. From ancient times to the present, immortals and sages have followed one another to dwell there in meditation, and there is now a deva temple that still observes the traditional rites. In the past, the Tathāgata also resided here and preached the profound Dharma extensively for devas and humans. To the south of the great city is a stūpa where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for three months. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the three past Buddhas. Not far to the west of the walking paths of the three Buddhas is a stūpa; this is the birthplace of the bhikṣu Śroṭaviṃśatikoṭi (唐言聞二百億; the old translation "Koṭikarṇa" [億耳] is incorrect). In the past, there was a wealthy and noble elder in this city who had a child late in life. Whenever a messenger arrived, he would bestow two hundred koṭis of gold coins, and thus he named his son Śroṭaviṃśatikoṭi (He who heard of two hundred koṭis). By the time he reached adulthood, he had never once walked upon the ground, and thus the hair on the soles of his feet was over a foot long, lustrous, fine, and soft, with a color like yellow gold. Cherishing this child, his parents provided him with every kind of luxury; from his residence all the way to the Snow Mountains, post-stations were linked together and servants lined the roads, so that whenever a rare medicine was required, the word was passed along and the item delivered in succession, arriving in no time at all—such was the extent of his great wealth. The World-Honored One, knowing that his roots of goodness were about to sprout, commanded Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子) to go and convert him. Upon arriving at his gate, he found no way to announce himself. The elder’s family worshipped the Sun Deity, and every morning they would face east to bow. At that time, the Venerable One used his supernatural powers to descend from the solar disc and stand before them. The elder’s son, suspecting he was the Sun Deity, offered him fragrant rice; the Venerable One then returned, and the aroma of the rice filled the entire city of Rājagṛha (王舍城). At that time, King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王) was astonished by the extraordinary fragrance and ordered a messenger to investigate; it was discovered that Maudgalyāyana of the Bamboo Grove Monastery (竹林精舍) had brought the rice from the elder's house, and thus, learning that the elder's son possessed such a wonder, the king summoned him. The elder accepted the command, but pondered how to travel safely. To travel by boat and ply the oars carried the danger of wind and waves; to ride in a carriage or on an elephant brought the fear of stumbling or falling. Thereupon, from his residence to the city of Rājagṛha, he excavated a canal for transport and filled it with mustard seeds, so that the boat could rest securely and be towed along by a long rope. Upon arriving at the city of Rājagṛha, he first paid homage to the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One said to him, "King Bimbisāra has ordered a messenger to summon you for no other reason than to see the hair on the soles of your feet." "If the king wishes to see them, you should sit in the cross-legged position. To extend your feet toward the king is a capital offense according to the laws of the country." The elder's son accepted this instruction and went to the court, where he was led in to have an audience. When the king wished to see the hair, he sat in the cross-legged position; the king praised his courtesy and came to cherish him deeply. Once he was able to return, he went back to the place of the Buddha. At that time, the Tathāgata (如來) preached the Dharma and offered him instruction; upon hearing it, he was moved to realization and immediately renounced the household life. Thereupon, he practiced with diligent effort, seeking to realize the fruits of enlightenment; he engaged in walking meditation without rest until his feet began to bleed. The World-Honored One said to him, "Good man, when you were at home as a layman, did you know how to play the lute?" He replied, "I did." "If that is so, take this as an analogy. If the strings are too tight, the sound will not be in harmony; if the strings are too loose, the melody will not be refined. Neither too tight nor too loose, the sound is then harmonious. The practitioner of the path is also like this. If one is too urgent, the body becomes exhausted and the mind weary; if one is too lax, the passions expand and the will becomes dissipated." Having received the Buddha's instruction, he followed it faithfully, and before long, he attained the realization of the fruit.

At the western border of the country, south of the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) River, one reaches the Small Isolated Mountain (小孤山; Skt. asura). Its layered peaks are lofty and precipitous. In the past, the Buddha spent three months of the rainy season retreat here, subduing the yakṣa Bakula (薄句羅). On a large rock below the southeastern cliff of the mountain, there is a trace of where the Buddha sat, which penetrates the stone by more than an inch; it is five feet two inches long and two feet one inch wide, and a stūpa has been built upon it. Next, to the south on the stone, there is a trace where the Buddha placed his kuṇḍikā (捃稚迦) (Original note: This is a washing vessel. The old term was *junchi*, which is a simplified and corrupted form), which is more than an inch deep and fashioned with an eight-petaled flower design. Not far to the southeast of the Buddha’s sitting trace is the footprint of the yakṣa Bakula, which is one foot five or six inches long, seven or eight inches wide, and slightly less than two inches deep. Behind the yakṣa’s footprint is a stone seated image of the Buddha, six or seven feet high. Not far to the west is a place where the Buddha walked in meditation. On the summit of the mountain is the former dwelling of the yakṣa. Next, to the north, is a footprint of the Buddha, one foot eight inches long, over six inches wide, and about half an inch deep; there is a stūpa above this trace. In the past, the Tathāgata subdued the yakṣa, causing him to stop killing people and eating meat, and to respectfully receive the Buddha’s precepts, after which he was reborn in the heavens. To the west of this are six or seven hot springs, the water of which is extremely hot. In the great mountain forests at the southern border of the country, there are many wild elephants, which are immense in size.

From here, traveling east for more than three hundred li along the southern bank of the Ganges (Gaṅgā) River, one arrives at the country of Campā (瞻波國), within the borders of Central India. The country of Campā is more than four thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country has the Ganges River to its north and is more than forty li in circuit. The land is low and damp, and the crops are lush and abundant. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are simple and honest. There are several dozen saṃghārāmas, most of which are dilapidated, with more than two hundred monks who study the teachings of the Hīnayāna. There are more than twenty deva temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together. The walls of the capital city are built of brick, several chang high, with lofty and steep foundations and high, precipitous battlements. In the beginning of the kalpa, when human beings first appeared, they lived in the wild and dwelt in caves, not yet knowing of palaces or houses. Later, a celestial maiden descended among humans and, while wandering by the Ganges and bathing in its currents to please herself, she was spiritually moved and became pregnant, eventually giving birth to four sons. They divided Jambudvīpa among themselves, each ruling over a region, building capitals and constructing towns, and marking out boundaries and borders. This city was the capital of one of those sons, and it was the beginning of all the cities in Jambudvīpa.

Traveling east from here for more than four hundred li, one reaches the country of Kajaṅgala (羯朱嗢祇羅國) (the local people sometimes call it the country of Kayaṅghara [羯蠅揭羅國]; it is within the borders of Central India). The country of Kajaṅgala is more than two thousand li in circuit. The land is moist and marshy, the crops are abundant, the climate is temperate, and the customs are agreeable. The people value high talent and esteem learning and the arts. There are six or seven saṃghārāmas with more than three hundred monks. There are ten deva temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together. For several hundred years, the royal line has been extinct and the country has been subject to neighboring states; for this reason, the walled cities are in ruins, and the people mostly dwell in villages and towns. Therefore, when King Śīlāditya (戒日王) traveled to East India, he built a palace here to manage the affairs of the various states; when he arrived, he thatched a building with grass, and when he departed, he set fire to it. In the southern borders of the country, there are many wild elephants.

From here, crossing the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) to the east and traveling over six hundred li, one arrives at the country of Puṇḍravardhana (奔那伐彈那國) (within the territory of Central India). The country of Puṇḍravardhana is over four thousand li in circuit. The capital city is more than thirty li in circuit. The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, and ponds, pavilions, and flower groves are interspersed throughout. The land is low and damp, and the crops are lush and abundant. The *panasa* (般核娑) fruit is both plentiful and highly valued; the fruit is as large as a winter melon, and when ripe, it turns yellowish-red. When sliced open, it contains several dozen smaller fruits as large as crane eggs, and when these are further broken, they yield a yellowish-red juice with a sweet and delicious taste. Some grow on the tree branches like the fruits of other trees, while others grow from the roots, like *fuling* (伏苓) in the soil. The climate is temperate and pleasant, and the customs favor learning. There are more than twenty saṃghārāmas (伽藍) with over three thousand monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles with equal diligence. There are one hundred deva temples, where followers of various heterodox sects dwell together, and the Nirgrantha (尼乾) ascetics, who go naked, are particularly numerous among their groups.

From here, traveling east for over nine hundred li and crossing a great river, one reaches the country of Kāmarūpa (迦摩縷波國) (in the territory of East India). The country of Kāmarūpa is over ten thousand li in circuit. The capital city is over thirty li in circuit. The land is low and moist, and crops are sown at the proper seasons. Although there are many *panasa* (般核娑 - jackfruit) and *nārikela* (那羅雞羅 - coconut) trees, they are considered very precious. Rivers, lakes, and ponds encircle the cities and towns. The climate is mild and pleasant, and the customs are simple and honest. The people are short in stature and dark in complexion. Their language differs slightly from that of Central India. Their nature is very fierce and impetuous, but they are determined to study diligently. They revere and serve the heavenly gods and do not believe in the Buddha-dharma. Therefore, from the time the Buddha appeared until the present, no monasteries have been built to gather monks. Those who have pure faith only pay homage in secret. There are several hundred deva temples and tens of thousands of non-Buddhists. The reigning king is a descendant of the god Nārāyaṇa and belongs to the Brahman caste; his name is Bhāskaravarman (婆塞羯羅伐摩) (in the language of Tang, "Sun-Armor"), and his title is Kumāra (拘摩羅) (in the language of Tang, "Youth"). Since he first occupied this territory, his family has ruled for a thousand generations down to the present king. The king is fond of learning, and the common people follow his example; men of high talent from distant lands, admiring his righteousness, come to travel as his guests. Although he does not sincerely believe in the Buddha-dharma, he respects learned śramaṇas. Previously, having heard that a śramaṇa from the country of Cīna (至那國) was at the Nālandā (那爛陀) Monastery in Magadha, having come from afar to study the profound Dharma of the Buddha, the king sent cordial invitations back and forth three times, but the monk had not yet complied with the request. At that time, the Master of Treatises Śīlabhadra (尸羅跋陀羅) said, "If you wish to repay the Buddha’s kindness, you must propagate the True Dharma. You should go; do not fear the long journey. The family of King Kumāra (拘摩羅王) has followed non-Buddhist paths for generations, and his invitation to a śramaṇa is a virtuous deed. If he changes his course because of this, the benefits will be vast and far-reaching. You previously aroused a great mind and made a grand vow, wishing to travel alone to foreign lands, casting aside your body to seek the Dharma and universally save all sentient beings—how could this be limited to your own country? You should forget about gain and loss, disregard honor and disgrace, propagate the holy teachings, enlighten the deluded, put others before yourself, and forget personal fame to spread the Dharma."  Thereupon, being unable to decline, he accompanied the envoy and went to meet him. King Kumāra said, "Although I am without talent, I have always admired those of high learning. Having heard of your fame and noble character, I ventured to invite you." He replied, "I am of little ability and narrow wisdom, yet I have undeservedly received your attention."  King Kumāra said, "Excellent! You admire the Dharma and love learning, regarding your own body as light as a feather, crossing heavy dangers to travel far to foreign lands. This is the source of royal transformation and the reason why the customs of your country value learning. Now, in all the countries of India, there are many who sing the 'Music of the King of Qin Breaking the Battle Lines' (秦王破陣樂) of the country of Mahācīna (摩訶至那國); I have heard it for a long time. Is this not the country of the Great Virtuous One?" He replied, "Indeed, this song praises the virtues of my sovereign."  King Kumāra said, "I did not realize that you, Great Virtuous One, were a man of this country. I have always admired its refined culture and have long looked toward the East, but as the mountains and rivers block the way, I have had no means to go there myself." I replied, "The sacred virtues of our great monarch spread far and wide, and his benevolent influence reaches distant lands; those from foreign regions with different customs who come to the imperial palace to pay homage and declare themselves subjects are numerous indeed." King Kumāra said, "Since his grace covers all like heaven and earth, I have long hoped to send tribute. Now King Śīlāditya (戒日王) is in the country of Kajuṅghira (羯朱嗢祇羅國), where he is about to hold a great almsgiving to cultivate merit and wisdom; all the Śramaṇas and Brahmins of the five Indias who possess learning have been summoned to assemble. He has now sent an envoy to invite me, and I wish for you to travel with me." I therefore went with him.  In the eastern part of this country, mountains and hills are interconnected, and there are no large capital cities; as its borders adjoin the Southwest Yi (西南夷), its people resemble the Man (蠻) and Lao (獠) tribes. I inquired in detail about the local customs and learned that one could reach the southwestern borders of Shu (蜀) in about two months' travel; however, the mountains and rivers are treacherous and obstructed, the mountain mists are noxious, and poisonous snakes and herbs cause great harm. In the southeast of the country, wild elephants roam in violent herds, which is why the elephant corps of this country is particularly numerous.

From here, traveling south for one thousand two hundred or one thousand three hundred li, one reaches the country of Samataṭa (三摩呾吒國) (in the territory of eastern India). The country of Samataṭa is more than three thousand li in circuit. It borders the great ocean, and the land is low and damp. The great capital city is more than twenty li in circuit. The crops are lush and the flowers and fruits are abundant. The climate is temperate and the customs are harmonious. The people are fierce by nature, short in stature, and dark in complexion; they are diligent in learning and believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are more than thirty saṃghārāmas with over two thousand monks, all of whom follow the teachings of the Sthavira school. There are one hundred deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths live together, and the naked Nirgrantha ascetics are particularly numerous. Not far from the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. In the past, the Tathāgata preached the profound and wonderful Dharma here for seven days for the sake of devas and humans. Nearby are the sites of the four Buddhas' sitting and walking meditation. Not far from this, in a saṃghārāma, there is a green jade Buddha image eight feet high, with all the physical marks perfectly complete, which frequently manifests miraculous responses.  From here, to the northeast, in a valley by the seaside, is the country of Śrīkṣetra (室利差呾羅國). Next, to the southeast, in a corner of the great ocean, is the country of Kamalāṅkā (迦摩浪迦國). Next, to the east, is the country of Dvāravatī (墮羅鉢底國). Next, to the east, is the country of Īśānapura (伊賞那補羅國). Next, to the east, is the country of Mahācampā (摩訶瞻波國), which is what is called Linyi (林邑) here. Next, to the southwest, is the country of Yamanadvīpa (閻摩那洲國). Regarding these six countries, the mountains and rivers make the roads difficult, so I did not enter their borders; however, their customs and territories can be known by hearsay.

Traveling west from the country of Samataṭa (三摩呾吒國) for over nine hundred li, one reaches the country of Tāmraliptī (耽摩栗底國) (within the borders of East India). The country of Tāmraliptī is about one thousand four or five hundred li in circuit. The capital city is over ten li in circuit. It is situated near the edge of the sea; the land is low and damp. Crops are sown in their proper seasons, and flowers and fruits are abundant. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are impetuous and fierce. The people are courageous and brave, and they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are more than ten saṃghārāmas and over one thousand monks. There are more than fifty deva temples, where followers of different paths live together. As the country is situated on a sea corner where water and land routes meet, rare and precious treasures are gathered here in abundance, and for this reason, the people of the country are generally wealthy. Beside the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. Nearby are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas.

From here, traveling northwest for over seven hundred li, one reaches the country of Karṇasuvarṇa (羯羅拏蘇伐剌那國) (in the territory of East India). The country of Karṇasuvarṇa is four thousand four or five hundred li in circuit. The capital city is over twenty li in circuit. The inhabitants are prosperous and the households are wealthy. The land is low and damp; crops are sown in their proper seasons, and various flowers and precious fruits grow in abundance. The climate is temperate and the customs are honest and harmonious. The people value learning and the arts, and they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are more than ten monasteries with over two thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Sāmmitīya school of the Hīnayāna. There are more than fifty Deva temples, and the number of non-Buddhists is very large. Separately, there are three monasteries where the monks do not consume milk or cream, following the legacy of Devadatta.

Beside the great city is the Raktamṛttika Monastery (Raktamṛttika; Chinese: Red Clay). Its courtyards and buildings are spacious and open, and its towers and pavilions are lofty and steep. The highly talented and profoundly learned scholars of the country, as well as those of renowned intelligence, all assemble therein to assist one another through mutual admonition and to cultivate their morality and virtue.  Formerly, before this country believed in the Buddha-dharma, there was a heretic from South India who bound his belly with copper plates, wore a bright torch upon his head, and, leaning on a staff, walked with proud strides into this city, where he struck the drum of debate and sought to engage in discussion. Someone asked him, "Why do you wear a torch on your head and plates on your belly?" He replied, "My learning and skills are so vast that I fear my belly might burst; I pity the ignorance of others, which is why I carry this light."  Ten days passed, and no one came to question him. They inquired among the eminent and wise, but there was no one who could match him. The king said, "Within the borders of this realm, can there be no wise and enlightened men? To leave a guest's challenge unanswered is a deep shame for the country. We should search further and inquire among those living in seclusion."  Someone said, "In the great forest there is an extraordinary man who calls himself a śramaṇa; he is dedicated to arduous study and has lived here in quiet seclusion for a long time. Were he not one who embodies the Dharma and accords with virtue, how could he live like this?"  The king heard this and went in person to invite him. The śramaṇa replied, "I am a man of South India staying here as a traveler; my learning is superficial, and I fear I may fall short of what you have heard. However, I dare to accept your command and will no longer firmly decline. If I am not defeated in the debate, I request that you build a monastery, gather monks together, and glorify and promote the Buddha-dharma." The king said, "I respectfully hear your words and dare not forget your virtue." The śramaṇa accepted the invitation and went to the site of the debate. The non-Buddhist then recited his tenets, totaling more than thirty thousand words. Their meaning was profound and their phrasing concise; they encompassed all names and characteristics, capturing the sight and hearing of the audience. The śramaṇa, having heard and examined them once, found no errors in the logic or the phrasing, and with a few hundred words, he debated and refuted them, then questioned the non-Buddhist on his tenets. The non-Buddhist, his arguments exhausted and his logic defeated, sealed his mouth and could not respond. Having been refuted in his reputation, he retreated in shame. The king deeply respected the śramaṇa’s virtue and built this monastery; from that time thereafter, the Buddha-dharma was widely propagated. Not far from the side of the monastery is a stūpa, which was built by King Aśoka (無憂王); in the past, the Tathāgata stayed here for seven days to preach the Dharma and provide guidance. Beside it is a mūla-gandha-kuṭī (精舍), the place where the past four Buddhas left traces of sitting and walking in meditation. There are several stūpas, all of which are places where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma, and they were built by King Aśoka.

Traveling southwest from here for over seven hundred li, one reaches the country of Uḍra (烏荼國) (in the region of East India). The country of Uḍra is over seven thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the kingdom is over twenty li in circuit. The land is rich and fertile, and the crops and grains grow luxuriantly; all kinds of fruits are much larger than in other countries, and the exotic grasses and famous flowers are difficult to describe. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are fierce and impetuous. The people are tall and robust in appearance, and their complexions are dark. Their speech and mannerisms differ from those of Central India. They are diligent in learning and mostly believe in the Buddhadharma; there are more than one hundred saṃghārāmas and over ten thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. There are fifty deva temples, where followers of different paths live together. There are more than ten stūpas in total, all of which are places where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma, and were built by King Aśoka.

On the southeastern border of the country, facing the coast of the great ocean, is the city of Caritra (折利呾羅城; translated in Chinese as "Departure"). It is over twenty *li* in circuit and serves as a thoroughfare and stopping place for seafaring merchants and travelers from distant lands. The city is solid and steep, and it contains many rare treasures. Outside the city, five monasteries stand in a row; their terraces and pavilions are lofty, and the sacred images are exquisitely crafted. To the south, the country of Siṃhala (僧伽羅國) is over twenty thousand *li* away; gazing into the distance on a quiet night, one can see the light of the precious pearl atop the Buddha-tooth stūpa of that land, shining clearly like a torch suspended in the air.

From here, traveling southwest through a great forest for more than one thousand two hundred li, one reaches the country of Koṅgoda (恭御陀國) (in the region of East India). The country of Koṅgoda is more than one thousand li in circuit. The capital city is more than twenty li in circuit. It borders the seashore; the mountains and hills are rugged and undulating, the land is low and damp, and crops are sown in their proper seasons. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs of the people are bold and fierce. Their stature is large, and their complexion is black. They possess a rough sense of propriety and righteousness, and are not very deceitful. As for their writing, it is the same as that of Central India, but their language and manner of speech differ considerably. They revere non-Buddhist sects and do not believe in the Buddha-dharma. There are more than one hundred Deva temples and over ten thousand followers of non-Buddhist paths. Within the borders of the country, there are several dozen small towns situated near mountain ranges and occupying the junctions of sea routes. The city walls are strong and steep, and the soldiers are brave and daring; their power dominates the neighboring lands, and thus they have no formidable enemies. The country borders the sea, and there are many rare treasures; conch shells, pearls, and precious stones are used as currency. They produce large dark-colored elephants, which are capable of traveling long distances when ridden.

From here, traveling southwest into a vast wilderness with deep forests and giant trees that reached the sky and obscured the sun, one proceeds for one thousand four or five hundred *li* to the country of Kaliṅga (羯𩜁伽國) (in the region of South India). The country of Kaliṅga is more than five thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city is more than twenty *li* in circuit. Crops are sown in their proper seasons, and flowers and fruits are abundant; forests and marshes stretch continuously for hundreds of *li*. It produces dark wild elephants, which are prized by neighboring countries. The climate is hot, and the customs are impetuous and violent; the people are by nature impatient and fierce, yet they value faith and righteousness. Their speech is rapid and light, their tone is simple and direct, and their diction and style are quite different from those of Central India. Few believe in the true Dharma, and most follow non-Buddhist paths. There are more than ten monasteries with over five hundred monks, who study the teachings of the Mahāyāna Sthavira school. There are more than one hundred *deva* temples, and the number of heterodox practitioners is very great, most of whom are followers of the Nirgrantha. In former times, the country of Kaliṅga was prosperous and densely populated, with shoulders rubbing and wheel hubs clashing, and the raising of sleeves would form a curtain. A sage possessing the five supernatural powers was dwelling in the rocks and cultivating purity; because people insulted and provoked him, he lost his supernatural powers and used evil spells to slaughter the people of the country, leaving no one, young or old, and destroying both the wise and the foolish. Human habitation was cut off for many years. Gradually, people have moved back, but it is still not fully populated; therefore, the number of households in this country is currently small. Not far south of the city is a *stūpa* more than one hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka. Beside it are the sites of the traces of the sitting and walking meditation of the four past Buddhas.

From here, traveling northwest through mountains and forests for over 1,800 li, one reaches the country of Kosala (憍薩羅國) (in the region of Central India). The country of Kosala is over 6,000 li in circumference, with mountain ranges encircling its borders and forests and marshes connected throughout. The capital city of the country is over 40 li in circumference. The soil is rich and fertile, and the land is highly productive. Villages and hamlets look out upon one another, and the households are prosperous and substantial. The people are large in stature and dark in complexion. Their customs are fierce and impetuous, and their nature is brave and violent. They believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings, and they are highly skilled in the arts. The king is a Kṣatriya. He reveres the Buddha-Dharma and is deeply compassionate and far-reaching in his benevolence. There are over one hundred saṃghārāmas, and the number of monks is just under ten thousand; all of them study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. There are over seventy Deva temples, where followers of different paths live together. Not far to the south of the city is an old saṃghārāma, and beside it is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata once manifested great supernatural powers at this place to subdue non-Buddhists. Later, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna (龍猛菩薩) resided in this saṃghārāma. At that time, the king of this country was named Sātavāhana (娑多婆訶) (in Chinese, "Leading the Righteous"). He cherished and respected Nāgārjuna, and he guarded the gates of his residence. At that time, the Bodhisattva Deva (提婆菩薩) came from the country of Siṃhala (執師子國) to seek a debate, and he said to the gatekeeper, "I would be grateful if you would announce my visit." The gatekeeper then went to report this. Nāgārjuna, already well aware of his reputation, filled a bowl to the brim with water and instructed his disciple, saying, "Take this water and show it to that Deva." When Deva saw the water, he silently dropped a needle into it. The disciple took the bowl and returned, feeling puzzled. Nāgārjuna asked, "What did he say?" The disciple replied, "He said nothing, but merely dropped a needle into the water." Nāgārjuna said, "How wise he is, this man! To know the subtle is divine; to perceive the minute is to be a sage. With such great virtue, he should be invited in immediately." The disciple asked, "What does this mean? Is this what you call the marvelous eloquence of silence?" Nāgārjuna said, "Water takes the shape of its container, whether square or round; it adapts to the purity or turbidity of its surroundings; it permeates everywhere without gaps, and its clarity is unfathomable. I showed him the bowl filled to the brim to signify that my learning is complete; he dropped a needle into it, thereby exhausting its depths. This is no ordinary person; he should be summoned at once."  Nāgārjuna’s demeanor was awe-inspiring and commanded respect; all who spoke with him would bow their heads in submission. Deva had long admired his reputation and had long hoped to request instruction. Just as he was about to become a student, he first wished to display his own keen intellect, yet he was also intimidated by Nāgārjuna’s majesty. He ascended the hall, sat to one side, and they discussed the profound mysteries all day long, their discourse clear and lofty. Nāgārjuna said, "Your scholarship surpasses the world and your brilliant eloquence outshines your predecessors. I am but a feeble old man, and meeting such a talented youth truly allows me to pour the contents of my vessel into another and keep the lamp of transmission burning without end; the propagation of the Dharma depends on such a person. I hope you will move to the front seat so that we may discuss the profound mysteries."  Upon hearing this command, Deva, who had been confident in his own mind, prepared to open the storehouse of his arguments and first roam the garden of debate. He raised his points and looked up to challenge the meaning, but suddenly catching sight of Nāgārjuna’s majestic countenance, he forgot his words and fell silent. He moved his seat back, acknowledged his fault, and requested to become his student. Nāgārjuna said, "Sit down again. I shall now bestow upon you the most perfect and wonderful truth, the authentic teaching of the Dharma King." Deva prostrated himself, his five limbs touching the ground, and with a single mind surrendered his life, saying, "From this moment on, I dare to follow your instructions."  Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva was well-versed in the arts of medicine; by consuming elixirs to nourish his life, he lived for several hundred years, his spirit and appearance showing no signs of decline. The king, Sātavāhana (引正王), having obtained the wonderful medicine, also lived for several hundred years. The king had a young son who said to his mother, "At this rate, when will I ever be able to succeed to the throne?" His mother replied, "Judging by the present situation, there is no prospect. Your father the king has already lived for several hundred years, and many of his descendants have already grown old and died. This is all due to the power of Nāgārjuna’s merit and the efficacy of his medical arts. If the Bodhisattva were to pass away, the king would surely perish. Now, Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva possesses vast wisdom and profound compassion; he provides for all living beings and regards his own life as something to be cast aside. You should go to him and try to beg for his head. If you can fulfill this intention, your wish will be granted."  The prince respectfully obeyed his mother’s command and came to the monastery; the gatekeepers were awestruck and fearful, so he was able to enter. At that time, Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva was chanting and walking in meditation. Suddenly seeing the prince, he stopped and asked, "For what reason have you come to the monastery this evening, appearing so anxious and fearful, and rushing here in such haste?" The prince replied, "I have received the words of my compassionate mother, who spoke of those who practice the virtue of giving. She said that for all living beings, life is a precious treasure, and that according to the maxims of the scriptures, there has never been anyone who lightly cast aside their physical body to bestow it upon those who seek it." My compassionate mother said: "It is not so. The Sugatas of the ten directions and the Tathāgatas of the three ages, from the time they first resolved their minds until they attained the fruit of enlightenment, diligently sought the Buddha-way and practiced the precepts and forbearance. Some threw their bodies to feed hungry beasts, some cut their flesh to save a dove; King Candraprabha gave his head to a Brahmin, and King Maitrībala gave his blood to satisfy hungry Yakṣas; examples such as these are truly difficult to enumerate fully. In seeking the sages of the past, what age has been without such people? Now, Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna (龍猛菩薩) is firm in his noble ambitions. I have a request for a human head to use, but though I have sought one for many years, no one has yet offered theirs. If I were to commit a violent robbery and murder, the burden of my sins would be all the greater; to cruelly harm the innocent would make my defiled virtue manifest. Only you, Bodhisattva, who practice the holy path and look toward the distant fruit of Buddhahood, whose compassion moistens all sentient beings and whose kindness reaches the boundless, treat life as lightly as a floating bubble and hold your body as cheaply as rotten wood. Do not violate your original vow, but grant what I request!"  Nāgārjuna said: "Yes, these words are indeed true! I seek the holy fruit of Buddhahood and I learn from the Buddha the ability to renounce all. This body is like an echo, this body is like a bubble; it circulates through the four types of birth and comes and goes through the six realms. Bound by a long-standing great vow, I will not oppose the desires of living beings. However, Prince, there is one thing that is not possible; what shall be done about it? Once my body is finished, your father will also perish. Considering this, who will be able to provide for him?"  Nāgārjuna paced about and looked around, seeking a way to end his life. He cut his own throat with a blade of dry cogon grass as if with a sharp sword, and his head was severed from his body. Seeing this, the prince was terrified and fled. The gatekeeper went up and reported the matter, detailing the beginning and the end; upon hearing this, the king was overcome with grief and, as a result, he also passed away.

Three hundred or more li southwest of the country, one arrives at the mountain of Bhramaragiri (跋邏末羅耆釐山; Tang language: Black Bee). It rises abruptly and loftily, with precipitous peaks and cliffs; having neither slopes nor valleys, it appears to be a single solid rock. King Śātavāha (引正王) excavated this mountain for the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna (龍猛菩薩) to establish a monastery (saṃghārāma). Ten or more li from the mountain, a tunnel was excavated; directly beneath the mountain, they carved upward into the rock. Within it are long corridors and eaves, lofty terraces and multi-storied pavilions; the pavilions have five tiers, and each tier has four courtyards, all containing shrines (mūla-gandha-kuṭī; 精舍) where golden images of the Buddha's size have been cast with exquisite craftsmanship, while the remaining decorations consist entirely of gold and jewels. From the high peaks of the mountain, a waterfall pours down, flowing around the multi-storied pavilions and winding through the corridors and verandas. The outer chambers are perforated to allow light to illuminate the interior. Initially, when King Śātavāha was building this monastery, the labor force was exhausted and the treasury was empty; with the work not yet half finished, his heart was filled with deep sorrow. Nāgārjuna said to him, "Great King, why are you so burdened with worry?" The king replied, "I have given rise to a great aspiration and ventured to establish a supreme field of merit, hoping it would remain firm forever until the coming of Maitreya (慈氏). With the work not yet finished and the financial resources exhausted, I am constantly filled with this regret, sitting and waiting for the dawn." Nāgārjuna said, "Do not worry. The merit of cultivating such supreme goodness is inexhaustible; if one has raised a vast vow, there is no worry that it will not be fulfilled. Return to the palace today and enjoy yourself to the fullest; tomorrow morning, go out for an excursion, travel through the mountains and fields, and then come here to discuss the construction." The king, having received these instructions, followed them accordingly. The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna (龍猛菩薩) used a miraculous medicine, dripping it onto large rocks, which all turned into gold. When the king saw the gold during his excursion, he rejoiced in his heart and words; he drove his carriage back to Nāgārjuna’s place and said, "During my outing today, I was deluded by spirits and ghosts, for I repeatedly saw heaps of gold amidst the mountains and forests." Nāgārjuna replied, "It was not a delusion of ghosts. It is the result of your utmost sincerity that this gold has appeared. You should take and use it immediately to complete your noble undertaking." He then proceeded with the construction, and when the work was finished, there was still a surplus. Thereupon, in each of the five tiers, he cast four large golden statues, and the remainder was still abundant, filling the treasuries. He summoned one thousand monks to reside within and perform rites and recitations. The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna collected and classified the teachings proclaimed by Śākyamuni Buddha and the treatises composed by various Bodhisattvas, storing them within. Thus, the first tier at the top housed only Buddha images and various scriptures and treatises; the fifth tier at the bottom was for the residence of lay servants (淨人) and the storage of property and miscellaneous goods; and the three middle tiers were the lodgings for the monks. I have heard from the records of former sages that after King Śātavāha (引正王) had completed the construction, the cost of salt consumed by the workers was calculated to be nine koṭis (Original note: koṭi is translated into Chinese as one hundred million) of gold coins. Thereafter, the monks fell into disputes and went to the king to seek arbitration. At that time, the lay servants said to one another, "Since a quarrel has arisen among the monks and their arguments are contradictory, evil men will watch for an opening to destroy the monastery." Consequently, they barred the heavy doors to exclude the monks. From that time on, there has been no monastic community there. Looking at the mountain cliffs from afar, one cannot discern any gate or path. At times, those skilled in medical arts were brought inside to treat illnesses; they were blindfolded upon entering and exiting, and thus did not recognize the route.

From this great forest, traveling south for more than nine hundred li, one arrives at the country of Āndhra (案達羅國) (within the borders of South India). The country of Āndhra is more than three thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty li in circuit and is named Vengīpura (瓶耆羅). The land is fertile and rich, and the crops are abundant. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs of the people are fierce and impetuous. Their language and tone of speech differ from those of Central India, but as for their written characters, the rules are largely the same. There are more than twenty monasteries and over three thousand monks. There are more than thirty Deva temples, and the followers of heterodox paths are very numerous. Not far from the side of Vengīpura city is a large monastery with multi-storied pavilions and layered terraces, the craftsmanship of which exhausts the possibilities of carving; the sacred images of the Buddhas are of exquisite and ingenious design. In front of the monastery is a stone stūpa, several hundred feet high, which was built by the Arhat Ācāra (唐言所行, "one who practices" in the language of Tang). Not far to the southwest of the monastery of the Arhat Ācāra is a stūpa built by King Aśoka; in the past, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here, manifested great supernatural powers, and delivered immeasurable multitudes.

Traveling more than twenty *li* southwest from the monastery of the Arhat, one reaches the solitary hill (Vyāsa). On the mountain ridge is a stone *stūpa* where the Bodhisattva Dignāga (which means "bestowed" in the language of Tang) composed the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* (Treatise on Logic).  As for the Bodhisattva Dignāga, after the Buddha had passed away, he followed the tradition and donned the dyed robes. His wisdom and vows were vast and great, and his power of discernment was deep and firm. Pitying the world for having no refuge, he contemplated how to propagate the sacred teachings. Considering that the treatises on logic were profound in language and extensive in reasoning, such that students labored in vain and found it difficult to achieve success, he hid his traces in secluded cliffs and settled his spirit in silent meditation, examining the merits and demerits of past works and scrutinizing the verbosity and conciseness of their meanings.  At that time, the cliffs and valleys shook and echoed, the mist and clouds changed color, and a mountain god lifted the Bodhisattva up several hundred feet, proclaiming: "In the past, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, guided sentient beings through skillful means and, with a compassionate heart, preached the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra*, encompassing wonderful principles and investigating subtle words to their depths. Since the Tathāgata entered extinction, the great meaning has been cut off. Now, the Bodhisattva Dignāga, whose merit and wisdom are vast and far-reaching, and who deeply understands the sacred intent, shall once again propagate the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* on this day."  The Bodhisattva then emitted a great light, illuminating the darkness. At that time, the king of this country felt deep respect; seeing this manifestation of light, he suspected the Bodhisattva had entered the *vajra-samādhi* and therefore requested that the Bodhisattva certify the fruit of non-arising. Dignāga said: "I have entered meditation to observe and wish to explain the profound scriptures; my heart is set on perfect enlightenment, not on the fruit of non-arising." The king said: "The fruit of non-arising is something all sages admire; it severs the desires of the three realms and provides mastery of the three types of supernormal knowledge—this is a magnificent achievement, and I hope you will realize it quickly." At that time, Dignāga (陳那) was pleased by the king’s request and was about to realize and accept the holy fruit of the *aśaikṣa* (no-more-learning). At that moment, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī (妙吉祥菩薩) knew of this and felt it was a pity; wishing to warn him, he snapped his fingers to awaken him and said: "What a pity! How can you abandon the vast and great mind for a narrow and inferior intention, following a desire for individual salvation while discarding the vow to benefit others? If you wish to perform a virtuous benefit, you should widely propagate the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (瑜伽師地論) composed by the Bodhisattva Maitreya (慈氏菩薩) to guide and encourage later students; the benefit of this is truly great." The Bodhisattva Dignāga respectfully accepted this instruction and followed it faithfully. Thereupon, he pondered deeply and researched extensively the treatises on *hetuvidyā* (logic). Fearing that students might be intimidated by the subtlety of the text and the conciseness of the language, he extracted the essential meanings and synthesized the profound words to compose the *Nyāyamukha* (因門論) in order to guide those who would come after. From this time forward, he propagated the *Yogācāra* (瑜伽), and his flourishing work and disciples were known throughout the world.

From this forest and wilderness, traveling south for more than a thousand *li*, one arrives at the country of Dhānakaṭaka (馱那羯磔迦國; also called the Great Andhra country; it is within the borders of South India). The country of Dhānakaṭaka is more than six thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than forty *li* in circuit. The land is fertile and rich, and the crops are abundant. There is much wilderness and few settlements. The climate is warm and hot, and the people are dark in complexion. Their nature is fierce and impetuous, and they are fond of learning the arts. The monasteries are arranged like the scales of a fish, but they are already very desolate; those that remain number more than twenty, with over a thousand monks, all of whom mostly study the teachings of the Mahāsāṃghika school. There are more than a hundred Deva temples, and the followers of heterodox paths are very numerous.

To the east of the city, resting on a mountain, is the Pūrvaśaila (Eastern Mountain) Monastery; to the west of the city, resting on a mountain, is the Avaraśaila (Western Mountain) Monastery. These were built for the Buddha by a former king of this country. They are situated along rivers and connected by paths, with pavilions perched upon cleared cliffs, and long corridors and covered walkways resting against the rocks and joining the peaks; they are guarded by divine spirits and frequented by sages and saints. Within the millennium following the Buddha’s nirvana, a thousand ordinary monks would gather each year to enter the summer retreat; on the day the retreat concluded, they would all attain arhatship and depart by rising into the air through their supernatural powers. After the millennium, ordinary and holy monks lived there together. For over a hundred years, there have been no more monks, and the mountain spirits have changed their forms—sometimes appearing as jackals and wolves, other times as apes and monkeys—to terrify travelers; for this reason, the place is desolate and devoid of any monastic community.

To the west of the city, resting on a mountain, is the Avaraśaila (meaning "West Mountain") Monastery, which a former king of this country built for the Buddha. It is situated above a river and connected by paths, with cliffs cleared to support pavilions, long corridors, and covered walkways, all resting against the crags and joining the peaks; divine spirits guard and protect it, and sages and saints have frequented it to rest. Within the millennium following the Buddha’s nirvana, a thousand ordinary monks would enter the summer retreat there together each year; on the day the retreat concluded, they would all attain arhatship and depart by rising into the void through their supernatural powers. After that millennium, ordinary people and sages lived there together. For the past hundred years or so, there have been no more monks, and the mountain spirits have changed their forms—sometimes appearing as jackals or wolves, other times as apes or monkeys—to terrify travelers. For this reason, the place has become desolate and is devoid of any monastic community.

Not far to the south of the city is a great mountain crag, the place where the master of treatises Bhāviveka (in Tang language, Qingbian) resided in the palace of the Asuras, awaiting the appearance of Maitreya Bodhisattva to attain Buddhahood. The master of treatises possessed a refined character that was vast and far-reaching, and his supreme virtue was profound and deep; outwardly he displayed the attire of the Sāṃkhya, while inwardly he promoted the teachings of Nāgārjuna. Hearing that the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla in the country of Magadha was propagating the teachings of the Dharma and had several thousand students, he felt a desire to engage in discussion, so he took up his staff and set out. Upon arriving at the city of Pāṭaliputra, he learned that the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla was at the Bodhi Tree (Mahā-bodhi). The master of treatises then instructed his disciple, saying: "Go to the place of the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla at the Bodhi Tree and convey my words as follows: 'The Bodhisattva propagates the bequeathed teachings and guides the deluded; I have long looked up to your virtue with a humble mind. However, because my past vows have not yet been fulfilled, I have missed the opportunity to pay my respects. As for the Bodhi Tree, I vow not to see it in vain; when I see it, there must be a realization, and I shall proclaim you the teacher of gods and men.'" The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla said to his messenger: "The human world is like an illusion, and life is like a floating bubble; I am diligent and sincere in my thirst for the sun, and have no time for discussion." Messengers went back and forth, but they never met. After the master of treatises returned to his native land, he reflected in silence: "If Maitreya does not attain Buddhahood, who can resolve my doubts?" Before an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, he recited the *Hṛdaya-dhāraṇī* (Original note: *Suixin tuoluoni*), abstaining from grain and drinking only water for a period of three years. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva then manifested a wondrous physical form and said to the master of treatises: "What is your aspiration?" He replied, "I wish to preserve this body to wait until I see Maitreya (慈氏)." Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva said, "Human life is precarious and fragile, and the world is a floating illusion; you should cultivate superior and virtuous vows to be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven (覩史多天), where you may pay homage and meet him more quickly." The master of treatises said, "My will cannot be swayed, and my heart cannot be divided." The Bodhisattva said, "If that is the case, you should go to the mountain cave south of the city of the country of Dhānyakaṭaka (馱那羯磔迦國) to the abode of the Vajrapāṇi (執金剛) deity; if you recite the *Vajrapāṇi-dhāraṇī* (執金剛陀羅尼) with utmost sincerity, this vow shall be fulfilled." The master of treatises then went there and recited it. After three years, the deity asked him, "What is your wish, that you are so diligent and earnest?" The master of treatises said, "I wish to preserve this body to wait until I see Maitreya. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva directed me to come and request your aid; is it not in your power to fulfill my vow?" The deity then bestowed a secret method upon him and said, "Inside this rock is the Asura Palace (阿素洛宮); if you perform the ritual according to the Dharma and make your request, the stone wall shall open. Once it opens, you may enter and wait there to see him." The master of treatises said, "If I dwell in seclusion and see nothing, how will I know when the Buddha has arisen?" The Vajrapāṇi deity replied, "When Maitreya appears in the world, I shall inform you." The master of treatises accepted this instruction and practiced the recitation with focused intensity. After another three years had passed, without ever having a different thought, he enchanted mustard seeds and struck the rock with them; the stone wall suddenly split open. At that time, hundreds of thousands of people watched, forgetting to return home. The master of treatises (śāstra-master) stepped across the threshold and announced to the crowd, "I have long prayed, waiting to see Maitreya (慈氏); through the protection of the holy spirits, my great vow is now fulfilled. You should all enter here to witness the arising of the Buddha together." Those who heard this were terrified and none dared to step through the entrance, claiming it was a den of venomous snakes and fearing they would lose their lives. After he exhorted them repeatedly, only six people followed him inside. The master of treatises looked back to bid farewell to the crowd and entered with composure. Once he had entered, the stone wall closed back up. The crowd all lamented and sighed, regretting their previous words.

From here, traveling southwest for more than a thousand *li*, one reaches the country of Cuḷya (珠利耶國) (in the region of South India). The country of Cuḷya is two thousand four or five hundred *li* in circumference. The capital city is more than ten *li* in circumference. The land is wild and desolate, with marshes and wastes. The population is sparse, and bands of robbers operate openly. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are treacherous. The people are fierce and violent by nature, and they revere and believe in non-Buddhist paths. The monasteries are dilapidated, with only a few monks. There are several dozen *deva* temples, mostly belonging to the naked ascetics. Not far to the southeast of the city is a *stūpa* built by King Aśoka. In the past, the Tathāgata manifested great supernatural powers at this place, preached the profound and subtle Dharma, subdued the non-Buddhists, and saved various heavenly beings and humans. Not far to the west of the city is an old monastery, the place where the Bodhisattva Deva debated with an Arhat. Initially, the Bodhisattva Deva heard that there was an Arhat in this monastery named Uttara (Original note: *Uttara* is translated as "Superior" in Chinese), who had attained the six supernatural powers and was endowed with the eight emancipations; he therefore came from afar to seek him out and observe his demeanor. Upon arriving at the monastery, he requested to stay with the Arhat. The Arhat was of few desires and knew contentment, possessing only one bed. When Deva arrived, there was nothing to use as a seat, so he gathered fallen leaves and instructed him to sit upon them. The Arhat entered into meditation and did not emerge until midnight. Deva then presented his doubts and requested resolutions; the Arhat explained each difficulty as it was raised. Deva followed his words with repeated questioning, and by the seventh round, the Arhat remained silent and could not respond, so he secretly exercised his supernatural powers to go to the Tuṣita Heaven to consult Maitreya. Maitreya (慈氏) provided the explanation and told him: "That Deva (提婆) has practiced for vast kalpas and shall succeed to the Buddha's throne during the Bhadrakalpa (賢劫); this is beyond your knowledge, and you should pay him deep respect." In the space of a finger-snap, he returned to his original seat, whereupon he expounded the wonderful meanings and analyzed the subtle words. Deva said to him: "This is the explanation from the holy wisdom of Maitreya Bodhisattva; how could it be something you have investigated thoroughly on your own?" The Arhat replied: "Indeed, it is the intent of the Tathāgata." Thereupon, he left his seat to offer thanks and expressed deep reverence and admiration.

From here, traveling south into the wilderness for fifteen or sixteen hundred li, one reaches the country of Draviḍa (達羅毘荼國) (in the territory of South India). The country of Draviḍa is over six thousand li in circumference, and its capital city, called Kāñcīpura (逮志補羅), is over thirty li in circumference. The land is fertile and rich, with abundant crops, many flowers and fruits, and it produces precious treasures. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs of the people are brave and fierce. They are deeply devoted to faith and righteousness, and are noble and learned, though their language and script differ slightly from those of Central India. There are over one hundred saṃghārāmas and more than ten thousand monks, all of whom follow the teachings of the Sthavira school. There are over eighty Deva temples, mostly belonging to the naked ascetics. When the Tathāgata was in the world, he frequently traveled to this country to preach the Dharma and save people, and for this reason, King Aśoka (無憂王) built stūpas at all the sacred sites. The city of Kāñcīpura is the birthplace of the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla (達磨波羅) (in Tang language, "Protector of the Dharma"). The Bodhisattva was the eldest son of a high minister of this country. In his youth, he possessed a refined character, and as he grew, his aspirations became vast. When he reached the age of twenty, a princess was betrothed to him. On the evening of the wedding ceremony, he felt deeply distressed and prayed earnestly before an image of the Buddha. Moved by his utmost sincerity, a deity carried him far away to a mountain saṃghārāma several hundred li from there, where he sat within the Buddha hall. A monk opened the door and, seeing this youth, suspected him of being a thief and questioned him further. The Bodhisattva explained his situation in full and requested to leave the household life. The assembly was astonished and subsequently granted his wish. The king then issued a decree to search far and near, and thus learned that the Bodhisattva had been carried away to a distant land by a deity. Upon learning this, the king’s respect and wonder increased all the more. After the Bodhisattva had dyed his robes (i.e., entered the monastic life), he studied with diligent sincerity, and his excellent reputation and conduct are described in the preceding record. Not far to the south of the city is a large saṃghārāma where the wise and learned of the country gather and reside. There is a stūpa over one hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here, subduing the followers of external paths and extensively saving humans and devas. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas.

From here, traveling south for more than three thousand *li*, one reaches the country of Malakūṭa (秣羅矩吒國) (also called the country of Kumārī (枳秣羅國); it is within the borders of South India). The country of Malakūṭa is more than five thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city is more than forty *li* in circuit. The soil is salty and barren, and the land is not fertile. Many precious items from the islands of the sea are gathered in this country. The climate is hot, and the people are mostly dark-skinned. Their dispositions are fierce and unyielding, and they revere both heterodox and orthodox teachings. They do not value the arts, but are skilled only in the pursuit of profit. There are many ruins of old monasteries, but few remain standing, and the monks are also scarce. There are several hundred *deva* temples, and the followers of non-Buddhist paths are very numerous, many of whom are ascetics who go naked. Not far to the east of the city is an old monastery; its courtyards and buildings are desolate, but the foundations still remain, having been built by the Great King (Mahendra), the younger brother of King Aśoka. To its east is a *stūpa* whose high foundation has sunk, though the inverted-bowl dome still exists, established by King Aśoka. In the past, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here, manifested great supernatural powers, and saved immeasurable multitudes; this was built to mark these sacred traces. As time has passed, it has become increasingly miraculous, and prayers are sometimes fulfilled.

To the northeast of this mountain, by the seaside, there is a city which is on the route to the country of Siṃhala (執師子國) in the South Sea. I have heard from the local people that if one enters the sea from here and travels southeast for more than three thousand li, one reaches the country of Siṃhala (in the language of the Tang, this means "Holder of Lions"; it is not within the borders of India).

In the southeastern corner of the country is Mount Laṅkā (䮚迦山), with its steep cliffs and deep valleys where spirits and ghosts dwell; it is here that the Tathāgata formerly preached the Laṅkā Sūtra (the old name, Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra [楞伽經], is an error).

From the country of Draviḍa (達羅毘荼國), traveling north into the forests and wilderness, passing isolated cities and small towns where bands of brigands harm travelers, one journeys over two thousand *li* to reach the country of Konkaṇapura (荼建那補羅國) (Original note: in the region of South India). The country of Konkaṇapura is over five thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city is over thirty *li* in circuit. The land is fertile and crops are abundant. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are impetuous and fierce. The people are dark-complexioned and their temperaments are wild and violent. They are fond of learning and value virtue and the arts. There are over one hundred monasteries and more than ten thousand monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles with equal diligence. There are several hundred *deva* temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together. Beside the royal palace is a large monastery with over three hundred monks, who are truly men of outstanding talent. In the great *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) of this monastery, which is over one hundred feet high, is the precious crown of Prince Sarvārthasiddha (一切義成太子). It is slightly less than two feet high, adorned with precious jewels, and kept in a jeweled casket. Whenever a fast day arrives, it is brought out and placed on a high seat to be worshipped with incense and flowers, and at times it emits a brilliant light. Beside the city, in a large monastery, there is a *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* over fifty feet high, containing a sandalwood statue of Maitreya Bodhisattva (慈氏菩薩) over ten feet tall. On fast days, it sometimes shines with a divine light; it is said to have been made by the Arhat Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi (二百億羅漢). Not far to the north of the city is a forest of *tāla* trees, over thirty *li* in circuit. Its leaves are long and broad, and their color is glossy and smooth; all the various countries use them for writing. In the forest there is a stūpa, which is the site of the traces of the sitting and walking meditation of the four past Buddhas. Beside it is a stūpa said to contain the bodily relics of the Arhat Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi (二百億羅漢). Not far to the east of the city is a stūpa; its base has already collapsed and sunk, and it remains three *zhang* high. According to ancient records, it contains relics of the Tathāgata, and on fast days it sometimes shines with a divine light. In the past, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here and manifested his supernatural powers to save the multitudes of living beings. Not far to the southwest of the city is a stūpa over a hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). It is said that the Arhat Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi manifested great supernatural powers here to transform and save living beings. Beside it is a monastery, of which only the foundations remain, which was built by that Arhat.

From here, traveling northwest into a great forest and wilderness, one encounters ferocious beasts and cruel bands of robbers. After traveling two thousand four or five hundred li, one reaches the country of Mahārāṣṭra (摩訶剌侘國) (in the territory of South India). The country of Mahārāṣṭra is over six thousand li in circumference. The capital city borders a great river on the west and is over thirty li in circumference. The soil is fertile and the crops are abundant. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are simple and honest. The people are tall and sturdy in stature and proud and carefree by nature; they never fail to repay a kindness or avenge a grievance. If someone insults them, they will risk their lives to take vengeance; if someone is in desperate straits and seeks their aid, they will forget their own safety to assist them. When they intend to take revenge, they must first notify their opponent; both sides then don sturdy armor before engaging in battle. When pursuing a retreating enemy on the battlefield, they do not kill those who have surrendered. If a general or soldier suffers a defeat, he is not punished; instead, he is presented with women’s clothing, and, feeling ashamed, he will take his own life. The state maintains several hundred warriors. Whenever they are about to engage in a decisive battle, they drink until they are intoxicated; a single one of these men can break the vanguard, causing ten thousand men to lose their edge. If they happen to harm someone, the state does not impose punishment; whenever they go out, they have drums beaten to lead the way. Furthermore, they keep several hundred ferocious elephants. When they are about to engage in battle, these elephants are also given wine to drink; they then charge in a group, trampling everything, with no firm enemy able to stand before them. The king relies on these men and elephants to lightly treat and bully neighboring countries. The king is of the Kṣatriya (剎帝利) caste and is named Pulakeśin (補羅稽舍). His strategies and plans are far-reaching, and his benevolence is widely extended; his subjects serve him with the utmost loyalty. Currently, the great King Śīlāditya (戒日大王) campaigns from the east to the west, bringing distant lands to submission and near lands to order; only the people of this country alone refuse to acknowledge his suzerainty. Although he has repeatedly led the armored troops of the Five Indias and summoned the heroic generals of many nations to personally lead an invasion, he has yet to achieve victory. Such is their military, and such are their customs. The people are known for their love of learning, and they revere both the heterodox and the orthodox. There are over one hundred saṃghārāmas (伽藍) with more than five thousand monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles with equal diligence. There are hundreds of Deva temples, and the heterodox sects are very numerous. Inside and outside the great city, there are five stūpas (窣堵波), all of which are sites where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation, built by King Aśoka (無憂王).
