As for the other stone and brick stūpas, their number is so great that it is difficult to enumerate them all. Not far to the south of the city is an old saṃghārāma, in which there is a stone image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩); its spiritual efficacy is secretly felt, and those who pray for wishes often see them fulfilled.

On the eastern border of the country is a great mountain (Pravaragiri) with overlapping ridges and connected barriers, and layered peaks with sheer cliffs. There is a monastery situated in a deep valley, with lofty halls and spacious chambers built against the cliffs and peaks; its multi-storied pavilions and tiered terraces lean against the rocks and face the gully. It was built by the Arhat Ācāra (which means "the one who acts" in the language of the Tang). The Arhat was a man from West India. After his mother passed away, he observed where she had been reborn and saw that she had taken a woman's body in this country. The Arhat then came to this place, intending to guide and transform her, accepting her according to her capacity. He entered the village to beg for food and arrived at the house where his mother had been reborn. When the girl brought food to offer as alms, her milk began to flow; when her relatives saw this, they considered it an ill omen. The Arhat explained the original karmic causes, and the woman then attained the holy fruit. Feeling gratitude for the grace of his birth and cherishing the karmic conditions that brought it about, the Arhat built this monastery to repay her profound virtue. The great vihara (mūla-gandha-kuṭī) of the monastery is over a hundred feet high, and within it is a stone Buddha statue more than seventy feet tall. Above it are seven stone canopies, suspended in the void without any attachments, with a space of more than three feet between each canopy. I have heard from the records of those before me that this is sustained by the power of the Arhat’s vows; others say it is by the power of supernatural faculties; still others say it is the work of medicinal arts. Upon examining the actual records, the cause remains unclear. The four walls of the vihara are carved with stone reliefs depicting the various causal deeds of the Tathāgata when he was formerly practicing the Bodhisattva path. The auspicious signs of his attainment of the holy fruit and the spiritual responses upon his entry into nirvana are all carved in detail, leaving nothing out. Outside the gate of the monastery, there is a stone elephant at each of the four positions: south, north, left, and right. According to the local people, these elephants occasionally roar loudly, causing the earth to tremble. In the past, the Bodhisattva Dignāga (陳那) frequently resided in this monastery.

From here, traveling west for over a thousand li and crossing the Narmada River (耐秣陀河), one reaches the country of Bharukacchapa (跋祿羯呫婆國) (in the region of South India). The country of Bharukacchapa is two thousand four or five hundred li in circuit. The capital city is over twenty li in circuit. The land is saline and barren, with sparse vegetation. The people boil seawater to make salt and rely on the sea for their livelihood. The climate is hot, and swirling winds rise up frequently. The local customs are mean and thin, and the people’s nature is deceitful and cunning. They do not study arts or crafts, and they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are more than ten sanghārāmas (伽藍) with over three hundred monks, who study the teachings of the Mahāyāna Sthavira school. There are more than ten deva temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together.

From here, traveling northwest for more than two thousand li, one reaches the country of Mālava (摩臘婆國) (also known as the country of Lāṭa; it is within the borders of South India). The country of Mālava is more than six thousand li in circumference. The capital city is more than thirty li in circumference and is situated to the southeast of the Mahī River. The land is fertile, agriculture is flourishing, the vegetation is lush, and flowers and fruits are abundant. It is particularly suitable for winter wheat, and the people eat mostly cakes and parched grain. The nature of the people is gentle and compliant; they are generally intelligent, their speech is elegant and clear, and their learning and arts are profound. Within the borders of the Five Indias, two countries place great importance on learning: the country of Mālava in the southwest and the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) in the northeast; they value virtue, honor benevolence, and are brilliant and diligent in their studies. However, in this country, both heterodox and orthodox beliefs are practiced. There are several hundred saṃghārāmas with more than twenty thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Sammatiya school of the Lesser Vehicle. There are several hundred deva temples, and the number of heterodox practitioners is substantial; most of them are followers who smear themselves with ashes. The local records state: sixty years ago, there was a king named Śīlāditya (唐言戒日, "Sun of Virtue" in the language of Tang). His ingenuity and wisdom were brilliant, his talent and learning were vast and sharp, he cherished and nurtured the four types of living beings, and he revered and honored the Three Jewels. From his birth until his death, his countenance never showed anger, and his hands never harmed a living creature. When his elephants and horses drank water, he would have it filtered first, fearing that he might injure the life-force of the water. His benevolence was such as this. During his reign of more than fifty years, wild beasts became familiar with humans, and the people of the entire country refrained from killing. Beside the palace, he built a monastery (mūla-gandha-kuṭī) with the utmost craftsmanship and exquisite adornment, and within it were fashioned images of the seven World-Honored Buddhas. Every year, he regularly held a Great Pañcavārṣika Assembly, gathering monks from all directions to provide them with the four monastic requisites, whether in the form of the three robes and religious implements, or various rare treasures of the seven precious gems. This tradition has been passed down through successive generations, and this noble practice has never ceased.

More than twenty *li* northwest of the great city, one arrives at the Brahmin village (Brāhmaṇagrāma). Nearby is a deep pit; during the autumn and summer, despite heavy and persistent rains that last for ten days, and although it receives many streams, the water never accumulates. Beside it, a small stūpa has been built. According to ancient records, this is the place where a highly arrogant Brahmin fell into hell while still alive.  Formerly, in this village, there was a Brahmin who was naturally wise and widely learned, his scholarship surpassing that of the eminent men of his time. He had thoroughly investigated the profound mysteries of both internal and external scriptures, and the abstruse texts of astronomy and mathematics were as clear to him as if he were looking at the palm of his own hand. His character was noble and refined, and his reputation spread far and wide. The king held him in great esteem and respect, and the people of the country honored him. He had thousands of disciples who admired his way and were drawn to his influence.  He would often say, "I have appeared in this world to expound the sacred and guide the ordinary; neither the sages of the past nor the philosophers of the future can compare to me. People are all swept up in following Maheśvara, Vāsudeva, Nārāyaṇa, and the World-Honored Buddha; they propagate their doctrines, paint their images, and vie with one another to offer them worship. Now, since my virtue exceeds theirs and my fame dominates the age, if I do not do something different, how can I manifest my greatness?"  He then used red sandalwood to carve images of Maheśvara, Vāsudeva, Nārāyaṇa, and the World-Honored Buddha. He made a four-legged seat for them, and wherever he went, he carried them with him. Such was his arrogance. At that time, in Western India, there was a bhikṣu named Bhadraruci (in Chinese, "Virtuous Love" [賢愛]), who had attained the pinnacle of *hetuvidyā* (logic) and had deeply exhausted the study of heterodox doctrines. His moral conduct was pure and refined, the fragrance of his precepts was intense, and he was possessed of few desires and contentment, seeking nothing from the world. Upon hearing of this, he sighed and said, "Alas! The times are devoid of men, allowing that foolish fellow to dare to practice such wicked deeds." Thereupon, he shouldered his khakkhara (monk's staff) and traveled from afar, arriving in this country, where he fully explained his long-held intention to the king. When the king saw his tattered robes, he did not feel much respect in his heart, yet he esteemed his ambition and reluctantly accorded him the proper courtesies. He then set up a debate seat and informed the Brahmin. The Brahmin heard this and laughed, saying, "Who is that person, that he dares to harbor such an ambition?" He ordered his followers to come to the debate arena, and hundreds of thousands of people gathered before and behind to listen. Bhadraruci wore his tattered, old robes and spread out grass to sit upon. The Brahmin sat perched upon the seat he had brought, denouncing the true Dharma and expounding his heterodox doctrines. The bhikṣu’s clear eloquence flowed like a stream, circling back and forth in argument. After a long time, the Brahmin admitted defeat. The king then said to him, "You have long abused a false reputation, deceiving your superiors and confusing the masses. The ancient codes record that one who loses a debate must be executed." He intended to use a red-hot iron seat to make him sit upon it. The Brahmin, in dire straits, surrendered and begged for his life. Bhadraruci took pity on him and petitioned the king, saying, "Great King, your benevolence and propriety are known far and wide, and your praises fill the roads; you should spread compassionate nurturance rather than practicing cruelty. Forgive his inadequacies and let him go as he pleases." The king ordered him to ride a donkey and announce his defeat throughout the city and its suburbs. The Brahmin, ashamed of this humiliation, became enraged and vomited blood. Upon hearing of this, a bhikṣu went to comfort him, saying, "Your learning encompasses both internal and external doctrines, and your reputation is known far and wide; you should clearly understand the nature of honor and disgrace, and when to advance or retreat. As for fame, what reality does it possess?" The Brahmin, filled with resentment, bitterly reviled the bhikṣu, slandered the Mahāyāna, and spoke with contempt of the ancient sages. Before his words had even died away, the earth split asunder, and he fell alive into the pit; the traces of this event still remain.

From here, traveling southwest into a maritime bay and then northwest for two thousand four or five hundred *li*, one reaches the country of Aṭali (阿吒釐國), which is within the borders of South India. The country of Aṭali is more than six thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty *li* in circuit. The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, and precious treasures are accumulated in abundance. Although agriculture is practiced, the people make their living through trade. The land is sandy and saline, and flowers and fruits are scarce. It produces the black pepper tree, the leaves of which resemble those of the Sichuan pepper. It also produces the frankincense tree, the leaves of which resemble those of the flowering pear. The climate is hot, and there is much wind and dust. The nature of the people is shallow and fickle; they value wealth and despise virtue. Their script, language, customs, and laws are largely the same as those of the country of Mālava (摩臘婆國). Most do not believe in merit, and even among those who do, they revere and serve the heavenly deities. There are more than ten temples, where various heterodox sects dwell together.

Traveling northwest from the country of Mālava (摩臘婆國) for three days, one reaches the country of Kaṭṭa (契吒國) (within the borders of South India). The country of Kaṭṭa is more than three thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city is over twenty *li* in circuit. The population is dense, and the households are wealthy. There is no great sovereign; it is subject to the country of Mālava, and its climate, products, and customs are consequently the same as that country. There are more than ten monasteries and over one thousand monks, who study both the Great and Small Vehicles with equal diligence. There are several dozen *deva* temples, and the non-Buddhists are numerous.

From here, traveling north for more than one thousand *li*, one arrives at the country of Valabhī (伐臘毘國) (also called the country of Bīlala; it is within the borders of Southern India). The country of Valabhī is more than six thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city is more than thirty *li* in circuit. The produce of the land, the suitability of the climate, and the customs and human nature of the people are the same as in the country of Mālava (摩臘婆國). The inhabitants are prosperous, and the households are wealthy; there are more than one hundred families who have accumulated wealth of one hundred *yuta* (hundreds of millions). Rare goods from distant regions are mostly gathered in this country. There are more than one hundred *saṃghārāma*s, with more than six thousand monks, who mostly study the teachings of the Hīnayāna Saṃmitīya school. There are several hundred *deva* temples, and the heterodox sects are very numerous. When the Tathāgata was in the world, he frequently traveled to this country; therefore, King Aśoka erected markers and built *stūpa*s at all the places where the Buddha stopped. The sites where the three past Buddhas sat, walked, and preached the Dharma are interspersed among them.  The current king is of the Kṣatriya caste; he is the nephew of the former King Śīlāditya of the country of Mālava and the son-in-law of the current King Śīlāditya of the country of Kanyākubja (羯若鞠闍國). His name is Dhruvabhaṭa (杜魯婆跋吒) (in the language of Tang, this means "Permanently Intelligent"). His temperament is impetuous, and his wisdom and strategy are shallow. However, he has pure faith in the Three Jewels. Every year, he holds a great assembly for seven days, offering rare treasures and superior delicacies to the community of monks. He gives away the value of the three robes and medicines, as well as rare and precious treasures of the seven kinds, and then redeems them at double their price. He values virtue and honors the worthy; he follows the Way and respects learning. He shows special reverence and respect to high-ranking monks from distant regions. Not far from the city is a great monastery (saṃghārāma) established by the Arhat Ācāra, where the Bodhisattvas Guṇamati and Sthiramati resided and composed treatises that are widely circulated.

From here, traveling northwest for over seven hundred li, one reaches the country of Ānandapura (in the territory of Western India). The country of Ānandapura is over two thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is over twenty li in circuit. The population is dense and the households are wealthy. There is no great sovereign, and it is subject to the country of Mālava. The soil, climate, and the rules of writing are also the same as there. There are more than ten sanghārāmas, with fewer than one thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Sāmmitīya school of the Lesser Vehicle. There are several dozen deva temples, where followers of various paths live together.

Traveling westward from the kingdom of Valabhī (伐臘毘國) for over five hundred li, one reaches the kingdom of Suraṭṭha (蘇剌侘國) (in the territory of Western India). The kingdom of Suraṭṭha is over four thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the kingdom is over thirty li in circuit and borders the Mahī River (莫醯河) to the west. The inhabitants are numerous and their households are wealthy. It is subject to the kingdom of Valabhī. The land is saline and alkaline, and flowers and fruits are scarce. Although the cold and heat are balanced, the wind blows incessantly. The local customs are shallow and the people’s temperament is impulsive. They do not care for learning arts, and they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are over fifty saṃghārāmas (伽藍) with more than three thousand monks, who mostly study the teachings of the Mahāyāna Sthavira school. There are over one hundred deva temples, where various non-Buddhist sects dwell together. As the country lies on the route to the Western Sea, the people all rely on the benefits of the sea, engaging in trade as their profession and exchanging goods to supply what is lacking.

Traveling north from the country of Valabhī (伐臘毘國) for more than 1,800 li, one reaches the country of Gūrjara (瞿折羅國) (in the region of Western India). The country of Gūrjara is more than 5,000 li in circuit. The capital city is named Bhīlamāla (毘羅摩羅), and it is more than 30 li in circuit. The soil, climate, and customs are the same as those of the country of Surāṣṭra (蘇剌侘國). The inhabitants are prosperous, and their households are wealthy. They mostly serve non-Buddhist paths and have little faith in the Buddha’s teachings. There is one monastery with more than 100 monks, who study the teachings of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) according to the Sarvāstivāda school. There are several dozen Deva temples where followers of various non-Buddhist paths live together. The king is of the Kṣatriya caste; he is in the prime of his youth, his wisdom and courage are far-reaching, he deeply believes in the Buddha’s teachings, and he holds noble and extraordinary talents in high regard.

Traveling southeast from here for over 2,800 li, one reaches the country of Ujjayanī (鄔闍衍那國) (in the territory of South India). The country of Ujjayanī is over 6,000 li in circuit. The capital city is over 30 li in circuit. The soil, climate, and customs are the same as those of the country of Surāṣṭra (蘇剌侘國). The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, and the families are wealthy. There are several dozen saṃghārāmas, most of which are dilapidated, with only three or five remaining in use. There are over 300 monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles. There are several dozen Deva temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together. The king is of the Brāhmaṇa caste; he is widely read in heterodox texts and does not believe in the true Dharma. Not far from the city is a stūpa, which is the site where King Aśoka created a hell.

Traveling northeast from here for more than a thousand *li*, one arrives at the country of Zhizhituo (擲枳陀國) (within the borders of South India). The country of Zhizhituo is more than four thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city of the country is fifteen or sixteen *li* in circuit. The soil is described as fertile, and the crops are abundant; it is suitable for beans and wheat, and there are many flowers and fruits. The climate is temperate and pleasant, and the people are gentle and compliant by nature. They mostly believe in non-Buddhist paths and have little respect for the Buddhadharma. There are several dozen *saṃghārāmas* (monasteries), but few monks. There are more than ten *deva* temples, and over a thousand followers of non-Buddhist paths. The king is of the Brahmin caste; he is a devout believer in the Three Jewels and holds virtuous people in high esteem, so many learned scholars from various regions gather in this country.

From here, traveling northward for more than nine hundred li, one reaches the country of Maheśvarapura (in the region of Central India). The country of Maheśvarapura is more than three thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty li in circuit. The soil, products, and customs are the same as those of the country of Ujjayanī (鄔闍衍那國). They revere and honor non-Buddhist paths and do not believe in the Buddha-Dharma. There are several dozen Deva temples, and most of the inhabitants are followers who smear themselves with ash. The king is of the Brahmin caste and does not have much faith or respect for the Buddha-Dharma.

From here I returned to the country of Gurjara (瞿折羅國), then traveled north through wild wastes and dangerous deserts for over one thousand nine hundred li, crossed the great Sindhu (信度) River, and arrived at the country of Sindhu (in the territory of Western India). The country of Sindhu is over seven thousand li in circuit. The capital city is named Viṣambhapura (毘苫婆補羅), and it is over thirty li in circuit. The land is suitable for grain crops and is abundant in winter wheat; it produces gold, silver, and brass, and is suitable for raising cattle, sheep, camels, and mules. The camels are small and have only one hump. It produces much red salt, the color of which is like red stone, as well as white salt, black salt, and white rock salt; people in distant foreign lands use these as medicine. The people are fierce and straightforward by nature, frequently quarrel, and are prone to slander. They are not widely learned, but they deeply believe in the Buddhadharma. There are several hundred monasteries with over ten thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Sammitīya school of the Hīnayāna; for the most part, they are indolent, and their character and conduct are corrupt. However, those who are diligent, virtuous, and good dwell alone in quiet seclusion, keeping their traces far from the mountain forests, and, working day and night without slackening, many attain the holy fruits. There are over thirty Deva temples, where followers of different paths live together. The king is of the Śūdra caste; he is pure and simple by nature and respects the Buddhadharma. In the past, the Tathāgata traveled extensively in this country, and therefore King Aśoka built several dozen stūpas at the sites of the holy traces. The great arhat Upagupta (優波毱多) frequently traveled to this country to preach the Dharma and provide guidance. At every place he stayed, he marked the sacred traces, either by building a monastery (saṃghārāma) or erecting a stūpa; these rise up here and there, and can be briefly described. Along the side of the Sindhu River (信度河), in the midst of marshes extending over a thousand li, there are several hundred thousand households residing there. Their nature is fierce and violent, and they are devoted solely to killing. They herd cattle to sustain their lives and have no other means of livelihood. Whether male or female, noble or base, they shave their hair and beards and wear the kaṣāya (monastic robes), appearing like bhikṣus while engaging in secular affairs; they stubbornly hold to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) views and reject the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna). I have heard from the records of the ancients: "In the past, the common people of this land were hardened and cruel, devoted only to violence." At that time, an arhat took pity on their fallen state and, in order to transform them, came through the void, manifesting great supernatural powers and displaying rare wonders, causing the multitude to believe and accept his teachings, which he introduced gradually. The people were respectful and pleased, and wished to follow his instructions. The arhat, knowing that the hearts of the multitude were compliant, administered the three refuges to them, calmed their ferocity, caused them to completely cease killing, and had them shave their hair, dye their garments, and respectfully practice the teachings of the Dharma. As the ages grew distant and the world changed with the passage of time, their adherence to goodness faltered, yet the remnants of their old customs were not extinguished; although they wear the robes of the Dharma, they have never possessed the precepts or virtue. Their descendants, generation after generation, have made this their custom.

From here, traveling east for over nine hundred li and crossing to the eastern bank of the Indus River (Sindhu), one arrives at the country of Mūlasthānapura (茂羅三部盧國) (in the region of Western India). The country of Mūlasthānapura is over four thousand li in circuit. The capital city is over thirty li in circuit. The inhabitants are numerous and the households are wealthy. It is subject to the country of Takka (磔迦國). The land is fertile and productive, and the climate is temperate and regular. The customs of the people are honest and straightforward; they are fond of learning and value virtue. They mostly serve the heavenly deities and have little faith in the Buddha-dharma. There are more than ten sanghārāmas, most of which are dilapidated; there are few monks, and they do not specialize in any particular study. There are eight deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths live together. There is a Temple of the Sun God, which is extremely magnificent and beautiful; the image of the Sun God is cast in gold and adorned with rare jewels. Its spiritual influence is profound and mysterious, and its divine efficacy is secretly bestowed. Female musicians play in rotation, bright torches burn continuously day and night, and offerings of incense and flowers are never interrupted. The kings and noble families of the five Indias never fail to donate precious treasures here and establish charitable houses to provide food, drink, and medicine to the poor and the sick. People from various countries come here to offer prayers, often numbering in the thousands. Around the deva temple, the ponds and flowery woods are most pleasant for sightseeing.

From here, traveling northeast for more than seven hundred li, one reaches the country of Parvata (鉢伐多國) (within the borders of Northern India). The country of Parvata is more than five thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty li in circuit. The inhabitants are prosperous and numerous. It is subject to the country of Takka (磔迦國). There is much early-ripening rice, and it is suitable for growing wheat and barley. The climate is temperate, the customs are simple and honest, the people’s temperament is impetuous and hasty, and their speech contains vulgar expressions. They are deeply learned in the arts and sciences, and they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are more than ten monasteries with over a thousand monks, who study both the Mahayana and Hinayana teachings. There are four stūpas, which were built by King Aśoka. There are twenty Deva temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together. Beside the city is a large monastery with over a hundred monks, all of whom study the Mahayana teachings; this is where the former śāstra master Jinaputra (唐言最勝子, "Most Victorious One") composed the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-vyākhyā*, and it is also the place where the śāstra masters Bhadraruci and Guṇaprabha originally entered the monastic order. This large monastery was burned by celestial fire and is now ruined and desolate.

Traveling southwest from the country of Sindhu (信度國) for fifteen or sixteen hundred li, one reaches the country of Audumbatira (阿點婆翅羅國) (within the borders of West India). The country of Audumbatira is over five thousand li in circuit. The great capital city is named Khasvara (朅䶩濕伐羅), and it is over thirty li in circuit. It is situated in a remote western region, bordering the Sindhu River and adjacent to the shore of the great sea. The buildings are magnificent and contain many precious treasures. Recently, it has had no sovereign and is under the jurisdiction of the country of Sindhu. The ground is low and damp, the soil is saline, and foul weeds grow in abundance. The fields are little cultivated; although all types of grain are present, the *śāli* rice and wheat are particularly abundant. The climate is slightly cold, and the winds are fierce and strong. It is suitable for cattle, sheep, camels, mules, and similar livestock. The people are impetuous and do not like to study. Their language differs slightly from that of Mid-India. Their customs are simple and honest, and they revere the Three Jewels. There are more than eighty saṃghārāmas and over five thousand monks, most of whom study the teachings of the Sthavira-Saṃmitīya school of the Lesser Vehicle. There are ten deva temples, mostly inhabited by ash-smearing heterodox ascetics. In the city, there is a temple to Maheśvara (大自在天). The temple is carved and adorned, and the image of the deity is spiritually responsive; ash-smearing heterodox ascetics reside within it. In the past, the Tathāgata traveled extensively in this country, preaching the Dharma to save people and guiding the commoners to benefit the populace; therefore, King Aśoka (無憂王) built six stūpas at the sites of these sacred traces.

Traveling west from here for less than two thousand li, one reaches the country of Laṅgala (狼揭羅國) (within the borders of Western India). The country of Laṅgala measures several thousand li in each of the four directions. The capital city is over thirty li in circumference and is named Sthūlīśvara (窣菟黎濕伐羅). The land is fertile and moist, and crops are abundant. The climate and customs are the same as those of the country of Adhyavakila (阿點婆翅羅國). The inhabitants are prosperous and possess many precious treasures. It borders the great ocean and is the route to the country of the Western Women (西女國). There is no great monarch; the people occupy the river valleys and establish themselves independently, not acknowledging the authority of one another, and are subject to the country of Pārsi (波剌斯國). Their writing is largely the same as that of India, though their spoken language differs slightly. They believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are over one hundred monasteries with more than six thousand monks, who study and practice the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. There are several hundred Deva temples, and the ash-smearing heretics are extremely numerous. Inside the city is a temple of Maheśvara (大自在天), magnificent and grand, which is the place of worship for the ash-smearing heretics.

From here, going northwest, one reaches the country of Pārsa (波剌斯國) (although it is not a country of India, it is appended here as it lies along the route; the old name was Bosi (波斯), which is an abbreviation). The country of Pārsa is several tens of thousands of li in circumference. The great capital city of the country is named Sūlāsātǎngnà (蘇剌薩儻那), which is more than forty li in circumference. The land is vast and the climate is also distinct, being generally warm. Water is diverted to irrigate the fields, and the households are wealthy and prosperous. It produces gold, brass, quartz, crystal, and rare treasures and precious gems. The people are skilled at weaving large brocades, fine woolens, and rugs, and there are many fine horses and camels. For currency, they use large silver coins. The nature of the people is impetuous and violent, and their customs lack propriety and righteousness. Their script and language differ from those of other countries. They have no interest in academic arts but are skilled in crafts; all their manufactures are highly valued by neighboring regions. Marriages are promiscuous, and when people die, they are mostly abandoned as corpses. The people are large in stature, wear their hair cut level, and go bareheaded; they wear leather and wool garments and dress in brocade and felt. Regarding household taxes and levies, each person pays four silver coins. There are many deva temples, and the followers of the Dinaba (提那跋) heretics are those who revere them. There are two or three saṃghārāmas with several hundred monks, all of whom study the Hīnayāna teachings of the Sarvāstivāda school. The alms bowl of the Śākya Buddha is in the king’s palace here.

Traveling north from the country of Adembasila (*Aṭembasila*) for more than seven hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Pi-to-zhi-luo (臂多縶羅國) (within the borders of Western India). The country of Pi-to-zhi-luo is more than three thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city is more than twenty *li* in circuit. The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous; they have no great sovereign but are subject to the country of Sindhu (信度國). The land is sandy and saline, and the cold winds are biting. There is much wheat and barley, but few flowers or fruits. The customs of the people are fierce and violent. Their language differs from that of Central India. They do not care for the arts or learning, yet they are sincere in their faith. There are more than fifty monasteries with over three thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Sāmmitīya school of the Lesser Vehicle. There are more than twenty *deva* temples, all belonging to the ash-smearing non-Buddhists. In a large forest fifteen or sixteen *li* north of the city, there is a *stūpa* several hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka. Inside it are relics that occasionally emit light. This is the place where the Tathāgata, in a former life as a *ṛṣi*, was harmed by a king. Not far to the east of this is an old monastery, which was established by the great arhat Mahākātyāyana. Beside it are the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas, where *stūpas* have been built to mark the sites.

From here, traveling northeast for three hundred li, one arrives at the country of Avaṇḍa (阿軬荼國) (in the region of West India). The country of Avaṇḍa is two thousand four or five hundred li in circuit. The capital city is over twenty li in circuit. There is no great monarch; it is subject to the country of Sindhu (信度國). The land is suitable for agriculture; millet and wheat are especially abundant, while flowers and fruits are scarce, and trees and vegetation are sparse. The climate is windy and cold, and the nature of the people is fierce and impetuous. Their speech is simple and plain, and they do not value academic pursuits, yet they are pure and faithful in their devotion to the Three Jewels. There are over twenty saṃghārāmas with more than two thousand monks, most of whom study the teachings of the Hīnayāna Saṃmitīya school. There are five Deva temples, all belonging to the ash-smearing heretics.  Not far to the northeast of the city, in a large bamboo grove, are the remaining foundations of a saṃghārāma; this is where the Tathāgata once permitted the bhikṣus to wear *jīvashī* (亟縛屣) (in Tang language: boots). Beside it is a stūpa built by King Aśoka; although the base has collapsed, it is still over one hundred feet high. In the *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) beside it, there is a standing Buddha image made of blue stone, which sometimes emits divine light on fast days.  Eight hundred paces further south, in the forest, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. The Tathāgata once stayed here; because the night was cold, he covered himself with his three robes, and the next morning, he permitted the bhikṣus to wear quilted robes. In this forest, there is a place where the Buddha walked in meditation. There are also several stūpas, arranged like fish scales facing one another, which are the places where the four past Buddhas sat. Inside that stūpa are the hair and nail relics of the Tathāgata, which often emit divine light on fast days.

From here, traveling northeast for more than nine hundred li, one reaches the country of Varaṇa (伐剌拏國) (in the territory of West India). The country of Varaṇa is over four thousand li in circuit. The capital city is more than twenty li in circuit. The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, and they are subject to the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國). The land has many mountains and forests, and crops are sown in their proper seasons. The climate is slightly cold, and the customs are fierce and violent. The people are impetuous and irritable, and their dispositions are base and corrupt. Their language is somewhat similar to that of Mid-India. They revere both heterodox and orthodox teachings, and they do not care for learning or the arts. There are several dozen monasteries, most of which are ruined and desolate; there are over three hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. There are five Deva temples, mostly belonging to the ash-smearing ascetics. Not far to the south of the city is an old monastery where the Tathāgata in the past preached the Dharma, manifesting teachings to bring benefit and joy, and enlightening living beings. Beside it are the seats of the four past Buddhas and the places where they walked in meditation. I have heard from the local people that to the west of this country, bordering the country of Jīmna (稽畺那國), the people live in the valleys among the great mountains; they have separate rulers and no great monarch. There are many sheep and horses. Those who possess good horses have animals that are large and beautiful in form; they are a rare breed among the various countries and are treasured by the neighboring regions. Traveling northwest from here again, crossing great mountains, traversing wide rivers, and passing through small towns and cities, one travels over two thousand li, leaves the borders of India, and reaches the country of Jāguḍa (漕矩吒國) (also called the country of Caoli (漕利國)).

The country of Jaguḍa (漕矩吒國) is over seven thousand li in circuit. The great capital city of the country is called Ghasna (鶴悉那), which is over thirty li in circuit; sometimes the capital is at the city of Ghasala (鶴薩羅城), which is also over thirty li in circuit, and both are steep, rugged, and well-fortified. The mountains and rivers are undulating, and the fields and ridges are high and dry. Crops are sown in their proper seasons, winter wheat grows in abundance, vegetation is lush, and flowers and fruits are flourishing. The land is suitable for saffron (欝金香), and it produces the hingu herb (興瞿草), which grows in the Rāmēndu (羅摩印度) valley. In the city of Ghasala, there are gushing springs that flow in various directions, which the people of the country utilize to irrigate their fields. The climate is cold and harsh, with frequent frost and snow. The people are impulsive by nature and their dispositions are often deceitful. They are fond of learning arts and possess many technical skills; they listen but do not understand, yet they can recite tens of thousands of words a day. Their script and language differ from those of other countries. They often embellish empty talk and accomplish few practical results. Although they worship the hundred gods, they revere and honor the Three Jewels. There are several hundred monasteries and more than ten thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. The present king is sincere in his faith, having inherited the throne through successive generations; he is devoted to performing meritorious deeds, and is intelligent and fond of learning. There are more than ten stūpas built by King Aśoka (無憂王). There are several dozen deva temples, where followers of different sects live together. Most of the people are non-Buddhists, and their disciples are extremely numerous; they worship the deity Śuna (䅳那) (Original note: pronounced like *si* and *gou*, and so on below). This deity formerly moved from Mount Aruṇa in the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國) to reside in Mount Śunāśīra (䅳那呬羅山) on the southern border of this country, where he displays his power, bestows blessings, and commits acts of violence and evil; those who believe and pray to him have their wishes fulfilled, while those who despise him incur calamity. Thus, those far and near revere him, and those high and low stand in awe of him. The rulers, ministers, officials, and commoners of neighboring countries with different customs gather without appointment on auspicious days each year; they bring gold, silver, and rare treasures, or offer cattle, horses, and domestic animals, competing to present offerings to express their sincerity. Consequently, gold and silver are spread upon the ground and sheep and horses fill the valleys, yet no one dares to covet them, as all are intent only on making offerings. Those who follow non-Buddhist paths and practice asceticism with a disciplined heart are granted incantations by the celestial deity; the non-Buddhists who practice them find them highly effective, and those treated for illnesses are often healed.

From here, traveling southeast, crossing ridges and traversing valleys along dangerous canyon paths for more than three hundred li, one reaches the country of Kuraṇa (屈浪拏國). The country of Kuraṇa is the former territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). It is more than two thousand li in circumference. The land, topography, and climate are the same as those of the country of Yambagan (淫薄健國). The customs lack laws and regulations, and the people’s nature is base and violent. Most do not cultivate merit, and few believe in the Buddha-Dharma. Their appearance is ugly and wretched, and they mostly wear felt and coarse wool. There are rocky mountains that produce much gold essence; one must chisel and break the stones to obtain it. The monasteries are few, and the monks are also scarce. Their king is simple and sincere, and he reveres and honors the Three Jewels.

From here, traveling northeast, climbing mountains and entering valleys along a difficult and dangerous path for over five hundred li, one arrives at the country of Dharmasthiti (達摩悉鐵帝國) (also known as Zhenkan [鑊侃], and also called Humi [護蜜]). The country of Dharmasthiti lies between two mountains and is the former territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). It is over one thousand five or six hundred li from east to west, and four to five li wide from north to south, while at its narrowest it does not exceed one li. It borders the Vakṣu River (縛芻河), winding and twisting with uneven mounds and hillocks; sand and stones drift and spread, and the cold winds are harsh and piercing. They only plant wheat and beans; there are few forests and a lack of flowers and fruits. They produce many good horses; although the horses are small in stature, they are enduring in running and traveling. The customs lack propriety and righteousness, and the people’s nature is fierce and violent. Their appearance is base and ugly, and they wear felt and coarse wool garments. Their eyes are mostly emerald green, which is different from other countries. There are more than ten saṃghārāmas, but the number of monks is small.

From this valley, traveling southeast, one climbs mountains and traverses dangerous paths where there are no human habitations, only much ice and snow. After traveling more than five hundred li, one reaches the country of Kharbanda (朅盤陀國). The country of Kharbanda is over two thousand li in circuit. The capital city is built upon a large rocky ridge, with the Sītā River (徙多河) at its back, and it is over twenty li in circuit. The mountain ranges are connected, and the valleys and plains are narrow. Grain crops are scarce, but beans and wheat are abundant; trees are sparse, and there is little fruit or flowers. The plains and marshes are desolate, and the cities and towns are empty. The customs lack propriety and righteousness, and the people have little learning or skill. Their nature is fierce and violent, yet they are also brave and valiant. Their appearance is ugly and wretched, and they wear garments of felt and coarse wool. Their script and language are largely the same as those of the country of Khāsa (佉沙國). However, they are sincere in their faith and deeply revere the Buddhadharma. There are more than ten monasteries and over five hundred monks, who study the teachings of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) according to the Sarvāstivāda school. The current king is simple and honest, respects the Three Jewels, is refined and elegant in his demeanor, and is devoted to learning. Since the founding of the kingdom, many years have passed. The people claim to be the descendants of the *Cīna-deva-gotra* (至那提婆瞿呾羅) (in the language of the Tang, this means "the celestial race of the Han"). The origin of this country was a desolate valley in the Onion Range (Pamirs). Long ago, a king of Persia (波利剌斯) married a princess from the land of Han and was escorting her back when they reached this place. At that time, there was a military rebellion, and the roads to the east and west were blocked. He therefore placed the princess upon an isolated peak, which was extremely steep and dangerous, accessible only by ladders to ascend or descend, and he stationed guards all around to keep watch day and night. Three months passed, and the bandits were finally pacified. When he intended to continue on the road home, the princess was already pregnant. The envoy was terrified and said to his retinue, "The King ordered us to welcome his bride, but we encountered this rebellion; camping in the wild barrens, we cannot even plan for the next morning. Through the virtue of our King, the baleful atmosphere has been cleared, and now we are to return to the kingdom, yet the King’s bride is pregnant. Considering this, we are in distress, not knowing how to face death; we should identify the ringleader, or perhaps we will be executed later." There was a clamor of questioning, but no one could determine the truth. At that time, a maidservant said to the envoy, "Do not blame one another; it was a divine encounter. Every day at high noon, a man would arrive here on horseback, descending from the solar disc." The envoy said, "If that is the case, how can we clear ourselves of this guilt? If we return, we will surely be executed; if we stay, we will also be punished. With advancement or retreat being thus, what is the proper course of action?" They all agreed, "This matter is not trivial; who would willingly face such severe punishment? Let us await our fate outside the borders and delay for a while."  Thereupon, they built a palace and quarters on the stone peak, with a circumference of more than three hundred paces. They built a city wall around the palace, established the woman as sovereign, and instituted officials and laws. When the time came, she gave birth to a son, whose appearance was beautiful and refined. The mother managed the affairs of state, and the son assumed the royal title. He could fly through the void and control the wind and clouds; his majesty and virtue reached far and wide, and his reputation and teachings spread to distant lands. Neighboring regions and foreign countries all paid him homage. When the king died at a ripe old age, he was buried in a stone chamber within a large mountain (Skt. Pravaragiri) over a hundred *li* southeast of this city. His corpse was preserved like a mummy and remains intact to this day; resembling an emaciated person, he looks as if he were fast asleep, and his clothes are changed periodically while incense and flowers are constantly placed before him. His descendants have continued through the generations down to the present day. Because in the time of their ancestor, the mother was a person from the land of Han (China) and the father was of the seed of the Sun God, they call themselves the "Han-Sun-God Clan." However, their royal family resembles the people of the Middle Kingdom (China) in appearance; they wear square crowns as head ornaments and dress in foreign clothing. Later, their descendants declined and were pressured by powerful states. King Aśoka (無憂王) appeared in the world and built a stupa within their palace. The king later moved his residence to the northeast corner of the palace and converted his former palace into a monastery for the venerable Shastra Master Kumāralāta (童受論師), with lofty, spacious terraces and pavilions and solemn, majestic Buddha statues. The venerable master was a native of the country of Takṣaśilā (呾叉始羅國); he was brilliant from childhood, renounced the secular world early, devoted his mind to the scriptures, and focused his spirit on the profound mysteries, daily reciting thirty-two thousand words and writing another thirty-two thousand. Thus, his learning surpassed the scholars of his time, and his fame was high in the world; he established the True Dharma, refuted heterodox views, and his lofty discourses were clear and elevated, leaving no difficulty unaddressed, so that he was universally esteemed throughout the five Indias. The treatises he authored number several dozen; they are all widely circulated and studied, for he is the founding master of the Sautrāntika school. At that time, there was Aśvaghoṣa in the east, Deva in the south, Nāgārjuna in the west, and Kumāralāta in the north; they were known as the "four suns that illuminate the world." Therefore, the king of this country, having heard of the venerable master's great virtue, mobilized his troops to attack the country of Takṣaśilā and obtained him by coercion; he then built this monastery to manifest his reverence.

To the northeast of the great cliff, crossing ridges and traversing dangerous paths for over two hundred *li*, one arrives at Puṇyaśālā (translated in the Tang language as "House of Merit"). It is situated on the eastern ridge of the Onion Range (葱嶺), amidst four mountains, in a basin over one hundred *qing* in area, sunken in the center. Snow accumulates there throughout winter and summer, and the wind is cold and fierce. The fields and ridges are saline and barren, so crops do not grow; there are no trees, only fine grass. Even during the heat of summer, there is much wind and snow; as soon as travelers enter, clouds and mist arise, and merchant caravans suffer greatly from these hardships and dangers.  I have heard from the elders: once there were merchants with a following of over ten thousand and several thousand camels, carrying goods in pursuit of profit, who encountered wind and snow, and both people and animals perished. At that time, there was a great Arhat in the kingdom of *Kharbanda* (朅盤陀國) who saw them from afar; pitying their peril, he desired to exercise his supernatural powers to rescue them from their plight, but by the time he arrived, the merchants had already perished. He then collected their various treasures, gathered all that remained, constructed a building, stored up provisions, purchased land in neighboring countries, and bought households in border cities to provide relief for those traveling to and fro. Therefore, travelers and merchant caravans today all receive support from this.

Traveling north from here for over five hundred li across mountains, gravelly plains, and wilderness, one arrives at the country of Khāsa (佉沙國) (Original note: What was formerly called Shule is actually the name of its capital city. The correct pronunciation should be Śrī-kṛtati; the term Shule is a corruption). The country of Khāsa is over five thousand li in circumference. There is much gravel and sand, and little fertile soil. Agriculture is flourishing, and flowers and fruits are abundant. It produces fine felt and coarse wool, and they are skilled at weaving fine rugs and carpets. The climate is mild and pleasant, and the winds and rains follow their proper seasons. The people are fierce and violent by nature, and their customs are full of deceit; they treat ritual and righteousness lightly, and their learning and arts are superficial. It is their custom to compress the heads of newborn children to make them flat; their appearance is coarse and vulgar, and they have tattooed bodies and green eyes. Their writing system is modeled after that of India; although there have been deletions and corruptions, it still retains the original structure. Their language and tone of speech differ from those of other countries. They are sincerely devoted to the Buddha-dharma and diligently engage in meritorious works. There are several hundred saṃghārāmas with over ten thousand monks, who study the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teachings of the Sarvāstivāda school. They do not delve deeply into the principles but mostly recite the texts; therefore, many have mastered the recitation of the Tripiṭaka and the Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra.

From here, traveling southeast for more than five hundred li, I crossed the Sītā River, passed over a great sandy range, and reached the country of Cukuka (formerly called Juqu). The country of Cukuka is more than one thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than ten li in circuit; it is solid, steep, and secure, and the households are numerous and prosperous. The hills and mounds are connected, and the ground is covered with gravel and stones. It borders two rivers and is quite suitable for cultivation. Grapes, pears, and crabapples—these fruits are abundant. The climate is cold, and the people are impetuous and violent. Their customs are characterized by deceit and trickery, and they practice robbery openly. Their script is the same as that of the country of Gostāna (瞿薩旦那國), though their spoken language is different. Their sense of propriety and righteousness is slight, and their learning and arts are shallow. They are sincerely devoted to the Three Jewels and take pleasure in performing meritorious deeds. There are several dozen sanghārāmas, though many are in ruins, and there are more than one hundred monks who study the teachings of the Great Vehicle.

Going eastward from here, crossing mountains and valleys for more than eight hundred li, one reaches the country of Gostana (瞿薩旦那國) (in the language of Tang, this means "Earth-Nipple," which is the elegant form of the local name. In the vulgar tongue it is called the country of Huanna; the Xiongnu call it Yudun; the various Hu peoples call it Qidan; and in India it is called Qudan. The old name, Yutian, is a corruption). The country of Gostana is more than four thousand li in circumference. More than half of it is sand and gravel, and the arable land is narrow and restricted. It is suitable for grain crops and produces many kinds of fruit. It produces rugs and fine felt, and the people are skilled at spinning and weaving silk and pongee. It also produces white jade and black jade. The climate is mild and pleasant, though there are drifting winds and flying dust. The customs value propriety and righteousness, and the people are gentle and respectful by nature. They are fond of learning the arts and are broadly proficient in various skills. The populace is wealthy and happy, and the households are settled in their occupations. The country prizes musical sounds, and the people are fond of singing and dancing. Few wear coarse wool, felt, or furs; most clothe themselves in silk, pongee, and white cotton. Their deportment is refined, and their customs are well-ordered. Their writing and laws are modeled after those of India, though they have slightly altered the style and form, having undergone some evolution. Their language differs from that of other countries. They revere and uphold the Buddha-dharma. There are more than one hundred sanghārāmas (伽藍) and over five thousand monks, most of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. The king is very brave and martial, respects the Buddha-dharma, and claims to be a descendant of the deity Vaiśravaṇa (毘沙門天). In ancient times, this country was empty and uninhabited, and the deity Vaiśravaṇa resided here. After the crown prince of King Aśoka (無憂王) had his eyes gouged out in the country of Takṣaśilā (呾叉始羅國), the king angrily rebuked his ministers and exiled the powerful families to the north of the Snow Mountains to dwell among the desolate valleys. These exiles followed their herds and reached the western border of this land, where they elected their leader and established him as king. At that time, a prince from the eastern lands had been banished and had migrated to dwell on the eastern border of this region; his subordinates urged him to advance, and he also proclaimed himself king. As years and months accumulated, their customs and teachings remained disconnected. Each group, while out hunting, encountered the other in the desolate marshes; they inquired about each other’s lineage and consequently disputed who was superior. Anger manifested in their words, and they were about to engage in battle. Someone advised them, saying, "Why be so hasty now? To decide the battle while hunting does not fully display the sharpness of our weapons. It is better to return and prepare our troops, and gather at an appointed time." Thereupon, they turned their carriages and returned, each going back to his own country to drill their horses and soldiers and encourage their troops. When the appointed time arrived, the armies met, and their banners and drums faced one another. The next day they joined battle, and the Western Lord was disadvantaged; consequently, he was pursued in his retreat and his head was cut off. The Eastern Lord, riding the momentum of his victory, pacified and gathered the people of the defeated country, moved his capital to the central region, and began to build city walls. Worried that he lacked land and fearing that he might not succeed, he made a proclamation far and near, asking who knew the geography. At that time, there was an ash-smeared outsider (tīrthika) who carried a large gourd filled with water and stepped forward, saying, "I know the geography." He then let the water flow out in winding curves, returning to where it started, and then he hurried away and suddenly vanished. Following those water marks, the foundations were raised and the construction was successfully completed; this became the seat of government, and it is in this city that the current king has established his capital. The city is not high or steep, yet it is difficult to overcome by attack, and from ancient times until now, no one has been able to conquer it. By the time the king had moved the capital to build this city, established the state, and settled the people, his achievements were complete and he was in the twilight of his old age; yet he had no heir and feared the end of his ancestral line. He then went to the place of the god Vaiśravaṇa (毘沙門天神) to pray for an heir. From the forehead of the god’s statue, an infant was produced; the king took him in his arms and returned to his palace, and the people of the country celebrated. Since the baby would not drink milk, the king feared he would not live long, so he soon returned to the divine shrine to pray again for a way to nourish him. The ground in front of the deity suddenly rose up in the shape of a breast, and the divine child suckled from it until he grew to adulthood. His wisdom and courage surpassed his predecessors, and his moral influence spread far and wide; he then built a divine shrine to honor his ancestor. From that time on, the throne has been passed down through generations, and the kings have ruled the country without the line being broken. Therefore, the divine temple today contains many precious treasures, and offerings and sacrifices are made there without fail. Because he was nourished by the earth-breast, this became the name of the country.

More than ten li to the south of the royal city is a great monastery, which was built by a former king of this country for the Arhat Vairocana (meaning "Universal Shining" in Chinese). In the past, the Buddha’s teaching had not yet reached this country, but the Arhat came from the country of Kaśmīra to this forest, where he sat in quietude to practice meditation. At that time, those who saw him were startled by his appearance and attire, and they reported his condition in detail to the king. The king then went in person to observe his demeanor and said, "Who are you, staying alone in this secluded forest?" The Arhat replied, "I am a disciple of the Tathāgata, living in seclusion to practice meditation. Your Majesty should cultivate merit, propagate the Buddha’s teaching, build a monastery, and assemble the monkhood." The king asked, "What virtues and divine powers does the Tathāgata possess that you would dwell like a bird in the woods and so diligently follow his teachings?" He replied, "The Tathāgata compassionately cares for the four types of birth and guides the three realms; he sometimes manifests and sometimes remains hidden, demonstrating birth and demonstrating extinction. Those who follow his teaching escape birth and death; those who are confused by his teaching remain entangled in the net of desire." The king said, "If it is truly as you say, the matter transcends words and discussion. Since you speak of a Great Sage, manifest his form for me; once I have been able to gaze upon him, I shall build [a monastery], devote my heart to faith, and propagate the teaching." The Arhat said, "If the king builds a monastery, the merit will bring about a response." The king followed his request and built a sanghārāma; people from far and near gathered to celebrate the dharma assembly, but they lacked a ghaṇṭā to strike for summoning the assembly. The king said to the Arhat, "The monastery (saṃghārāma) is now completed, but where is the Buddha?" The Arhat replied, "You must be perfectly sincere; the Sage’s observation is not far off." The king then performed rites of petition, and suddenly he saw an image of the Buddha descend from the air and bestow upon the king a ghaṇṭā (揵稚). Because of this, he became sincerely faithful and propagated the Buddha’s teaching.

More than twenty li to the southwest of the royal city is the mountain of Gośṛṅga (瞿室𩜁伽山; in the language of Tang, "Cow Horn"). Two peaks rise up, and the rocky precipices are sheer on all sides. A monastery (saṃghārāma) is built between the cliffs and the valley, where the Buddha image within occasionally radiates light. In the past, the Tathāgata came to this place to briefly explain the essential Dharma for the various devas and humans, and he prophesied that a kingdom would be established here that would revere and honor the remaining Dharma and follow the practice of the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna). In the rocky cliffs of Mount Cow Horn, there is a large stone chamber where an arhat resides, having entered the samadhi of extinction to await the Buddha Maitreya; for several hundred years, offerings to him have never ceased. Recently, the cliff collapsed and blocked the entrance path. The king mobilized troops to clear away the fallen stones, but immediately a swarm of black wasps flew out and stung the people, and for this reason, the stone gate has not been opened to this day.

More than three hundred *li* to the east of the royal city, in the midst of a vast marsh, there is an area of several tens of *qing* where no vegetation grows and the soil is reddish-black. According to the elders, this is the place of a defeated army. In the past, an eastern country raised a million troops to invade the west. At that time, the King of Gostana (瞿薩旦那) also prepared hundreds of thousands of soldiers to resist the powerful enemy from the east. When the two armies met at this place, they immediately engaged in battle. The western army suffered defeat, and the victors, taking advantage of their success, slaughtered them cruelly, capturing their king, killing their generals, and massacring the soldiers until not a single one remained. The blood shed stained the ground, and the traces are still visible there.
